22811-the-staircase-at-the-heart-s-delig:
Police headquarters supplies the frame for The Staircase at the Heart's Delight, a detective story dated 1894. The narrator looks back on his younger self, a man full of ambition who refused to drop a case when his colleagues moved on. He kept watching and waiting, certain another victim would be reported.

His patience shapes the whole tale. Because he alone stays with the puzzle, he is ready when fresh word arrives, and the odd results he promises begin to unfold. The story belongs to the early years of modern detective fiction, when dogged legwork mattered more than clever gadgets. It suits readers who enjoy a murder inquiry told by the man who would not let it go.
a-spirit-in-prison-pg2994: Robert Hichens's 1908 A Spirit in Prison: an Italian romance of passion. Lush and dramatic in his best manner. The Garden of Allah author's romance. An Italian passion in Hichens's lush prose, romance behind bars, Hichens's lush Italian romance.
alchemy-and-chemistry-1894: Alchemy and Chemistry, 1894. The two sciences. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
arxiv-2512-00094:
Diffusion models are trained on huge image collections, sometimes including pictures used without permission. Kexin Li, Guozhen Ding, Ilya Grishchenko, and David Lie present HMark in a 2025 study from the University of Toronto. HMark is a watermarking method meant to expose unauthorized training.

The marks are radioactive, meaning they transfer into a trained model's outputs, where they can later be detected. A useful mark must also stay invisible, survive processing, and carry several bits of information. The work gives artists and dataset owners a technical tool for proving when their images were absorbed into a generative model. Ownership disputes over training data are now common in courtrooms as well as labs.
arxiv-2512-00394:
Graphene's promise for electronics depends on growing large sheets without grain boundaries or extra layers. Johanna Huhtasaari and a large team report wafer-scale single-crystalline monolayer graphene in 2025. Controlling growth kinetics to avoid those defects has remained challenging.

The team demonstrates single-crystalline graphene free from multilayer domains, made by one-step delamination of epitaxial graphene from silicon carbide. A clean wafer-scale sheet is key to realizing graphene's full potential in advanced applications, including twistronics. The result moves graphene production closer to the uniformity that chip manufacturing demands. Delamination avoids the transfer steps that usually wrinkle or contaminate graphene sheets. Silicon carbide is the standard substrate for epitaxial graphene growth. For labs that grow such sheets, the gain is a sheet that is one clean layer from edge to edge. It has no weak seams to fail in a chip.
arxiv-2512-00494:
Entanglement is a resource for sensing, letting correlated spins measure fields more finely than independent ones. Alexander and Mahesh demonstrate quantum sensing with large spin clusters in solid-state NMR in 2025. They create, manipulate, and detect clusters of correlated nuclear spins using multiple-quantum techniques.

The clusters sensitively detect jitter in the width of radio-frequency control pulses, at the level of tens of nanoseconds. The authors also identify the coherence order that works best for practical sensing. Their results show a tabletop NMR setup can act as a precise diagnostic for the control electronics used across quantum technologies. Pulse-width jitter is a practical nuisance in every pulsed quantum experiment.
arxiv-2512-00694:
Five authors, led by Mengzhu Xu, present a 2025 machine learning paper on continual learning for video and language models. Such models must keep learning as new data, domains, and question styles arrive over time. The hard part is knowing what should stay stable and what should change.

Many current methods blur that line, route tasks in fixed ways, or replay old videos, which strains memory and privacy. The team's affordance-first decomposition names the stable parts and the flexible parts up front. Giving stability a clear home could help models learn new video tasks without forgetting old ones or storing past footage.
arxiv-2512-00794:
Bo Guo, Sijia Wen, Yifan Zhao, Jia Li, and Zhiming Zheng improve 3D scene rebuilding in a 2025 computer vision paper. A method called 3D Gaussian Splatting builds scenes from many soft 3D blobs and has reached striking accuracy. It struggles, though, where light cues mislead, such as shiny or blank surfaces.

In those places, brightness alone cannot pin down the true shape. The team's method, PolarGS, adds polarimetric cues, information in how light waves are oriented after bouncing off a surface. Those cues help separate shape from shine. The payoff is cleaner geometry on the surfaces that fool other methods.
arxiv-2512-00894:
Leandro Lyra Braga Dognini revisits a puzzle in statistical physics in a 2025 paper. The Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution is the classic rule for how a system at a fixed temperature spreads over its states. It comes from maximizing a famous entropy formula under simple constraints.

Dognini generalizes that maximization using a nonadditive entropy with extra parameters. Nonadditive entropies do not simply add when systems combine, which suits some complex systems. The work connects this broader distribution to the electronic partition function paradox, a known tension in how electron states are counted. Fresh math on old paradoxes can clarify when classic formulas should bend.
arxiv-2512-00994:
Hang Wu, Qin Wu, Yue Liu, and Mengmeng Shi study inventory choices under two kinds of doubt in a 2025 paper. A newsvendor must order stock before knowing demand: order too much and goods spoil, too little and sales are lost. Online commerce has raised the stakes for pricing and stocking together.

The authors model a sequential game between two competing retailers. Each first sets prices in public, then chooses inventory in private, while demand stays uncertain. They back the theory with experimental evidence. The setup mirrors leading e-commerce platforms, where rivals watch prices but hide stock. Results show how strategic play changes classic ordering rules.
arxiv-2512-01394:
Hiroshi Noguchi studies patterns formed by active units on a grid. Each site on the grid holds a state that cycles in a loop. Past work gave each site just one loop. Real systems may host more than one loop at each site.

Noguchi asks what changes when loops compete at each site. He ran active Potts models on a square grid. Neighbor sites pull on each other in the usual way. The runs show how rival loops shift the patterns in space and time. The work helps link lab patterns to the rules that drive them.
arxiv-2512-01594:
Sina Abdollahi and co-authors build secure links between confidential virtual machines. Such machines shield work from even the host operator. Their split memory keeps data safe. It also makes sharing data between machines slow and clumsy.

On Arm CCA hardware, the team adds first-class sharing. Links are confidential, attestable, and fast at once. Each machine can prove what it runs before data flows. Fast safe sharing helps split sensitive work across machines in clouds without giving up the shield that made them useful. Attestation binds code identity to the link, so a peer machine knows both who it talks to and what software runs there.
arxiv-2512-01694:
Hui-Fa Liu, Qi Su, and Ding-fang Zeng compute quasinormal modes of charged AdS black holes. Those modes are the ringdown tones of a perturbed hole. Boundary rules at the AdS edge shape the tones a lot. Choice of rules is thus a physics choice, not just math.

The team sets rules from two principles. The boundary metric must not deform. Electromagnetic energy flux at the edge must vanish. Under those rules they find the mode spectrum. Ringdown spectra test gravity theory and holography links to field theory. Field-vanishing rules also keep the dual field theory clean, which matters for holography uses of these black hole spectra.
arxiv-2512-01794:
Jian Liang and Hua-Yang Wang find solutions to supercritical nonlinear Schrodinger equations on an annulus. They seek positive solutions with prescribed mass. The supercritical regime breaks standard variational tools. An annulus adds shape constraints that complicate the search.

Their Hopf reduction turns the task into a lower-dimensional one. Reduction via the Hopf fibration tames the geometry. Existence proofs in this regime extend nonlinear optics and condensate theory, where mass-fixed states on ring domains model real traps and fibers. Prescribed mass matches experiment, where atom number or beam power is fixed first and the state must form under that exact total.
arxiv-2512-01994:
Some crystals pair up two different magnetic atoms into tiny two-spin units, and squeezing such a crystal can rewrite its magnetic behavior. A 2025 paper by M. J. Coak and a large team studies one such material, a copper-vanadium compound, whose copper and vanadium spins form antiferromagnetic pairs linked weakly through hydrogen bonds.

The team places the material under hydrostatic pressure, squeezing it evenly from all sides, and watches how its properties respond. Weak links between the spin pairs make the system sensitive, so pressure can tip it between different magnetic states. Such experiments show how to tune quantum magnets by force rather than by chemistry.
arxiv-2512-02094:
Simulating how light travels through the cosmos is slow, so cosmologists often cheat by slowing light itself down in the calculation. Nickolay Gnedin's 2025 paper examines a flaw in that reduced speed of light approximation: in some regimes it makes photons quietly disappear.

Gnedin shows the missing photons can be counted exactly for certain numerical schemes, turning a hidden error into a measurable one. He then explains how to almost fix the problem, restoring conservation where it matters. Radiative transfer underlies simulations of galaxy formation and cosmic reionization, so photon bookkeeping errors can distort big conclusions.
arxiv-2512-02194:
Sparse autoencoders are popular tools for opening up neural networks, extracting human-readable features from their inner activity. Sophie Wang and co-authors note in 2025 that those features are unstable, changing with random seed and settings, and propose ordered sparse autoencoders to fix the wobble.

Their design extends Matryoshka autoencoders in two ways: it imposes a strict ordering on the latent features, and it uses every feature dimension deterministically instead of sampling approximations. Ordered features should mean the same concept lands in the same place across runs. Consistency like that is what interpretability research needs before its findings can be trusted and compared.
arxiv-2512-02394:
Radar that senses in four dimensions promises perception that survives fog and darkness, but radar semantic segmentation is starved of open data and labels. A 2025 paper reproduces and extends the RaDelft radar dataset work, adding camera assistance to produce the labels the original release lacked.

The original dataset was a landmark yet offered only LiDAR annotations and no public code to generate radar labels, limiting reproduction and downstream research. Camera-assisted labeling uses the camera's view to help assign meanings to radar returns. Open labels and code are the kind of infrastructure that lets a whole research direction move faster.
arxiv-2512-02494:
Zihao Zhao and four co-authors speed up a key building block for learning systems that must decide. Differentiable optimization layers let a model solve a small optimization problem as part of its own reasoning. Learning through such a layer usually needs a gradient found by implicit differentiation.

That gradient step solves a linear system with second order terms, which costs heavy compute and memory. The team's algorithm finds the gradient using only first order information instead. Cheaper gradients could let decision aware models run on larger problems and smaller machines, widening their use in planning and control. That gain grows as models take on more choice points in each task they face.
arxiv-2512-03094:
Quantum computers may one day beat classic ones at learning tasks. Tomás Villalba-Ferreiro, Eduardo Mosqueira-Rey, and Diego Alvarez-Estevez test that claim in this 2025 study. They compare two quantum methods with classic models for sorting data into groups.

One method uses quantum support vector ideas, the other uses quantum neural nets. They test all models on the Iris data set and a reduced form of MNIST. The authors report that quantum models tend to do better as tasks grow harder. That trend, if it holds, hints where quantum learning may first prove useful. For quantum computing teams, the pair of test data sets shows where gains first appear.
arxiv-2512-03594:
Chip routing is one of the slowest steps in design. Afsara Khan and Austin Rovinski present a routing method in this 2025 work. Detailed routing must place wires while obeying strict, shrinking design rules.

Prior routers use iterative pathfinding for each net, which converges slowly. The authors accelerate convergence through offline reinforcement learning. Learned guidance can steer the router away from dead ends sooner. Faster routing shortens chip design cycles for ever denser processors. Offline learning reuses past routing runs, so no costly live trials are needed, and the router improves from data it already owns.
arxiv-2601-06694:
Richard Kerner proposes a Z3-symmetric quantum chromodynamics in 2026. His description gives colour triplets of quarks an entangled graded structure. Lee-Wick type fields, graded by Z3, carry the colour degrees.

One field has real mass in his construction of the theory. The two remaining fields have mutually conjugate complex masses, he specifies. Colour is attributed to six Pauli spinors in his scheme. Three carry colours and three carry anti-colours among them. All six unite into one twelve-component generalized coloured Dirac spinor. Such symmetry could reorganize how quark colour is written mathematically. Particle theorists get an alternative formalism to test against standard QCD. Whether nature uses it is separate; the structure itself is new.
arxiv-2601-06894:
Sonia Yeh and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how ports plan new ideas. The paper links three things: how a port is run, who owns it, and Living Labs. A Living Lab is a test site where new tools are tried in real use. Ports matter for cuts in carbon and for strength in a crisis.

Past studies tell of green and digital pilot work at ports. But they say little on how who owns a port shapes that work. They also say little on who holds the right to choose. Work on Living Labs gives strong ideas, yet few facts from ports. The authors bring the two fields face to face. They ask how well lab ways fit the way ports are run.
arxiv-2601-06994:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Guillaume Dubus and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers magnetic winds in resistive compact binary discs. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Dwarf Novæ and low-mass X-ray binaries are eruptive binary systems comprised of a Roche-lobe overflowing solar-type star and an accreting compact object.

Their recurrence time can be explained by a low-accreting phase. The quiescence, during which the angular momentum transport parameter is inferred to be α ≈ 0.01 0.01 by the Disc Instability Model. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07494:
Chengyuan Huang and a large team of colleagues study how to write tiny electronic devices in oxide materials. Their 2026 preprint concerns reconfigurable oxide nanoelectronics, devices whose circuits can be drawn and redrawn at very small scales. The writing tool is conductive atomic force microscope lithography, which uses a fine probe tip. Complex oxide interfaces are prized for quantum engineering because new effects emerge there.

One limit shapes the study: the usual writing process works only in air. Device decay also follows a pattern described as a water-cycle mechanism. The authors pursue tip-induced electron delocalization, a different route to changing the material. Readers in nanoelectronics get both the promise of the platform and the practical barrier this work attacks.
arxiv-2601-07694:
Liam T. Powers and Stephen M. Durbin report seeing a classic quantum effect with x-rays instead of visible light. They observed Hong-Ou-Mandel interference using high-brightness synchrotron x-rays. The setup used a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and produced two-photon states. Such states interest scholars in x-ray quantum optics. Their 2026 preprint presents the observation.

Hong-Ou-Mandel interference happens when two identical photons meet and bunch together. It is a standard test that photons are truly indistinguishable. The paper recalls Dirac's famous claim that a photon interferes only with itself. Extending these tests to x-rays opens quantum optics at far shorter wavelengths. That could later support imaging and measurement methods with x-ray resolution. Physicists working on quantum light are the main readers.
arxiv-2601-07994:
Nayoung Choi, Jonathan Zhang, and Jinho D. Choi present DyCP, a method for pruning dialogue history on the fly. Large language models increasingly work over long conversations with frequent topic shifts. Extended context windows exist, but inference cost and latency still demand efficient history management. DyCP runs outside the model itself. It dynamically identifies and retrieves the dialogue segments relevant to the current turn. No offline memory construction is needed. Their 2026 preprint describes the method.

Pruning well means keeping what matters and dropping the rest without losing the thread. Conditioning retrieval on the current turn ties memory to immediate need. A lightweight external method can wrap many different models. That portability suits products that swap models often. The paper serves conversational AI engineers. It treats context as a budget to spend where it counts.
arxiv-2601-08094:
Zheng Zhou, Isabella McEvoy, and Camilo Valderrama work on reading emotions from brain signals. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets EEG emotion recognition that works across new people. Brains differ a lot between subjects, and short, noisy recordings make robust learning hard.

The team proposes a fusion framework with two parts. One part uses local descriptors for each EEG channel, and the other uses global descriptors for each trial. Merging both aims to improve how well the system generalizes to unseen subjects. They test the approach on the SEED-VII dataset, a standard benchmark for EEG emotion research.
arxiv-2601-08194: Shakyani Jayasiriwardene and co-authors explore chatbots whose personality can shift with context. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that conversational agents are now expected to adapt across settings. Most agents, though, stay static once configured, even as user expectations evolve. The study examines how expectations form and change when personality is made dynamically adjustable. It asks what users want from an agent that can be tuned during interaction. Findings speak to designers of assistants for work, learning, and care, where tone can help or harm.
arxiv-2601-08594: Rishi Leburu, Levon Nurbekyan, and Lars Ruthotto wrote a 2026 arXiv primer on how to take rates of change through equations with noise. The paper was sent to the editors on January 13, 2026. Such equations, called stochastic differential equations, model systems in physics, finance, and economics, and now in machine learning too. A core task is to gauge how a result shifts when a value in the system shifts. Cases in view are air-based values, financial Greeks, and the tuning of neural networks.
arxiv-2601-09494:
Konrad Pawlik, Maksym Prodius, Pedro R. Nicácio Falcão, and Jakub Zakrzewski review a phase of matter that refuses to thermalize. Their 2026 arXiv paper surveys many-body localization, a robust form of ergodicity breaking in interacting quantum systems. The review was presented at a meeting on strongly correlated quantum matter.

The authors compare the many ways disorder can be put into a system. Random disorder and quasiperiodic patterns lead to different flavors of the localized phase. In this phase, a system keeps a memory of its start instead of settling to a uniform state. The survey organizes a fast-moving field for readers entering it.
arxiv-2601-09594:
Russell M. Martin and Steven H. Collins help robots learn from pricey experiments. Their 2026 arXiv paper improves CMA-ES, a popular optimization algorithm, for noisy robot tuning. Each test of a candidate policy can take seconds to minutes of real robot time.

Short tests iterate fast but read noisy; long tests read clean but slow the search. The authors add Adaptive Sampling CMA-ES, which gives each candidate time based on predicted sorting difficulty. Easy calls get quick tests; close calls get longer ones. The aim is steady precision without wasting robot hours.
arxiv-2601-09694:
Sai Varun Kodathala and Rakesh Vunnam let software agents shrink large language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents adaptive pruning guided by agents. Pruning after training cuts compute costs while trying to keep performance.

Methods like SparseGPT and Wanda reach high sparsity, but they set per-layer sparsity by uniform rules or hand-made heuristics. The authors replace those rules with agents that adapt the ratios. Smarter layer budgets could keep more skill at the same size. Cheaper, smaller models matter for any team that serves language models at scale on tight budgets.
arxiv-2601-10094:
Han Wang, Yi Yang, Jingyuan Hu, Minfeng Zhu, and Wei Chen teach sight and text models with no marked data. Such models have grown strong at tasks that mix image and text. But top grades rest on vast marked sets. Those sets cost much time and pay to build.

The team made V-Zero, a post train plan that needs no marks. It uses raw images with no tags at all. The model makes its own tasks and checks from those images. It then learns from its own work. The plan aims to lift skill while it cuts the need for hand marked sets.
arxiv-2601-10194:
Weitang Li, Jiajun Ren, Lixue Cheng, and Cunxi Gong let AI agents run quantum sims on their own. Tensor nets are a strong tool for quantum work. They pack a vast state into linked small parts. But their use takes years of training to learn.

The team gave the task to large language model agents. The agents plan, code, and run the sims. Across a set of base tasks, they hit a high rate of success. The rate is near nine in ten. The work hints that agents can take on expert sim work. That may widen who can do such work.
arxiv-2601-10294:
Yuansen Liu, Yixuan Tang, and Anthony Kum Hoe Tun name a new way to trick an AI sorter. Most safety work guards the goal of a model. A trick may try to swap its task, say from sum to phish. The team say that view is too thin.

A sorter can be tricked at the level of its rules. An attack can slip in fake marks for what counts as safe or not. The model keeps its goal but grades by the fake marks. The team call this reasoning hijacking. They show how it works and why goal guards miss it. The work calls for guards at the rule level too.
arxiv-2601-10494:
Luke Yerbury, G. C. Livingston Jr, and Ricardo Campello group power users by how they act, from smart meter data. Grid firms face wild swings as green power grows. They can pay users to shift use in peak times. That plan works best when users are grouped by true acts.

Smart meters give vast rows of use data. The team made CROCS, a two stage group plan. It groups users by their act forms, not by bills or house size. Groups built on acts should take shift plans more well. The work aims to make peak shave plans hit their mark.
arxiv-2601-10894:
Helmut Prodinger counts features of skew Dyck paths that allow two kinds of down-steps. Dyck paths are lattice walks that rise and fall but never drop below their start. A recent interest in walks from hexagonal circle packings brought this skew family to attention. Its steps come in several types, with two variants of down-step.

Prodinger studies the height of such paths, a classic statistic in enumerative combinatorics. Height laws describe how tall a typical path grows. Results of this kind feed the analysis of algorithms and random structures, where Dyck-like paths encode stacks, trees, and queues.
arxiv-2601-11694:
Xinjue Wang, Xiuheng Wang, Esa Ollila, and Sergiy Vorobyov sharpen hyperspectral images. Their 2026 preprint uses anisotropic tensor deconvolution for the task. Hyperspectral images record many wavelength bands per pixel. Deconvolution must undo blur in that rich data cube.

The problem is ill-posed and hard by nature. High dimensionality makes naive solvers slow and unstable. The team frames the latent image as a tensor. A low-rank canonical polyadic decomposition models that tensor. The frame uses few parameters for the whole cube. Anisotropic terms respect unlike blur along each axis. Cleaner hyperspectral data aid land, crop, and mineral surveys.
arxiv-2601-12094:
John Banovetz, Claire-Alice Hébert, Peter B. Denton, and their co-authors plan how the Vera C. Rubin Observatory can catch the next supernova in our own galaxy. Such blasts occur about once or twice a century in a galaxy like ours. Yet the last one seen by humans was almost 1,000 years ago.

New neutrino detectors and scopes now give a real chance to catch the next one. Rubin can map its light in detail if alerted fast. A near blast would test star death physics like no far event can. The plan sets out that watch.
arxiv-2601-12294:
Dawei Li, Yuguang Yao, Zhen Tan, Huan Liu, and Ruocheng Guo build a test set for process reward models in tool-using agents. Reward-guided search lifts tool agents by steering their sampling over complex act spaces. Process reward models give step-level scores for that steering.

No firm test set yet exists for such models in tool settings. Their bench, named in the work, fills that gap. It also tests ways to advance the models. Sound step scores are key to agents that plan in many steps.  Step scores guide search in long tool use chains.
arxiv-2601-12794:
Dae San Kim and Taekyun Kim introduce a probabilistic form of the degenerate logarithm and new Stirling numbers. They start with a random variable whose moment generating function exists near the origin. Probabilistic Stirling numbers of both kinds have been introduced before. Early definitions often failed basic orthogonality and inverse relations, though.

Those early forms could also clash with classical numbers when the random variable is constant. The team build heterogeneous Stirling numbers that fix those flaws. Classical relations should survive any honest generalization. Numbers of this kind count partitions and track falling factorials in combinatorics. A probabilistic upgrade links counting with chance in a clean way.
arxiv-2601-13094:
Gelei Xu, Yuying Duan, Jun Xia, and co-authors tackle uneven skill in AI tools for medical diagnosis. A tool may work well for one group of patients and poorly for a next group. Gaps can stem from how often a disease shows up, how scans look, or how risk is spread.

Many past fixes try to hide group traits from the tool. In care work, the authors note, those traits often hold key clues for a right call. Hiding them can cut skill and trust where stakes are high. In place of hiding, the team uses patient tuned offsets that shift with each case. Their aim is calls that stay sound across groups while still using the clues each patient brings.
arxiv-2601-13294:
Yipeng Wang, Huy Gia Han Vu, and Mohit Singhal score the trust of posts on Telegram by their tags, not their links. Telegram is now a top route for false news. Old tools judge a post by the fame of its linked sites or by its words. Those tools fit long news from known sources.

High risk posts on Telegram are short and hold few links. That form breaks link and word tools. The team makes the tag on a post the signal. Tags travel with posts and mark their line. A tag based score can work where link scores have no data. For trust and safety teams, the route fits the true shape of the risk.
arxiv-2601-13394:
Munkaila Dasumani, Suzanne Lenhart, and co-authors use optimal control to plan species boosts in predator prey webs. A boost adds bred or moved stock to aid a rare species. It is a stock tool to guard bio range and halt loss of species.

The team works in discrete time, where steps fall in a set order. In such steps, the order of birth, death, and boost can flip the out come. They apply control theory to two boost models for linked hunter and prey crowds. Each model asks when and how much to boost for the best long run. For wild life teams, the work shows how step order must shape a boost plan.
arxiv-2601-13494:
Swapnil Guragain and Gokarna Sharma study an on line repair route task where a learner gives hints. In the task, calls land over time on a line. A repair worker must serve each call. The aim is low wait. In the classic form no hints are given, and calls are a surprise as they land.

In the learnt form, a machine learner hints where calls will land. A good rule uses hints when they help and guards when they err. The team builds such rules for the line case. For service fleets, hint led routes can cut wait if the hint trust is set with care.
arxiv-2601-13794:
Mehrdad Nasernejad and Jonathan Toledo build a unified frame for persistence in commutative algebra in 2026. Their objects are filtrations of ideals, chains of ideals that grow step by step. Persistence asks if a trait of one step must carry to later steps. Classic notions cover ordinary and symbolic powers of ideals.

The pair define F-persistence and F-strong persistence for a general filtration F. These new notions extend the classic ones to a broad class. A unified frame lets results proved once serve many cases. Commutative algebra gains a cleaner map of how ideal traits endure.
arxiv-2601-13994:
Mingyuan Chi releases a PyTorch library for sparse linear algebra that can learn in 2026. Industrial scientific computing uses sparse matrices for unstructured data. Finite element meshes, graphs, and point clouds all take sparse form. The library, torch-sla, enables GPU-accelerated, scalable, and differentiable sparse linear algebra.

Differentiable means gradients flow through the matrix solves, for training. Adjoint solvers and sparse tensor parallelism are built in. Parallelism lets big problems split across many GPUs. Engineers could then fit physics solvers inside AI training loops. The code is open source, so teams can adapt it to their own rigs. That should speed uptake in labs and in firms alike.
arxiv-2601-14194:
Anagh Venneti, Sarmistha Banik, and Bijay Agrawal test how lab data on nuclei shapes neutron star models in 2026. They construct posterior distributions of the equation of state for neutron star matter. The matter in view lies beyond the star's inner crust. Finite-nuclei constraints enter within relativistic mean-field models.

Those constraints are implemented in three complementary ways. One uses theoretical bounds, one works via nuclear matter parameters, and one enforces experimental values directly. The experimental values are binding energies and charge radii of selected nuclei. Lab nuclei thus guide models of the densest stars known.
arxiv-2601-14494:
Mohamed Omar studies a counting polynomial in this 2026 math paper. The domination polynomial of a graph counts its dominating sets by size. A dominating set is a set of vertices such that every vertex is in the set or next to one in it. The polynomial's coefficients record how many dominating sets have each size.

The open question is unimodality: do those counts rise, peak once, then fall? Omar brings new perspectives to that question. The abstract gives the definition in full formal terms. Readers get fresh angles on a clean graph theory problem, where a simple shape claim about a sequence of counts has resisted full proof.
arxiv-2601-14594:
Lianying Chao and a team of nine co-authors improve video captioning in this 2026 paper. Video captioning models convert frames into visual tokens, then generate descriptions with large language models. Encoding all frames is prohibitively expensive, so uniform sampling is the default choice. Uniform sampling enforces equal temporal coverage. It ignores how unevenly events are distributed in a real video.

The team built LFS, a Learnable Frame Selector. It selects frames that are temporally diverse and event-relevant. The title calls the system event-aware. Readers get a smarter front end for video captioning, one that spends its frame budget where the action actually happens.
arxiv-2601-14694:
Pengfei Ding, Yan Wang, and Guanfeng Liu rethink graph unlearning in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Graph unlearning removes nodes, edges, or features from trained graph neural networks. It is crucial in Web applications, where graph data may contain sensitive, mislabeled, or malicious information. Deleting a person from a social graph must also delete their imprint on the model.

The authors re-understand graph unlearning through memorization. What a network memorized decides what unlearning must erase. That lens reframes how removal methods should be built and judged. Readers get a fresh theoretical base for a task that privacy law increasingly demands.
arxiv-2601-14794:
Dimitrios G. Patsatzis, Alessandro Della Pia, Lucia Russo, and Constantinos Siettos present neural decoders in this 2026 paper. Their decoders, RANDSMAPs, are numerical analysis-informed and explainable. They are designed to explicitly respect conservation laws. The target task is the ill-posed pre-image problem in manifold learning. That problem asks for the original data point behind a low-dimensional embedding.

The team starts by proving an equivalence. Vanilla random Fourier feature neural networks match Radial Basis Function interpolation in the deterministic limit. They also match the double Diffusion Maps decoders based on Geometric Harmonics. RANDSMAPs add random features at multiple scales plus mass preservation. The checks are strict. A map that breaks a known law of the data is sent back, not used. Readers get decoders whose outputs obey the physics of the data.
arxiv-2601-14894:
Nicolas Lazzari, Valentina Presutti, and Antonio Vergari work on joining neural networks with formal logic. Their 2026 arXiv paper sits in neuro-symbolic AI. The aim is to make a network's choices obey rules drawn from domain knowledge.

Those rules are often stored in an ontology, a structured map of facts about a field. The authors note that current methods lack native support for such maps. They aim to build a method whose outputs always fit the ontology. Their route compiles the logic into probabilistic circuits, a form that can be checked.
arxiv-2601-14994:
Chaymaa Abbas, Nour Shammaa, and Mariette Awad study a quiet flaw in how language models are tested. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with data contamination. A test loses its force when the model has already seen the test items in training and can recall them.

Most checks for this flaw were built for English tests. That leaves other languages poorly understood. The authors bring evidence from Arabic corpora, large bodies of Arabic text. They show how translation can hide contamination, so a model may seem to generalize when it is in fact recalling text it has seen before.
arxiv-2601-15194:
Oliver Baker and Carl P. Dettmann ask how the shape of a space changes the randomness of a network built in it. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with soft random geometric graphs. Points are scattered in a space, and pairs link with a chance that fades with distance.

The team studies the entropy of these graph ensembles, a gauge of their disorder. When the link range is small, entropy depends only on the dimension of the space, not its shape. At large ranges, the domain's boundaries take over. Geometry thus matters in one regime and not the other.
arxiv-2601-15294:
Elif Uskuplu, Lawrence S. Moss, and Valeria de Paiva draw maps of how math results depend on each other. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a gap in how math knowledge is stored. Textbooks and lecture notes hide the dependency structure of a proof.

Formal proof libraries show every detail, but in a form few humans can read. Dependency graphs offer a middle ground. KnowTeX makes those graphs visible for results, definitions, and proofs. A reader can then see at a glance what a given theorem truly rests on and uses.
arxiv-2601-15494:
Miklós Koren, Gábor Békés, Julian Hinz, and Aaron Lohmann study how AI coding changes open source in a 2026 arXiv paper. Generative AI is reshaping how software gets made and used. In vibe coding, an AI agent builds software for the user. It picks and assembles open-source parts on its own. Users often never read the docs or talk to maintainers.

That shift can weaken the feedback loop open source relies on. Fewer bug reports and less contact mean less support for maintainers. The authors study the equilibrium effects on the whole ecosystem. Their title states the worry bluntly: vibe coding kills open source. The paper tests that claim with economic reasoning. Funders and maintainers alike have a stake in the answer.
arxiv-2601-15794:
A 2026 arXiv paper listed only under an asterisk is about a detector for the CBM experiment. The device is the Forward Spectator Detector, or FSD. CBM studies highly compressed nuclear matter. That work will take place at the future FAIR site. The FSD watches collision participants at the SIS-100 accelerator. It must work at high collision rates. It is built from scintillator parts. From its signals, teams rebuild the reaction plane. They also gauge how head-on each collision was.

The record carries no author names. Its abstract reads as a design overview. It covers the technical design of the FSD. It also covers tests of how well the detector works. Such reports guide the teams who will build it. They also guide the teams who will run it.
arxiv-2601-15994:
A. Foisseau and a large team report a bright blazar flare caught by a new mission in a 2026 arXiv paper. The blazar is 1ES 1959+650, one of the X-ray brightest known. On December 6, 2024, it underwent a high-amplitude X-ray outburst. The SVOM satellite detected it. The team calls it the first such discovery with this mission. Blazars are active galaxies whose jets point near our line of sight. Their flares test models of jet physics.

SVOM and the Swift observatory followed the source afterward. Monitoring ran from December 2024 to March 2025. Multi-wavelength follow-up is the record's other theme. Watching a flare rise and fade across bands shows how the jet spends energy. A mission's first big catch also proves the instrument in action.
arxiv-2601-16294:
Evangelos Georganas, Alexander Heinecke and Pradeep Dubey use space fill curves to ease matrix times. Their 2026 preprint deals with the core sum of deep learning and big maths. That sum, called GEMM, has been tuned for years by top teams. New chips give much math per byte of data moved. High ratios make a best fit build hard to reach by old ways.

Curves that fill space order the work to cut data moves. Less moves mean the chip spends its time on math, not waits. A plain build path with top speed has wide worth. The team frames curves as all the tool the task needs. Tests span deep and big maths loads.
arxiv-2601-16394:
Yihao Wang and four coauthors find the mark for phrase based cuts with entropy cues. Their 2026 preprint deals with cuts that use free phrase cues. The task, called RES, cuts the thing a phrase names in a pic. It backs tools like pic edit and robot sight. Past tools oft miss the true thing when pics hold more than one fit.

The team uses entropy to find prime points that pin the thing. Points then guide sight thought to the right zone. Sharp zone thought should lift cut grade on hard pics. The work, named ResAgent, adds a point find step. It seeks cuts that match the phrase sense well.
arxiv-2601-16494:
Partha Ghose draws loose cause order from a fail to glue in sense terms. His 2026 preprint deals with acts whose cause order is not fixed. Past paths span high order acts like the quantum switch. They span the process matrix frame and space based claims. Each path has gaps in how it grounds the loose order.

Ghose builds loose order from sense terms and a time term. Fail to glue means two views can not join in one frame. That fail yields order that is loose in a firm sense. A new ground may join split camps in the field. The work is a pure thought study of cause.
arxiv-2601-16894:
P. S. Koliogiannis, T. Ghosh, E. Yüksel, and N. Paar link lab atom facts to dead stars. Dense stars' size rests on how stiff their core stuff is. That stuff's rules stay blurred by wide doubt. One lab gauge is how much an atom's charge cloud stretches. Their 2026 preprint ties that stretch to star squeeze.

Such ties are called universal, since most models share them. A shared tie lets lab data bound star traits. It cuts the sway of which model one picks. The team tests the tie across many models. Firm ties help scopes read star mass and width right.
arxiv-2601-17094:
Junichiro Niimi splits world sense from word skill in chatbot design. Chatbots write smooth text with great ease. Yet that ease may hide a thin grasp of the world. His 2026 preprint sets a rule in plain words. The mouth is not the brain, he says. Word parts and world parts should sit apart in the build.

His design joins energy-based world models to text tools. World parts track how things work and shift. Text parts then speak of that tracked world. Split builds could make bot claims more true. They may also show where a bot's grasp fails.
arxiv-2601-17194:
Cheyu Lin and Katherine Flanigan read minds from how bodies move in built space. Built halls should now back care, bonds, and shared strength. Moves in those halls hint at how folks feel. Such moves are called kinesic acts in the field. Their 2026 preprint builds ways to read those acts by machine. It ties the reads to hall design aims.

A wave of pride, stress, or ease can show in gait. Tools that read it could tune light, space, and flow. That tune may help folks feel at home in halls. The work joins care sense to build craft.
arxiv-2601-17294:
Ryutaro Misawa builds point sets on spheres with a special evenness trait. A spherical t-design spreads points so that averages match the whole sphere for a class of functions. Such sets serve tests, codes, and sensor layouts. Misawa builds them from tight t-fusion frames. Those frames are sets of subspaces in a Grassmannian with tight balance.

For each subspace, points are placed by a fixed recipe. The question is when the full set earns design status. Clear conditions let others build designs on demand. That beats hunting for lucky sets by trial. The work gives geometers a bridge from frame theory to sphere design. Both fields gain new stock to share.
arxiv-2601-17494:
Uygun Jamilov and Manuel Ladra study how a family of quadratic operators acts on a simplex. The operators blend non-Volterra quadratic stochastic maps. One parameter, alpha, sets the blend. The authors track where repeated use sends each start point. Such maps model trait spread in populations across generations.

They show that for alpha from zero up to but not past one, all paths meet at a fixed point. That means long-run outcomes do not depend on the start. Fixed long-run states simplify forecasts for such systems. The result is a clean case in a field full of chaos. It gives biologists and algebraists a shared anchor.
arxiv-2601-17594:
Anton Arnold, Marlies Pirner, and Gayrat Toshpulatov study the long-time behavior of quantum Fokker-Planck equations. The equations are space-inhomogeneous and sit on a classical kinetic phase space. A nonlinear factor, f times one plus or minus f, shapes the model. It appears in both transport and collision terms. The plus and minus signs encode boson and fermion rules.

That factor captures inclusion for bosons and exclusion for fermions. Long-time results tell where the system settles. Such knowledge guides gas and plasma models at quantum scales. It also tests numeric codes over long runs. The work joins kinetic theory with quantum statistics. It gives a firm view of the end state.
arxiv-2601-18294:
Samuel Mallick and co-authors join reinforcement learning with model predictive control to run truck platoons on less fuel. Their 2026 preprint deals with cooperative control of autonomous vehicle groups. Platoons can cut drag and smooth traffic, and joint control of speed and gear choice adds further gains. Gear changes are discrete, which makes the joint problem awkward for smooth optimizers. The team pairs distributed MPC with a learning layer that handles the gear side.

Learning can tune what fixed rules miss, while MPC keeps the plan safe and feasible. Fuel savings scale across fleets and years. The work targets freight, where small percentage gains mean large sums and emissions cuts.
arxiv-2601-18994:
Michael Borinsky, Chiara Meroni, and Maximilian Wiesmann count colored regular graphs as they grow huge. A regular graph gives each node the same number of links, and colors on the edges add a further rule. The team proves a formula for how many such graphs exist when the count grows large.

The formula hangs on special points of a polynomial that encodes what may sit at each node. As a use case, they work out how many proper edge colorings a large random regular graph should have on average. Counts like this guide both combinatorics and models of random networks.
arxiv-2601-19194:
An unnamed team improves a speech system that names who said what in a crowd. Speaker attributed recognition must both transcribe speech and assign each line to the right speaker. Many systems do well only after tuning to one domain and fail on new kinds of recordings.

Their earlier system used speaker diarization, the split of audio by speaker, to guide the Whisper recognizer. The new version enrolls itself, needing no outside speaker samples. Strong results across languages and domains, with little tuning, would make meeting and media transcription far more useful.
arxiv-2601-19394:
Xudong Han and seven co-authors regularize model parameters by domain so models travel to new data safely. Domain generalization asks a model to do well on distributions it never saw, a must for real use. Most methods chase features that stay the same across source domains.

Their method, DSP-Reg, instead regularizes the parameters themselves with domain sensitivity in mind. Not all weights should be held equally loose or tight, and domains hint at which. Better travel to unseen data matters anywhere the world shifts after training, from hospitals to highways.
arxiv-2601-19494:
Lei Zhang and fourteen colleagues build a test for a new kind of software tool. Large language models can now review code and comment on changes, much like a human reviewer. Judging whether such reviews are any good takes a benchmark, a fixed set of tasks with known answers. Many current tests look at single files or small snippets, which misses how real projects fit together.

Their benchmark, AACR-Bench, judges automatic code review with the whole repository in view. A reviewer that sees the full project can catch faults that only make sense across files. The tasks are built to reflect that wider context. Good scores on the bench should mean a tool is ready for real code bases. The work gives labs and firms a shared yardstick for this fast-growing use of language models.
arxiv-2601-20094:
Haibin Wu and a large team of colleagues build the decoder behind a phone-based speech synthesiser. Neural audio codecs compress speech into acoustic features; the Mimi codec streams them for real-time text-to-speech. A decoder must turn those features back into natural audio on the phone itself. Their system, T-Mimi, is a transformer-based decoder for the Mimi codec.

It is designed for real-time, on-device use. Phones impose tight limits on latency and compute. A transformer decoder that fits those limits can give apps natural voices without the cloud. On-device synthesis also keeps voice data private. The work pushes high-quality speech generation onto everyday hardware.
arxiv-2601-20194:
Huichao Men and five colleagues present AirAgent, an agent framework for smart home air systems. It uses a voice dialogue interface to manage indoor air quality on its own. The system extracts feature labels from talks with a device, then plans how to host the device across several dimensions.

The design links perception, reasoning, and control in one loop, driven by a large language model. It aims to give each household personal control of air quality rather than fixed settings. As appliances gain smart features, such agents may become the layer that turns raw sensors into comfort people can feel.
arxiv-2601-20394:
Giovanna Broccia and five colleagues evaluate a language workbench, a tool for defining programming languages and reusing their parts. Workbenches aim to streamline language development. Whether designers adopt one depends in part on how easy its meta-language, the language for defining languages, is to comprehend.

The authors run a family of experiments that separates comprehension from adoption. A tool can be understood yet not adopted, or adopted despite being hard to learn. Knowing which barrier binds helps workbench builders spend effort where it counts, and helps language designers judge new tools.
arxiv-2601-20494:
Anika Beckers and Jan Friedrich present numerical schemes for two-dimensional systems of nonlocal conservation laws. Their schemes build on well-known monotone numerical flux functions, after approximating the nonlocal terms in a suitable way. The systems are weakly coupled through those nonlocal terms.

The underlying flux function is kept general, so the results apply to a wide range of common nonlocal models. Such laws describe traffic, crowds, and other flows where drivers or particles react to conditions ahead, not just at their own spot. Reliable schemes let engineers simulate those flows without spurious wiggles.
arxiv-2601-20694:
Hao Liang, Jiayu Cheng, Sean Sinclair, and Yali Du ask a sharp question about decision making under uncertainty. Their 2026 paper studies exogenous Markov decision processes, or Exo-MDPs. In these models, all randomness comes from outside inputs. Those inputs evolve on their own, untouched by the learner's actions. Demand, arrivals, and prices are classic examples.

Such models are common in operations work: inventory control, energy storage, and resource allocation. The authors study them with linear function approximation, a compact way to represent value. Their question is in the title: is pure exploitation enough? That means always taking the action that looks best now, with no probing of new options. The answer shapes how simple a good policy for these systems can be.
arxiv-2601-20794:
Jiaming Chen asks how rarely a noisy heat flow stays small on a curved space. The 2026 paper studies small ball chances for the stochastic heat equation. The heat spreads on a compact smooth curved space with no edge. Random noise drives the heat at each point. A small ball chance is the odds that the whole flow stays in a tiny tube.

The noise is Gaussian and white in time. The drift term rests on time, place, and the flow itself. The shape of the space shapes how heat and noise mix. Sharp rates for these small chances guide tests of the equation. They also guide simulations that must respect rare calm events. The paper extends flat-space ideas to worlds with shape.
arxiv-2601-20994:
Md Muhtasim Munif Fahim and Md Rezaul Karim argue that language models should grow wide, not deep. Their 2026 paper challenges a quiet assumption in scaling laws. Scaling laws describe how loss falls as parameters and data grow. They treat architecture as interchangeable. A billion parameters could form a shallow, wide model. Or they could form a deep, narrow one. The title calls the preference for depth a delusion.

The authors compare these shapes head to head. A shallow-wide network has few layers but broad ones. A deep-narrow network stacks many thin layers. If width wins, training and serving could both get cheaper. The paper is an argument backed by this comparison. It speaks to labs deciding how to spend a fixed parameter budget.
arxiv-2601-21094:
Minjae Kwon, Josephine Lamp, and Lu Feng test whether safe learning stays safe when patients change. Their 2026 paper studies safety generalization in safe reinforcement learning. Such algorithms are usually evaluated under fixed training conditions. The authors ask if training-time safety guarantees transfer to deployment under distribution shift. Their testbed is diabetes management, a safety-critical domain. A unified clinical simulator hosts the comparison.

The benchmark reveals a safety generalization gap. Policies that obey constraints in training often break them on unseen patients. That gap is the paper's central warning. A diabetes policy that fails new patients is not safe in any useful sense. The study urges the field to test safety where it will actually be used. It gives researchers a shared simulator for that harder test.
arxiv-2601-21294:
Anders Gjølbye, Emma Kargaard, Ida Kargaard, and Lars Kai Hansen study what missing data does to a classic method for paired datasets. The method finds shared structure by looking at how two views of the same items vary together. Real paired data, such as scans plus test scores, often have holes in both views.

The authors study random holes in a high-dimensional model with a hidden spike of signal. They find sharp phase changes: past a point, the shared structure suddenly becomes hard or easy to recover. Knowing where that edge lies helps researchers judge when their data are too patchy to trust.
arxiv-2601-21494:
Ishan Jindal, Sai Prashanth Akuthota, Jayant Taneja, and Sachin Dev Sharma cut the cost of careful reasoning in language models. A popular trick samples many full reasoning chains and takes the majority answer. That works, but it pays full price for every chain, including the doomed ones.

Their method watches the opening steps of each chain. Chains that agree early tend to share a fate, so weak branches can be dropped early. They call the approach the path of least resistance. Saving compute on reasoning lets the same budget cover more questions, or deeper thought on the hard ones.
arxiv-2601-21594:
A. Aghajani and J. Kinnunen sharpen estimates for the size of a sum of two nonnegative functions. The problem traces to a question posed by Carbery in two thousand six. Later teams strengthened the bounds on these Lp norms, and later work refined them to a form that is optimal in a certain sense.

The authors add new inequalities to this line of work. Such bounds sit under harmonic analysis, where sums of functions model overlapping signals. Sharper constants mean sharper guarantees wherever the estimates are used. The paper continues a careful twenty-year effort to pin down the exact shape of the inequality.
arxiv-2601-21694:
Shuo Li, Jiajun Sun, and twelve co-authors build a benchmark for editing charts end to end from user intent. Charts are a basic format for structured data analysis. Editing one on request sounds simple but demands fine control and global consistency at once.

A changed label must not break the scale, and a new color scheme must stay readable. Their benchmark grades systems on full editing tasks, not toy tweaks. End-to-end skill here would save analysts hours of fiddly manual work. The benchmark also exposes where current AI tools still mangle the structure they were asked to preserve.
arxiv-2601-21894:
Lukas Twist and co-authors ask what kind of code actually teaches language models to reason. Models often improve at reasoning after training on code, and they produce step-by-step chains of thought. Yet most studies treat code as a generic training signal, as if any code helped equally.

The team's 2026 preprint takes a data-centric view and asks which properties of code drive the gains. Complexity is a prime suspect: simple scripts and intricate systems code may teach very different lessons. Knowing which code helps, and why, would let trainers pick data deliberately instead of hoarding it. That could make future models both smarter and cheaper to train.
arxiv-2601-21994:
Florian Kayatz, Annica Black-Schaffer, and Jorge Cayao study superconductivity in atom-thin materials placed next to an ordinary superconductor. Transition metal dichalcogenides are promising for spin-triplet superconducting phases because their spins are locked to their motion by strong Ising spin-orbit coupling. Most earlier studies used oversimplified models, though.

The team instead models a single layer with a three-orbital model, tracking the real orbital makeup of the material. Their 2026 preprint examines which superconducting properties arise in proximity to a conventional superconductor under this richer description. Triplet superconductivity is a building block for topological quantum devices, so knowing when it truly appears, beyond toy models, guides experimental design.
arxiv-2601-22094:
Hanzhuo Huang and co-authors generate images guided by three-dimensional assets. Reference-based image generation usually starts from a single flat reference picture and leans on large pretrained diffusion models. The result can copy appearance, but it has no true grasp of the object's shape.

Their 2026 preprint proposes RefAny3D, a diffusion model that takes real 3D assets as its reference. Conditioning on an actual model could hold an object's geometry steady while its setting, lighting, and style change around it. That control matters for product design, games, and film, where a hero object must look like itself from every angle a director or customer chooses.
arxiv-2601-22294:
Serhii Kryhin, Tatiana Mouzykantskii, and Vivishek Sudhir study how to forecast a hidden signal buried in harsh noise. Their 2026 preprint deals with scale-free noise, where bursts come at all sizes and no scale stands out. The task is to build a filter that reads past data and calls the next value.

Forecasting sits inside a long line of signal work, from Wiener to Kalman. Scale-free noise breaks many of the usual tricks. The team seek a filter that stays causal, using only what has been seen. Sharp forecasts help in fields from physics to finance.
arxiv-2601-22594:
Aryaman Arora, Zhengxuan Wu, Jacob Steinhardt, and Sarah Schwettmann find that language model circuits are sparse when read in the neuron basis. Circuits are the small sub-networks that carry out a task inside a model. Their 2026 preprint notes that most scholars hunt circuits with sparse autoencoders, since single neurons seemed too messy.

Their result says the neuron basis itself holds sparse circuits. That simplifies the hunt: no extra tool may be needed. Clear circuits aid safety checks and edits. The work reopens a path the field had set aside. It may change how models are mapped.
arxiv-2604-01194:
AgentWatcher is a rule-based monitor for prompt injection attacks in 2026. Large language models and their agent applications are highly vulnerable. Prompt injection can steer an agent through text it merely reads.

State-of-the-art detection methods carry two limitations, the authors argue. First, effectiveness degrades significantly as context length increases in long inputs. Second, they lack explicit rules defining what prompt injection is. Detection decisions thus stay implicit, opaque, and hard to reason about. A rule-based watcher aims to fix both problems at once. Explicit rules make each flag explainable to a human reviewer. Security readers get a monitor designed for long, real agent contexts.

blake-songs-innocence-experience-1794:
William Blake wrote, illustrated, and hand-printed Songs of Innocence in 1789, then added the darker Songs of Experience five years later. The combined book appeared in 1794. Blake called the two sets the two contrary states of the human soul.

Short lyric poems pair off against each other. The Lamb answers The Tyger, and happy childhood scenes face the grim streets of London. Simple words carry deep questions about God, freedom, and cruelty. Few books of English poetry are quoted more often, and Blake's own pictures for the poems are just as famous as the words.
burton-first-footsteps-east-africa-1894:
Richard Burton traveled in disguise to the forbidden city of Harar in 1854 and 1855. First Footsteps in East Africa tells how he did it; the 1894 edition is the fuller text, printed after his death. Harar, in what is now Ethiopia, barred Christians on pain of death.

Burton posed as a Muslim merchant, relying on his languages and his nerve. He spent ten days in the city, met its ruler, and got out alive, the first European known to do so. The return brought a spear attack that scarred his face for life. The book mixes danger, learning, and dry wit.
chopin-bayou-folk-1894:
Kate Chopin published Bayou Folk in 1894, her first collection of stories, after years of writing about the Louisiana she had married into. Chopin lived in New Orleans and in the Cane River country around Cloutierville. The twenty-three stories draw on Creole and Acadian life she observed at close range.

Désirée's Baby, the most famous piece, turns on a young mother's unknown ancestry and her husband's pride, ending in one of American fiction's great shocks. Other tales follow planters, servants, children, and wanderers through fairs, feuds, and romances. Chopin writes dialect with care and judgment without cruelty. Bayou Folk founded Creole local color and announced a writer far ahead of her time.

Erasmus Darwin published Volume 1 of Zoonomia; Or, the Laws of Organic Life in 1794. Darwin, a doctor and poet in Lichfield, was the grandfather of Charles Darwin. In Zoonomia he set out a full system of life, disease, and change in living things.
