Ernest Rhys edited a one-volume selection of Thomas Dekker's plays for the Mermaid series in 1894. The Mermaid volumes brought the old English dramatists back to common readers in cheap, handy form. Dekker, Shakespeare's cheerful contemporary, had long been hard to find in print.

Rhys chose from Dekker's best work, the comedies and city plays that made his name. Dekker's London of apprentices, shoemakers, and rogues comes alive in these pages. His prose pamphlets on plague and coney-catching share the same warm eye. The selection served for years as the standard way to meet Dekker, and its notes and glossary still help new readers.
doe-osti-3383765-closeout-document-usdoe: DE-FG02-94ER40870 got closeout-documented, and this DOE grant covers the closeout. The pages detail the document findings. The researchers get their data. The grant was USDOE. The data were researcher. The 94ER40870 were grant. The document were closeout.
dorsey-a-study-of-siouan-cults-1894:
Dorsey followed his Omaha study with this wider 1894 report comparing the cults of the Siouan peoples. Drawing on his knowledge of the Omaha, Ponka, Osage, and Dakota, he set their religions side by side for the Bureau of American Ethnology.

The study covers sacred societies, mystery rites, dances, and the beings each group honored. Dorsey shows how shared ideas about power and spirits took different forms in each tribe. He prints prayers, songs, and ritual terms in the native languages with translation. Though dense, the report is a key early attempt to compare Native American religions as systems.
dubois-pithecanthropus-erectus-1894:
Eugene Dubois, a Dutch army doctor, published his monograph on the Java fossils in 1894, in German. Digging near the Solo River at Trinil, he had found a skullcap and a thigh bone. He named the creature Pithecanthropus erectus, the upright ape-man.

Dubois argued the bones formed a link between apes and humans. Many scholars first doubted or dismissed the claim. The find was the first fossil hominin reported outside Europe. Now classed with Homo erectus, it vindicated the search for human ancestors in Asia. Dubois guarded the fossils jealously for years, which only sharpened the long controversy.
erman-life-ancient-egypt-1894:
Adolf Erman rebuilt the daily life of old Egypt in Life in Ancient Egypt, in English from 1894. Erman led the Berlin school, the most strict crop of sages then at work. H. M. Tirard turned his German text to English. House by house, shop by shop, he shows how folk there dwelt, dressed, ate, wed, and worked.

He draws each scene from texts and finds, not dreams. Kings get brief room; plain folk get the book. Few works on Egypt have been used so much since. It is the lost world at home, at ease.
europmc-pmc10013894:
Douglas, Ewell, and Brauer compare the quality of survey data from five online research platforms in a 2023 study. Online studies now recruit large numbers of people fast and cheaply. Yet researchers worry about careless respondents and automated bots filling in answers.

The team collected data through MTurk, Prolific, CloudResearch, Qualtrics, and SONA, then checked each set for signs of poor attention. Their comparison shows which sources gave cleaner data. It names clear steps that labs can take before they collect data. The paper offers practical guidance for anyone who runs or reads online human research.
europmc-pmc10172194:
Sun and colleagues map cell-level chemical changes in gastric cancer using spatial multi-omics in a 2023 study. Gastric cancer forms in the stomach lining and is often found late. How a tumor rewires its chemistry, cell by cell and place by place, shapes its growth and its talks with nearby healthy cells.

The team combined imaging and molecular profiling to chart that rewiring in place. Their maps show which tumor regions run which fuel programs and how tumor and non-tumor cells interact. The work may help design treatments aimed at the tumor's chemistry.
europmc-pmc10190894: A medical paper with the prophylaxis of tetanus, a summary. The lockjaw prevention. This article preserves that immunology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc10225594:
Mitra and co-authors trace CAR T cell therapy from bench to bedside in a 2023 review. In this therapy, a patient's own T cells are engineered in the lab to hunt cancer. The approach won its first approval in 2017 for children and young adults with a form of leukemia that had resisted other care.

The review recounts the decades of work behind that breakthrough. It explains how the engineered cells are made and given, and their striking results in blood cancers. It also covers side effects and the push to make the therapy work in solid tumors.
europmc-pmc10250194:
Punjani and Fleet present 3DFlex, a method that finds the structure and motion of flexible proteins from cryo-electron microscopy, in a 2023 paper. Cryo-EM photographs vast numbers of frozen molecules and averages them into a three-dimensional shape. Flexible molecules break that averaging, since each copy bends in its own way, and modeling them is a top challenge in the field.

3DFlex learns how a molecule bends and sorts the images by pose. It then rebuilds both the shape and the range of motion. The method reveals moving parts of molecular machines that older tools blurred away.
europmc-pmc10301994:
Al Kuwaiti and colleagues review the role of artificial intelligence in healthcare in a 2023 paper. AI tools have spread fast through medicine, from scan reading to virtual nursing. The authors base their review on the published literature and sort the field into key areas of use.

They cover imaging and diagnosis, virtual patient care, drug discovery, and hospital management. For each area they weigh proven gains against risks such as bias and privacy loss. The review gives readers a structured tour of where AI already works in care and where caution is due.
europmc-pmc10468394:
Watson and a large team gave a method in 2023 to design brand-new proteins with AI. Proteins are cell machines whose shape sets their job. Past design tools each fit a narrow task. The team adapted diffusion models, the AI type that builds images from noise, to protein shapes.

Their tool, RFdiffusion, starts from the RoseTTAFold prediction network, tuned to clean noisy shapes. It can build plain chains, binders that grip a target, and symmetric multi-part forms. Watson built and tested hundreds of the designs in the lab. One binder's true shape, read by a cold electron scope, matched the design near exactly. The binder gripped a flu protein as planned.
europmc-pmc12094094:
Lagier and a large team reported growing gut microbes once thought uncultivable in 2016. DNA methods had revealed vast numbers of unknown gut species. Growing them in pure culture had fallen out of fashion. Yet culture stays key to learning what each microbe does. The journal later retracted the article.

Their approach, called culturomics, tries many growth conditions at once. Fresh samples and new protocols widened the catch. The team reported 1,057 species from the human gut. Of those, 531 were new to the gut list. Readers should weigh the findings with the retraction in mind.
europmc-pmc12148494:
Bunne and many co-authors laid out a plan for a virtual cell in 2024. Cells drive health and disease, yet models capture them poorly. New artificial intelligence tools and rich cell data change that outlook. A virtual cell would simulate molecules, cells, and tissues together.

Such a model could predict how cells act in new states. It could guide lab work and speed discovery. Building it demands shared data, open science, and teamwork across fields. Bunne sets priorities and chances for the effort. The vision treats the cell as a system computers can learn.
europmc-pmc1240994:
Greer and colleagues dosed volunteers with perchlorate to find safe levels in 2002. Perchlorate taints groundwater across the Southwest at low levels. It blocks iodide from entering the thyroid gland. That blockade is both its drug use and its toxic risk.

Thirty-seven volunteers drank perchlorate water for 14 days at four dose levels. Thyroid uptake of radioactive iodine was measured before, during, and after dosing. Uptake at 8 and 24 hours tracked each other closely. Greer charts how uptake falls as dose climbs. Those curves anchor health limits for water contamination. Thyroid uptake returned to normal 15 days after the dosing stopped. No sex gap appeared in the response.
europmc-pmc1241394:
Schantz, Widholm, and Rice reviewed PCB exposure and child brain function in 2003. PCBs are industrial chemicals that persist in soil, water, and food. Better chemistry now profiles single PCB types in human tissue. Different types carry different toxic profiles.

Cohorts in Taiwan, Michigan, New York, Holland, Germany, and the Faroe Islands were compared. Each reported negative links between prenatal PCB exposure and child test scores. Memory, attention, and related skills were affected. The pattern held across settings and exposure routes. Schantz weighs how this growing record should shape risk assessment.
europmc-pmc12857194:
Verma and a large team mapped genetic architecture across 2,068 traits in 2024. Human genetics has under-sampled diverse populations. The VA Million Veteran Program is among the largest American biobanks. About 29 percent of its members trace to non-European reference groups.

Over 635,000 participants contributed health record linked data. More than 44.3 million genetic variants were genotyped. The scale supports association studies across many ancestries at once. Missing causal factors and health disparity roots are the targets. Verma shows diversity at scale can fill long-standing gaps. It appeared in Science in 2024. In total, the scan found 26,049 links between gene variants and traits across groups.
europmc-pmc1324794:
Schaffer and co-authors imaged brain surface blood flow after vessel blockage in 2006. A dense arteriole network overlies the mammalian cortex. The team asked whether it reroutes blood after an occlusion. Rodent cortex was imaged with two-photon microscopy at single-vessel scale.

Flow returned quickly past a blocked vessel by reversing direction. The first branch downstream regained perfusion through one reversed vessel. Blocking the main middle cerebral artery flipped flow in about half of distant downstream vessels. Schaffer shows collateral rerouting is fast and widespread. That rerouting may limit stroke damage in surface networks.
europmc-pmc1434494:
A pig germ caused a severe outbreak in China in the summer of 2005. Tang and co-authors investigated cases of toxic shock, a crash marked by fever, low blood pressure, and organ failure. The germ was Streptococcus suis type 2, a microbe of pigs that rarely harms people.

The team studied sick people and pigs, and grew 45 germ strains from samples. Tests in pigs and gene checks showed the strains were strong and closely matched. Tang also linked the outbreak to a like event in 1998. Their report marks the first clear proof that this pig germ can cause toxic shock in people.
europmc-pmc1456994:
Ernst and Bar-Joseph built a tool in 2006 for a common lab bind. Gene activity studies over time are often short, with just three to eight points, due to cost. Generic tools fit such short runs poorly. Their program, STEM, was made for short series from the start.

STEM groups genes by how their activity rises and falls. It can compare two runs and chart the trends. It also links groups to a gene function database for sound biological reads. Ernst notes that most time series studies are short, so a tool shaped for them fills a real gap. STEM is free for academic use.
europmc-pmc2020494:
Rosen, Fox and Gill reviewed in 2007 how well HIV treatment programmes in sub-Saharan Africa keep patients in care. Antiretroviral therapy, drugs that suppress HIV, was expanding fast across the region. Long-term retention is vital for those programmes to succeed. The team searched databases, conference reports and project documents from 2000 to 2007 for non-research programmes.

They found 32 publications covering 33 cohorts and 74,192 patients in 13 countries. Reported retention was 79.1 percent at six months, 75.0 percent at one year, and 61.6 percent at two years, with wide variation between programmes. Loss to follow-up caused 56 percent of attrition, and death caused 40 percent. The authors warn that short reports may overstate retention, and urge better patient tracing.
europmc-pmc2125494: A medical paper on the absorption of fat in partially and completely depancreatized dogs. The pancreasless fat. This article preserves that physiology. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2125794: A medical paper on the neutralization of antipneumococcus immune bodies by infected exudates. The blocked antibodies. This article preserves that immunology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128394: A medical paper with studies on the disease of guinea pigs due to Bacillus abortus. The guinea pig disease. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2128494: A medical paper on roentgen ray intoxication, intestinal lesions and acute intoxication. The X-ray gut. This article preserves that radiology. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2128594: A medical paper on allergic irritability, formation of anti-sheep hemolytic amboceptor. The sheep antibodies. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131494: A medical paper with studies on d'Herelle's bacteriophage, an inquiry into the mode of action. The phage's method. This article preserves that virology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2140394: A biology paper on the dark adaptation of the human eye. The night vision. This article preserves that physiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2359994:
O'Connor and colleagues reviewed a scanning method for testing blood vessel drugs in 2007. The method is DCE-MRI, a form of magnetic scan that tracks a contrast dye through tissue. Antiangiogenic drugs block new vessel growth, while vascular disrupting drugs attack vessels that already feed a tumor.

The authors explained that this scan type is now common in early trials of such drugs. For some vessel-blocking drugs, scans showed clear drug effects and stronger effects at higher doses. They set out the choices that shape scan quality, covering how data are collected and analysed in the T1-weighted form of the method. They also flagged weak points where the technique still needed work before results could be compared across trials.
europmc-pmc2373894:
Itoh and co-authors compared sex chromosome gene dosage in birds and mammals in 2007. Dosage compensation means evening out gene output between the sexes, since one sex carries two copies of the sex chromosome and the other carries one. Mammals manage this well, but birds, where males have two Z chromosomes and females one, were a mystery.

Using gene chips, they measured male-to-female activity ratios in zebra finch and chicken, plus mouse and human data. In birds, Z-linked genes ran clearly higher in males than ordinary genes did. In mouse and human, X-linked genes matched ordinary genes closely, showing effective balancing. Even the many human X genes that escape silencing did not break the balance. The authors called birds an unmatched case of living without real dosage compensation.
europmc-pmc2376094:
Galluzzi and co-authors reviewed how viruses control cell suicide at the mitochondria in 2008. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations, and they also hold a trigger for apoptosis, the program that makes infected cells kill themselves. Killing infected cells is an ancient defence, so many viruses must disable it to survive.

The review catalogues viral tricks on both sides of that switch. Some viral proteins mimic the host's own Bcl-2 family, the proteins that guard the suicide trigger, and block death so the virus can finish copying itself. Others push death along, killing immune cells or bursting infected cells to spread the virus. Still others, with no host look-alike, grip key parts of the death machinery directly. The authors focused on the mitochondrial step, where the decision to die is largely made.
europmc-pmc2488194:
Johnson and colleagues hunted hidden drug resistance in newly diagnosed HIV patients in 2008. Standard resistance tests read the dominant virus, missing rare resistant copies that can still wreck a first treatment. The team applied sensitive real-time PCR tests, each tuned to one resistance mutation, to patients in the United States and Canada.

Among 205 people whose virus looked fully drug-sensitive by standard testing, 17% carried one to three hidden resistance mutations, and 2% carried resistance to two drug classes at once. Samples that already showed resistance often hid extra mutations too. The clincher came from 316 patients starting an efavirenz-based regimen: hidden mutations appeared in 7% of those whose treatment failed, but under 1% of successes, a statistically sharp gap. The authors argued baseline testing should use sensitive methods so first regimens are not chosen blind.
europmc-pmc2592694:
van der Schaar and colleagues filmed individual dengue virus particles entering living cells in 2008 to map the virus's entry route step by step. Dengue is the world's most common insect-borne viral infection, yet how it invades cells was unclear. The team tracked single labelled particles alongside glowing markers of the cell's uptake machinery.

The virus moved by diffusion across the cell surface until a ready-made clathrin-coated pit, the cell's standard cargo intake dimple, snagged it. All entry used this clathrin route. Inside, particles rode compartments marked Rab5, which then matured into late endosomes by gaining Rab7 and shedding Rab5. Fusion between the viral membrane and the compartment membrane, the step that releases the virus's contents, happened mainly in those late endosomes. The timeline gives drug designers precise steps to block.
europmc-pmc2600394:
Lanciotti and colleagues characterised in 2008 the Zika virus behind a 2007 epidemic on Yap Island in Micronesia. Physicians there saw an outbreak of rash, conjunctivitis, and joint pain that a rapid test blamed on dengue virus. Samples sent to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention told a different story, and the team set out to identify the virus fully.

Antibody tests confirmed a recent flavivirus infection. Genetic sequencing of amplified fragments showed about 90 percent identity with Zika virus. That virus is mosquito-borne and was first isolated in Uganda in 1947. The team determined the full coding region sequence of the Yap virus and described its serologic properties, including how patient antibodies react. The episode was the first documented Zika outbreak outside Africa and Asia.
europmc-pmc2675494:
Cruz and Wishart reviewed in 2007 how machine learning, software that finds patterns in past data, is used to predict cancer. The field had grown fast on new gene and protein measurements too complex for hand analysis. The reviewers surveyed which methods were used, what data fed them, and how well they worked.

Clear trends stood out. Studies leaned hard on older neural network methods, and on prostate and breast cancers above others. Protein markers and gene chip data were the favorite inputs. Many studies also skipped proper testing on fresh data, a basic safeguard. In the well-tested work, learning methods beat standard prediction by 15 to 25 percent on who gets cancer, whose returns, and who dies of it. The methods, they add, are also teaching basic lessons about how cancers grow.
europmc-pmc2678294:
Rumble and co-authors presented in 2009 SHRiMP, a program for placing millions of very short DNA reads onto a genome. New sequencing machines read genomes in scraps of 25 to 70 letters. Mapping those scraps back to a reference genome is the first step of most studies, and it gets hard when the new individual differs from the reference at many spots.

SHRiMP pairs a fast first pass with careful alignment that handles both ordinary reads and a color-coded kind from one major machine. A statistical model weeds out false matches. The team tested it on a sea squirt, Ciona savignyi, an animal famous for its scrambled variation. The program mapped the second sequenced individual's reads accurately onto the reference despite the heavy differences. The run also confirmed just how variable this species is, a good sign for studies of wilder, less tame genomes.
europmc-pmc2715894:
Vanengelsdorp and co-authors surveyed in 2009 honey bee colonies hit by Colony Collapse Disorder, a sudden loss of adult worker bees in the United States over two winters. Hives were left with brood and food but few adults, and few dead bees nearby. No single cause was known when the study began.

Across sixty-one measured factors, from bee body state to pathogen and pesticide levels, no one measure stood out as the likely cause. Bees from collapsed colonies carried more pathogens at once than bees from healthy colonies. That pattern points to a mix of infection and other stresses, or to shared exposure, rather than to one agent acting alone.
europmc-pmc2791494:
Forristal and colleagues studied how low oxygen shapes human embryonic stem cells, which can become any cell type in the body. Embryos start life in low oxygen, yet labs usually grow these cells in room air. Their 2010 work compared growth at room air with growth at just five percent oxygen, mimicking the womb where embryos begin, and tested oxygen-sensing proteins called hypoxia inducible factors.

Cells in room air grew more slowly and made less of three proteins that keep stem cells flexible. Silencing one sensor, HIF2A, cut growth and lowered those same proteins, while a marker of early change rose. A third sensor, HIF3A, tuned the other two, and low oxygen clearly suited the cells better.
europmc-pmc2828994:
Jewkes and Morrell argued in 2010 that South Africa's HIV epidemic runs through cultural ideals of manhood and womanhood, not just private choices. Research already showed that unequal power in couples and partner violence raise women's HIV risk, and that violent men more often carry the virus themselves.

Drawing on the idea of hegemonic masculinity, the authors describe a dominant ideal of black African manhood prizing toughness, control over women, and many sexual partners. The matching ideal of womanhood prizes compliance and tolerance, even of cheating and violence, often traded for material security. Women with the fewest resources can least afford to break these scripts. The authors urge prevention aimed at changing gender ideals, rather than only coaching single behaviors.
europmc-pmc2837394:
Penny and colleagues argued in 2010 that brain model comparisons should judge whole families of models, not crown a single winner. Researchers compare math models of brain data by their evidence scores, then usually discard all but the best. That habit turns brittle when hundreds of models compete or when each person's best model differs.

Grouping models into families that share one trait, such as serial versus parallel processing, lets the data answer the trait question directly. Averaging parameters across a family then gives estimates that no longer hinge on one exact wiring diagram. The team demonstrates both moves on dynamic causal models of speech brain imaging data, asking which regions receive input and which links a task adjusts.
europmc-pmc2853094:
Northover and colleagues reported in 2010 the thirteen-year follow-up of ACT I, the first British randomized trial of chemoradiation for anal cancer. The trial's 1996 results had already made combined chemotherapy and radiation the standard over radiation alone. This update tracked all five hundred seventy-seven randomized patients for relapses and deaths through 2007.

The benefit endured and grew clearer with time. For every hundred patients given chemoradiation, about twenty-five fewer suffered local relapse and about twelve fewer died of anal cancer by twelve years. An early bump in deaths from other causes faded away by year ten. Only eleven patients relapsed locally after year five, a fact the authors say should shape how future trials choose their endpoints.
europmc-pmc2871794:
Frank and co-authors mapped in 2010 the microbes living in the human nose. They asked how those microbes relate to carriage of Staphylococcus aureus. That germ can cause skin, blood, and heart infections. About half of healthy adults carry it in the nose at least sometimes, and carriage usually comes before infection. The team sampled five healthy adults over time plus hospital patients classed as carriers or non-carriers.

Healthy noses were dominated by skin-like bacteria, mainly two groups that thrive on the face and nostrils. Hospital patients' noses held far more staphylococci and far fewer of those usual residents, most sharply in one group. The pattern suggests the resident community helps keep the dangerous germ in check, and disturbing that community may open the door to carriage.
europmc-pmc2885494:
Harrison and co-authors traced in 2009 how body inflammation drags mood down, with a focus on a small brain area called the subgenual cingulate. This area is strongly linked to depression, and immune signals are known to spark low mood. Sixteen healthy men got a typhoid shot or salt water in a crossover study. They viewed faces with feelings during brain scans.

The shot raised markers of inflammation and made mood worse within hours. The size of the mood drop tracked shifts in the cingulate's activity while the men viewed the faces. Inflammation also changed how the cingulate linked with reward and emotion areas. A clear brain circuit thus carries the effect of body inflammation into mood.
europmc-pmc2912394:
Van der Meijden and colleagues discovered in 2010 a new human polyomavirus hiding in the skin lesions of a heart transplant patient. The patient had trichodysplasia spinulosa, a rare skin disease seen only in people with suppressed immunity, marked by spiny facial growths. Rolling-circle amplification, a technique that copies small circular DNA, recovered the full viral genome from plucked spines.

The genome spans a little over five thousand DNA letters in the family's usual layout, with early genes for replication control and late genes for the shell proteins. Its closest relative infects orangutans, and it sits a step further from the Merkel cell virus that causes a rare skin cancer. Finding the virus exactly in diseased skin makes it the prime suspect for the condition and adds a member to the human virus roster.
europmc-pmc2952094:
Yamagishi and Matsui reviewed how sugar-damaged proteins drive kidney disease in diabetes, in a 2010 article written as worldwide diabetes counts headed toward several hundred million people. Kidney failure from diabetes had become a leading cause of dialysis.

Compounds called advanced glycation end products form faster under high blood sugar and collect in tissues. Acting through their receptor, they spark oxidative stress that injures kidney filters over time. Tight sugar and pressure control help but fall short, so the authors present this product and receptor system as a target for new treatments that might halt progression.
europmc-pmc2957394:
Spurling and a team of colleagues reviewed studies on how drug company promotion affects doctors' prescribing in a 2010 systematic review. Companies spend a large share of revenue courting prescribers while claiming the contact also educates.

Across the gathered evidence, the team found no sign that exposure to company material made prescribing better. Instead, several studies linked greater exposure with prescribing more often. Others linked it with choosing costlier options, or prescribing less well. With industry spending so large, the authors argue the information channel deserves scepticism. It also deserves tighter separation from clinical education and from everyday prescribing habits.
europmc-pmc3003694:
Marim and co-authors established a way to grow macrophages, key immune cells, from frozen mouse bone marrow in a 2010 methods study. Genetically altered mice made such cells a workhorse, yet no one had shown they could come from stored marrow.

Their freezing protocol kept marrow able to yield macrophages for over six years. Cells from frozen stocks matched fresh ones in switching on activation markers after bacterial cues or infection. They also handled two live invaders, a bacterium and a parasite, just as fresh cells did. Early tests suggest dendritic cells can be raised the same way.
europmc-pmc3070694:
Tiemersma and colleagues estimated in 2011 how long untreated tuberculosis lasts and how often it kills, using studies from before effective drugs existed. Many patients worldwide still go undiagnosed, so the natural course of the disease remains a live question, and disease models need honest numbers for it. The team reviewed the old literature for patients without HIV, split by whether their sputum carried visible bacteria.

For the more infectious form, roughly seven in ten patients died within ten years across the old studies. For the less visible form, the estimate was about two in ten. From first illness to cure or death took about three years on average for both forms, a year longer than many models assumed. The authors say model builders should keep the fatality figures but stretch the timeline. The work also frames what treatment programs prevent.
europmc-pmc3078894:
Chablais, Veit, Rainer, and Jaźwińska created in 2011 a heart attack model in zebrafish. Unlike earlier fish models, it starts like a mammal heart attack yet ends in full repair. Freezing a spot on the fish heart killed about a fifth of the wall, mimicking the massive cell death of a human infarct. Simple cutting models used before did not reproduce that death pattern.

Early healing looked mammalian: clotting, scar building cells, and collagen laid down in the wound. Then the paths split. Fish heart muscle cells reentered the growth cycle and invaded the damaged zone, while scar tissue was dismantled cell by cell. Within two months the wall was new muscle and heart tracings showed normal function restored. A distinctive support protein marked the busy border zone. The model lets researchers hunt for what mammals lack.
europmc-pmc3100594:
Sutherland asked in 2011 a pointed question about a much studied cell enzyme: which of its nearly one hundred proposed targets does it truly act on inside living cells? The enzyme, GSK3 in short, is proposed to tag proteins in almost every tissue and process, and it is a tempting drug target in diabetes, brain disease, and cancer. Many proposed targets rest on test tube evidence that may not hold in the cell.

The paper audits the evidence target by target, separating those with strong in vivo support from those with only suggestive data. The confirmed set still spans core processes such as sugar storage, cell division, and gene control, so the enzyme's importance is not in doubt. The dispute is over its exact reach. Sutherland argues that drug developers need this honest map, because blocking the enzyme will touch every genuine target at once, wanted or not.
europmc-pmc3192794:
Marwan Baliki and colleagues found that each chronic pain condition reshapes the brain in its own pattern in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Chronic pain is usually treated as a state of altered activity, but lasting pain may also physically reorganise the brain. Structural scans compared patients with chronic back pain, a regional pain syndrome, and knee arthritis against healthy controls.

Only the back pain group showed changed whole-brain grey matter volume, while each condition carried a distinct regional pattern and its own large-scale network signature. A shared set of regions tracked how long pain had lasted across all groups. Combining the patterns into one index classified individual brains to their condition with high accuracy, and back pain reorganised the brain more slowly but more extensively than the regional syndrome.
europmc-pmc3197594:
Ana Negredo and colleagues discovered a new Ebola-like virus in dead bats in Spain in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The virus family includes some of the most lethal primate pathogens known, previously found naturally only in Africa and the Philippines. The bats, from a cave in Asturias, had died in a wider European die-off, and their organs showed signs of viral pneumonia.

Genetic screening of lung and spleen found sequences of a filovirus unlike any known, provisionally named for the cave. Bats carrying African family members stay healthy, so this virus's role in the die-off is suggestive rather than proven. The find extends the family's known range into Europe and raises fresh questions about bat reservoirs on the continent.
europmc-pmc3203094:
Yang Zhang and colleagues described a simpler way to prepare rice protoplasts in this 2011 paper in Plant Methods. Protoplasts are plant cells stripped of their walls, widely used to test gene function quickly. Rice protoplasts usually came from cultured cells or seedlings grown in darkness, which limits studies of light and chloroplasts.

Their method isolates protoplasts directly from normally grown young green rice leaves, without special chemicals or vacuum equipment. The cells took up plasmids of many sizes with strikingly high efficiency, including several plasmids at once. The team verified the system with protein blotting, localization, and interaction assays. Because the protoplasts stayed photosynthetically active, turning on one light-related gene raised the activity of several photosynthesis genes.
europmc-pmc3207894:
Chaokun Li and colleagues presented FastCloning, a simpler way to insert DNA into plasmids, in this 2011 paper in BMC Biotechnology. Molecular cloning is often slow and frustrating, relying on purification steps, kits, or special enzymes. Their method needs only standard PCR and a high-fidelity polymerase.

The vector and the insert are amplified separately in few cycles, with short overlapping ends designed into the primers. After an enzyme step destroys the original template DNA, the mixture goes straight into bacteria, with no gel purification and no ligation kit. Fewer cycles also mean fewer random mutations. The authors showed the method is reproducible and versatile, handling chimera construction, insertions, and multiple mutations across a stretch of DNA.
europmc-pmc3279294:
Preethi Srikanthan, Andrea Hevener, and Arun Karlamangla asked whether low muscle mass worsens the metabolic cost of obesity, in this 2010 analysis in PLoS ONE. Muscle loss, or sarcopenia, often accompanies obesity and could compound insulin resistance. Using a large United States health survey of more than fourteen thousand adults, they measured muscle by electrical impedance and related it to insulin resistance and blood sugar control.

Sarcopenia was tied to insulin resistance in both non-obese and obese people, independent of other factors. Among the obese, it was also tied to poorer blood sugar control, though not among the non-obese. The links ran strongest in people under sixty. Because the data are a snapshot, cause cannot be proven. Still, the authors suggest low muscle may be an early warning sign of diabetes risk. They urge work on preventing the sarcopenic-obese state.
europmc-pmc3302894:
Laroui and co-authors worked out how a chemical used to trigger gut inflammation in mice actually does its damage, in a 2012 study. The chemical, known as DSS, reliably causes colon inflammation resembling human bowel disease, yet it harms living tissue while leaving lab grown cells alone. None of its breakdown parts explained the effect, which deepened the puzzle.

The team found that DSS latches onto medium length fatty acids that are naturally present in the colon. Together they form tiny fat coated particles that can merge with the membranes of colon cells. Once inside, these particles appear to switch on inflammatory signals. Most harm falls on the far end of the colon, and the authors suggest reshaping the chemical to keep its targeting while removing the damage.
europmc-pmc3321794:
Grandadam and colleagues reported the first locally caught cases of chikungunya in mainland France, in a 2011 paper. Chikungunya is a mosquito carried virus that causes fever and severe joint pain, and it had been spreading to new regions worldwide. In September 2010, people in southeastern France who had not traveled caught the infection near home.

The tiger mosquito that carries the virus is established in that part of France, which made local spread possible. The team read the genomes of viruses from travelers who imported the infection and from the locally caught cases. Comparing them revealed fresh features relevant to how the virus might emerge and spread in Europe. The short report stands as an early warning that tropical mosquito diseases can take hold in temperate Europe.
europmc-pmc3365894:
Gronenschild and co-workers tested whether the computing setup itself changes brain measurements from FreeSurfer, the standard software for measuring cortical thickness and anatomical volumes. Using thirty MRI scans, they varied the software version, the workstation type, and the Macintosh operating system version, then compared the outputs.

The newest software version differed significantly from its two predecessors, shifting volume results by around nine percent on average and thickness results by a smaller margin. Changing workstation or operating system produced differences roughly half as large — comparable to effects reported in disease studies. The authors advise against upgrading software or switching machines mid-study without repeating the analysis.
europmc-pmc3383994:
Reijns led a team reporting in 2012 that mice cannot develop without RNase H2, an enzyme that trims stray RNA building blocks out of DNA. Such ribonucleotides slip into DNA easily and weaken it. In simple yeast the enzyme is optional, but in people faulty versions cause a brain inflammation disease.

Mouse embryos lacking the enzyme stalled from an early stage onward. Their cells carried over a million stray ribonucleotides each, and the damage switched on a p53-driven alarm response. The work crowns RNase H2 as a key guardian of the mammalian genome. It also shows these stray blocks are the most common internal DNA flaw in dividing cells.
europmc-pmc3418594:
Pearce and a large team followed British children and young adults in 2012 to measure cancer risk after CT scans. The scans are clinically valuable but expose patients to ionizing radiation, and children are more sensitive than adults. The cohort covered well over one hundred seventy thousand patients first scanned before age twenty-two, tracked through national registries.

Risk of leukemia and brain tumors rose with the radiation dose absorbed. At the higher cumulative doses seen in the study, the risks roughly tripled compared with the lowest-dose group. Because these cancers are rare, the absolute danger stayed small, about one extra case per ten thousand head scans in the first decade. Still, the authors urge keeping doses low and choosing radiation-free tests when suitable.
europmc-pmc3433794:
Peyrot, Barnett, Meneghini, and Schumm-Draeger surveyed insulin users and their doctors across eight countries in 2012 about sticking to insulin therapy. Over fifteen hundred patients and more than twelve hundred physicians answered. The study asked how often doses get skipped and why, and how well doctors think treatment is going.

A third of patients admitted skipping or missing insulin at least one day in the past month, averaging over three days. Doctors estimated worse adherence than patients confessed. The top reasons matched on both sides: being busy, travel, skipped meals, stress, and embarrassment in public. Most doctors said their patients lack adequate control and that fear of low blood sugar stops them pushing doses harder. Less restrictive regimens are needed, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc3464294:
Xu and colleagues tested whether cell stiffness can reveal how likely ovarian cancer cells are to spread, in a 2012 PLoS ONE study. Knowing which tumors will spread helps doctors plan treatment for each patient. The team pressed on single cells with an atomic force microscope, a tool that measures how much a cell gives under a tiny probe.

Cancer cells from the ovary proved softer than healthy ovarian surface cells, and their stiffness varied less. The most invasive line was softer still than its less invasive parent line. Xu's group linked the softening to changes in the actin skeleton that holds a cell's shape. They propose stiffness as a simple physical marker of spread risk.
europmc-pmc3478794:
Liana and co-authors reviewed the fast-growing field of paper-based sensors in Sensors in 2012. Paper wicks liquid on its own, costs little, and can be burned after use, making it attractive for cheap test devices. Such sensors target clinic diagnosis, food safety checks, and pollution monitoring, above all where labs are scarce.

The review covers how the devices are printed and patterned, how results are read, and where they are already used. Simple strip tests give yes-or-no answers, while newer designs steer fluids through shaped channels for exact readings. Liana's team admits accuracy and sensitivity still lag behind lab gear. They expect better printing and reading methods to close that gap and widen use.

fontane-effi-briest-1894:
Theodor Fontane published Effi Briest in 1894, a German novel about a young wife in Prussian society. Effi is seventeen when she marries Baron von Innstetten, a man twice her age. Life in a dull town bores her, and she drifts into a brief affair. Years later her husband finds old letters.

Honor, as his class defines it, forces Innstetten to act. A duel and a divorce destroy Effi's health and standing. Her own parents shut their doors to her for a time. Fontane tells the story with calm sympathy and no easy blame. Critics place the novel among the finest works of German realism.
fox-journal-1694: The Journal of George Fox, founder of the Quakers, published in 1694. It records his spiritual journey and the movement's early days. This edition preserves that foundational Quaker text. The paper lived through the years. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
freeman-pembroke-1894:
Mary Wilkins Freeman meant Pembroke as a study of the human will gone diseased, she says in a sketch up front. The Harper printing scanned here dates from 1894. Barnabas Thayer stands as the strongest case of that bent will, drawn from life.

Barnabas can bend at last only through purer, selfless love for Charlotte Barnard. Deborah Thayer, Richard Alger, and Cephas Barnard show the same sickness in other forms. In the tale, a proud father clashes with his son over love, and a family breaks on his hard will. Darker than her famed stories, the novel builds a full tragedy from village flint.
frus-1861-d194:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 May 1861. The dispatch is document 194 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton's May letter reports a Russia that wished the Union well. The czar's court had freed its serfs that spring and felt kinship with Lincoln's stand. His dispatch gave Washington rare good news in a season of European doubt. The serf edict of March 1861 gave Lincoln's cause a warm echo in Russian talk. A warm echo from Russia was one of the few cheers of that grim spring.
frus-1861-d294:
In a letter dated 17 August 1861, William H. Seward gave Mr. Harvey his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 294 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d94:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 4 October 1861. Lyons was the British minister in Washington. The letter is document 94 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Lyons was the man Seward had to face across the table at home. Their letters dealt with the friction of war at sea: searches, seizures, and the rights of British trade. This October note shows that friction handled in formal, careful terms. Lyons and Seward met often in person, and their notes kept the formal record straight. Formal notes gave their talks a spine that mere chat could never supply.
frus-1862-d194:
Document 194 opens the Washington end of the British file: a note dated 3 December 1861 from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

December 1861 was the month of the Trent crisis, after a Union warship took two Confederate envoys off a British mail ship. War between Britain and the Union felt close. Notes between Seward and Lyons in those weeks carried the weight of that danger. Both men worked the problem in the same city, face to face. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d294:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed William L. Dayton in Paris on 10 July 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 294 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was the first Seward letter in the July run.

Seward wrote with the Richmond campaign lost and Northern morale shaken. His letters abroad in July had a repair job to do: present the retreat as a change of base, not a collapse. Dayton received this guidance as French interest in mediation grew. The letter is part of the administration's effort to manage the story of a bad month. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d394:
Bayard Taylor, of the American legation in St. Petersburg, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 October 1862. His letter closes the Russian file in this run as Document 394 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Taylor, a well-known travel writer serving as legation secretary, took up the post's pen after Simon Cameron's departure that fall. His October letter reached Washington as the European truce scheme was failing. It ends the file with the Russian channel in careful hands, its friendly tone unbroken through a hard year. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d494:
James Shepherd Pike reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward from The Hague on 9 April 1862. The dispatch is Document 494 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Pike wrote in the first shock of the Shiloh news reaching Europe, when casualty lists made the war look endless to foreign eyes. Dutch opinion, commercial to its core, asked how long American trade could bear the strain. His report gave Washington an honest reading of that doubt. Such candor was Pike's habit and his value. Seward could trust the Hague letters. They told him what the Dutch really thought, not what a minister wished they thought.
frus-1862-d594:
In Mexico City, Thomas Corwin received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 July 1862. The instruction is Document 594 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Seward wrote in the aftermath of the Seven Days. The Union's own position had darkened. Its protests over Mexico carried less weight in Paris. His instruction still held the established line: friendship for the republic, disapproval of the French enterprise, and prudence above all. Corwin needed that steadiness from home, since events in Mexico invited bolder gestures than Washington could back. The letter shows two governments' crises interlocked, each limiting what the other could do.
frus-1862-d694: William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to a Mr. McMath on 1 July 1862. The letter is document 694 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the second of his letters to McMath in the file. The evidence names the two men and the date but gives no post for McMath and no topic for the letter.
frus-1862-d94:
In a letter dated 9 July 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 94 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d194:
A dispatch dated 8 May 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 194 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d294:
Reporting on 18 September 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 294 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d394:
On 18 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 394 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war. Each side kept copies of the whole exchange, which is why the printed volume can show the argument from both desks.
frus-1863p1-d494:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 7 May 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d594:
On 23 July 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d694:
Lord Lyons sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 November 1863. It is document 694 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington and a key figure in wartime ties between the two nations.

Late November found the exchange still active and still tense in spots. British merchants, ship owners, and officials all had stakes in how the Union ran its war at sea. Lyons put their case to Seward in formal terms. The letter helps a reader hear the British voice in the record. It is not just the American one, near the close of a long year of notes.
frus-1863p1-d94:
On 26 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 94 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of a set often took the longer view: not one talk, but the drift of things. Adams wrote that way when the day's news allowed it. This letter is the middle of his 26 February three. With the Seward letter of the same date set nearby in the volume, the day shows both capitals writing hard. They wrote on the same war, an ocean apart.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d194:
Ambassador Averell Harriman cabled President Roosevelt from Moscow on 6 November 1943 about delivering Roosevelt's message on Turkey to Soviet foreign minister Molotov. Harriman handed it over in person, in the form of a letter, and reports that Molotov was highly pleased with it.

Molotov raised no objection to the safeguard clause in the message. He proposed that the American agreement be attached to the Turkey protocol he and Eden had signed, and that both papers become part of the conference's most secret military record. Harriman explains that Molotov faced gripes from Soviet military men for winning no action on Turkey at the conference, and he asks leave to accept.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d294:
A long secret summary went from Secretary of State Cordell Hull in Washington to President Roosevelt on 23 November 1943, as the Soviet army neared the Polish frontier. Poland's government in exile was growing frantic about its country's future, and Hull passes on the main points of its appeals.

The Polish premier's memorandum of 18 November begs Roosevelt to intervene with Stalin to restore Polish-Soviet relations and protect Polish life and property once Soviet troops enter. Poland refuses even to discuss giving up her eastern lands, which make up half her territory, and calls any vote held under Soviet occupation worthless. East Prussia, Danzig, and Silesia, the Poles argue, are needed for a stable peace and cannot count as fair payment for the east.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d394: The entry under this title is Roosevelt's own sketch of his concept for the United Nations organization, preserved in the Hopkins Papers and undated. The printed entry gives the editors' description of the drawing, since the sketch itself is a diagram of circles. The words inside the circles read: forty United Nations, Executive Committee, and Four Policemen. Below one circle stand the words International Labor Organization, Health, Agriculture, and Food. A later file note marks the sheet as Tehran miscellaneous.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d494:
The Shah of Iran wrote to President Roosevelt on December 6, 1943, a few days after the Tehran Conference ended in his capital. The young Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, had hosted Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin, and the three powers had signed a declaration pledging respect for Iran's independence. His letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Iran was occupied by Allied forces guarding the supply route to Russia, so its young ruler had much at stake in the leaders' goodwill. A letter from the Shah to Roosevelt shows a small, occupied country speaking directly to a superpower's president. It adds the host nation's voice to a record usually dominated by the Big Three.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d94: Ambassador Harriman wrote to Roosevelt from Moscow on November 4, 1943, days after the foreign ministers' conference ended in his host capital. The dispatch is Document 94 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Harriman's Moscow letters gave the president a direct reading of Soviet moods before Tehran. The record gives the date and the names and no topic. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d194:
At 10 a.m. on September 15, 1944, the Combined Chiefs cleaned up their record and closed the conference's business. Amendments to the previous meeting's minutes fixed small errors and one large planning assumption. For production and manpower planning, the date for the end of the war against Japan was set at eighteen months after Germany's defeat, adjustable as the war developed.

The chiefs then approved their final report to Roosevelt and Churchill, as amended in discussion. They also shaped the messages announcing Octagon's results. A paragraph on transferring power to the Pacific after Germany's collapse was added to the letter for Stalin. For Chiang Kai-shek, a sentence promised agreed operations to intensify the offensive, including opening a seaway into China.
frus-1944-quebec-d294: On 17 September 1944 the secretary of state wrote to President Roosevelt, one day after the second Quebec Conference had ended. The message is document 294 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering that meeting, issued by the Department of State. It preserves one piece of the follow-up correspondence between Washington and the president in the conference's immediate aftermath.
frus-1944-quebec-d94:
George Elsey prepared a memorandum dated September 8, 1944. Elsey assisted the President's naval aide at the White House. His paper appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It belongs to the final week of conference preparation.

Junior staff papers often preserve how decisions were arranged. Elsey worked close to the President's daily military briefings. A memorandum from his desk records staff-level handling of summit business. For readers, it shows the White House machine from inside. Young aides kept papers moving while senior men argued policy. Their notes help historians rebuild the conference's preparation.
frus-1945-50-intel-d194:
A text titled "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 9" bears the date 18 April 1947. Readers meet it as document 194 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

Directives were the rule books of the new system. A short one could fix the duties of a whole office. Directives set who may do what, what must be reported, and which office has the final say. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d294:
Dated 30 June 1948, this memorandum runs from the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). It stands as document 294 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d394:
Roscoe Hillenkoetter, the first Director of Central Intelligence, wrote to Secretary of State Dean Acheson on 19 August 1949. The letter appears as document 394 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Hillenkoetter led a young agency that had to prove its worth to older departments. Writing straight to the Secretary of State put the CIA's views before the man who ran American foreign policy. Short as it is, the letter shows the new intelligence chief dealing with the cabinet on equal terms. Papers of this rank were rare enough that each one carried weight beyond its length.
frus-1945-50-intel-d94:
Peurifoy, acting assistant secretary for administration, wrote to both Under Secretary Acheson and Secretary of State George Marshall on 31 January 1947. Marshall had held the secretary's chair for only days. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A paper addressed to both the under secretary and a brand-new secretary of state catches a department in transition at the top. Byrnes had gone; Marshall, the wartime Army chief, now ran State. The administration's business, intelligence included, had to be laid before the new chief in order. Readers should note the date's place in the larger story: within months, the National Security Act would remake the central system again. Papers like this one readied the ground.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d194:
Should France, Belgium, and Holland be rearmed at once? James Dunn put the British question to Under Secretary Stettinius on 10 November 1944. This excerpt from his “Preparation for Big Three Meeting” paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

London's embassy had asked the American view. New arms would let those countries' troops share in occupying Germany. They would also fit Britain's idea of a defensive grouping of itself with the states of Western Europe. The Joint Chiefs, asked for a purely military judgment, favor the rearming. Under the British plan, London would arm the Dutch and Belgians. The United States would arm the French, to the tune of eight to twelve divisions, all with fresh equipment.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d294:
When would the German war end? The British chiefs reviewed the planning date on 30 January 1945 in paper C. C. S. 772, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Their review leans on the latest study by the Joint Intelligence Subcommittee.

One path runs fast. If the Russians overrun Germany's eastern defences before they can be consolidated, the Germans must strip the west to reply. Allied advances on both sides might then force a collapse before mid-April 1945. On balance, though, the paper expects distance and stiffening resistance to halt the Russians near the line of Landsberg and the Giant Mountains. Industrial Silesia would be lost in that case. Its loss would cut finished armaments output, mainly land armaments, by a quarter or more within about six months.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d394:
Complete success, Roosevelt declared, as the plenary opened on February 8, 1945, and Bohlen's minutes follow the report. The President congratulated the foreign secretaries on their work and called on Eden to read their findings. Four subjects frame the session: the world security body, Poland, regular meetings of foreign ministers, and Yugoslavia and Greece.

Eden read the ministers' report on the world organization. It covered seats for two or three Soviet republics among the first members. It also covered which states to invite to the United Nations conference, and when and where to hold it. The bargain that created the United Nations enters the record here.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d494:
No basic quarrel divides us on Italy, Roosevelt assured Churchill in this letter of February 11, 1945. Churchill had voiced concern about their differing views on Italian policy. Roosevelt replied that Matthews, for the State Department, had gone over the ground with Alec Cadogan the day before. Differences in emphasis remained, as was natural.

But both men, Roosevelt wrote, agreed on the important fact. Whatever Italy's past attitude and actions, the allies faced a real problem of the future. Italy was and would remain an important factor in Europe. The letter, sent on the conference's last day, smooths a friction the formal record barely mentions.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d94:
Which choices would the Security Council actually vote on? A briefing book paper dated 15 January 1945 lists them, class by class. It was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Under the President's formula, every listed decision needs seven yes votes, including the permanent members. The sole break: a permanent member party to a dispute casts no vote on peaceful settlement steps. The classes begin with advice to the General Assembly on admitting, suspending, or expelling members and choosing the Secretary General. They run on through restoring a suspended member's rights, and then to the work of settling disputes without force.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d194:
Acting Secretary Grew gave London a guarded answer on war criminals in a letter dated July 7, 1945. The letter to Ambassador Halifax is document 194 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Halifax had proposed on June 29 that the heads of government discuss war criminals at their meeting.

The question is being given careful consideration by the American government, Grew replies. Much will depend, he says, on the discussions then taking place in London among British, American, French, and Soviet representatives. Those were the talks drafting the charter for trying the top Nazi leaders. The brief letter neither accepts nor refuses the British proposal; it keeps Washington's hands free while Justice Jackson's hard negotiations in London ran their course.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d294:
Washington sent Ambassador Harriman in Moscow a draft plan on June 23, 1945, for running the Allied Control Commission in Hungary in the armistice's second period. The Acting Secretary of State asked for his comments on the points. They were drawn from a draft by General Key, the American military chief in Hungary.

The draft would limit the commission to policing the armistice terms. A Soviet chairman would lead it, with the British and American mission chiefs as vice-chairmen, plus staff and a chief of staff. The cable shows Washington trying to write fair rules for a body the Soviets in practice ran alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d394:
Punishment of war criminals is laid out in a briefing book paper that traces the plan's short history. After first talks with the British in London in April 1945, Judge Rosenman, acting as President Truman's personal representative, presented a draft agreement at San Francisco in early May. The British, French, and Soviet representatives received the American plan there.

The draft rested on an earlier report to President Roosevelt by the Secretaries of State and War and the Attorney General. The Moscow Declaration of November 1, 1943, shaped its approach. European Axis criminals proven to have joined in specific atrocities would be returned to the lands where their crimes were committed. There they would be judged.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d494:
Bierut's attitude toward the old government's debts appears in an extract of Harriman's cable from Moscow of June 30, 1945. In their talk of June 25, Harriman reports, Bierut did not raise the constitutional question over the legality of the pre-war government's obligations. He did say he wished to scrutinize the transactions of the government in exile.

His purpose, Bierut explained, was to satisfy himself that those transactions were undertaken in the interests of the Polish state. That seemed a reasonable attitude to Harriman, given the controversies between the two Polish groups. Bierut and all the Poles, he adds, show the keenest desire to obtain, at the earliest moment, the Polish state's assets abroad and American economic help.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d594:
A United States delegation working paper holds a draft proclamation to Japan by the Allied heads of state. Undated but filed July 1, 1945, it is document 594 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The draft had won approval from the Secretaries of War and the Navy and the Acting Secretary of State.

The draft speaks in the names of the U.S. President, the British prime minister, and China's president. Bracketed lines would add the Soviet leader if his country joined the war. It offers Japan's people a chance to end the war on the terms stated. It points to the vast land, sea, and air forces poised to strike the final blows. It also holds up Germany's futile resistance as an awful example of what Japan faces.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d694:
Ambassador Wilson sent his own reflections on the Soviet-Turkish clash from Ankara on July 2, 1945. The urgent top secret wire is document 694 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Wilson reads Molotov's demands as an opening move, not a local quarrel.

First, he argues, the campaign runs on a broad front far beyond Turkey. Molotov's hint that Moscow might voice Balkan views points to the whole Balkan question. He cites a Bulgarian bid for an Aegean outlet and radio attacks on Greece's government. Second, the claim to Kars and Ardahan must be taken seriously. It is a matter of prestige to recover what the Czarist regime once held, and the lands guard the approaches to northern Iran. Third, he probes what Black Sea security would truly require of the Straits regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d94:
Ambassador Harriman sent Admiral Leahy a two-line answer from Moscow on June 24, 1945. The telegram is document 94 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Leahy had asked, on behalf of General Marshall and Harry Hopkins, how Stalin would take the American Chiefs of Staff traveling to Berlin with the President.

Molotov had consulted Stalin the night before, Harriman reports, and Stalin had no objection whatsoever to the President bringing his chiefs with him. The short cable closed a question Washington had worried over for days, since some officials feared the military gathering might alarm Stalin or send the wrong signal to Japan. The chiefs could now plan to attend.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1094: Edwin Pauley cabled Washington from Babelsberg on July 17, 1945, asking for material on Italian reparations. A staff officer named Reinstein was preparing a study of possible Italian reparations and restitutions. Pauley wants its outstanding features cabled to him at conference headquarters at once. He asks special stress on what Italy might have available for reparations, and what it could be worth. He also wants official estimates of the imports Italy will need to keep her economy running over the coming year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1194: Bissell, who ran the ship requirements desk of the War Shipping Administration, wrote inside his own agency on 22 July 1945. His desk counted hulls: how many ships the war effort needed, and where they had to be. Notes from that desk guided where merchant ships were sent. Fleets and armies moved on its sums.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1294:
The Acting Secretary of State set down this memorandum on 23 July 1945. Grew ran the department in Washington while the chief sat at Potsdam. His memoranda fixed the home office's views in the middle of the summit's second week.

A note from the acting chief could settle a desk dispute, record a decision, or frame a question for the team abroad. This one belongs to that daily staff work. It is the Washington end of the department thinking on paper, at a moment when half its mind was in Germany. The record keeps it among the summit's own papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1394:
A memorandum by Mikołajczyk dated 1 August 1945 closes his run of papers in the volume. It was written on the day the Potsdam Protocol was signed. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Ending the run with a formal memorandum, after days of diary pages, returns Mikołajczyk to his public role. The settlement of Poland was now a fact on paper, and his task turned from pleading to recording his position for the future. Readers who have followed the whole run hold a rare thing. Five memoranda and four diary entries give a near-daily account of a great settlement, from the side that lost most by it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-94:
Benjamin Cohen, a senior State Department lawyer and adviser, took these notes at Potsdam on July 24, 1945. Cohen's notes form one of the parallel American records of the conference. He sat in on talks where exact wording could shape a border or a payment. His pages were printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official Foreign Relations series.

Cohen wrote as a lawyer writes: close to the words used. His notes often catch the sense of a phrase that formal minutes smooth over. For readers, that makes them a sharp check on the official record. They show how much care went into each line agreed at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d794:
Reber wrote to Matthews, the director of European affairs, on July 16, 1945, in document 794. The special assistant reported to his own chief on the eve of the Potsdam Conference. Their office owned the Department's Europe files. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

An eve-of-summit letter inside an office shows final alignment. Reber could flag last facts before the leaders met. Readers see the Department's Europe team closing ranks. The document pairs the home staff with the traveling team: both worked the same files that week. It marks the quiet start of the volume's busiest fortnight.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d894:
The United States delegation put the paper on German reparations before the Potsdam Conference on July 17, 1945. It reports what the Allied Commission on Reparations had settled and what it had not. Seven basic principles stand agreed. One clause of an eighth principle remains in dispute.

The disputed clause says imports approved by the governments should be paid before reparation deliveries from current goods and stocks. America insists such imports must rank as a first charge on German exports. The paper also urges quick agreement on definitions of restitution, war booty, and reparations. It says the definitions and the sharing formula must be settled together.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d994:
Covey Oliver cabled Emilio Collado on July 25, 1945, with news that the Madrid embassy had jumped the gun. It had already joined the British in formally telling Spain that the powers occupying Germany claim title to or control of German-owned assets. Spain was asked to take no step that clashes with that control.

Oliver notes this wording marks the limit of British agreement for now. London will not name the Control Council as the source of authority. France had grudgingly consented to joint warnings before Madrid acted. Washington has now told its missions in Stockholm, Bern, Lisbon, and Ankara to take like steps, though Ankara must await British consent.
frus-1961-63v04-d294: A 1961-1963 FRUS telegram from the Vietnam volume, August to December 1963. The Diem regime fell. This entry holds that cable. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
gao-gaoreports-b-296094: Mathews Associates took its May 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296294: Kesser International took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296394: Vador Ventures doubled its August 2005 protest — the second round — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer each, and the record stays clean. The record stayed clean.
gao-gaoreports-b-297294: Shaw Environmental took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297994: Client Network Services took its April 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298694: Kellogg Brown & Root tripled its November 2006 protest — three case numbers, one services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one thorough answer. Three dockets, one thorough answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-305494: Chemical weapons demilitarization funds got a fiscal ruling in this March 2006 GAO call, which tests the obligation of the funds. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the dollars could legally move. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310794: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by S4, Inc. The February 12, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-194: FHA's new mortgage products needed risk controls in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were required to manage the dangers. The review writes the warning. The homebuyers deserved the safeguards. The risks had to be managed. The homebuyers deserved the safeguards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-294: Large pension plans' funding weaknesses got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says recent experiences illustrated the rules' flaws. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the retirees deserved sound funding. The weaknesses had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-394: Maritime intel sharing was better in 2005, and GAO's report says new structures improved the flow, though clearance processing needed more. The review credits the progress while flagging the backlog. The ports' information deserved the speed. The processing had to improve.
