gao-gaoreports-gao-06-294: Country grant numbers needed checking in 2006, and GAO's report says the funding figures had to be proven true. The findings demand the proof. The report warns that the rural dollars deserved honest counts. The counts had to be true. The rural dollars deserved honest counts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-494: Wounded soldiers were drowning in military debt in 2006, and GAO's report says hundreds of battle-injured troops struggled to resolve the debts. The findings expose the cruelty. The report warns that the injured should not fight paperwork too. The debts had to be resolved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-594: NOAA's buying shop needed strengthening in 2006, and GAO's report lays out next steps for its acquisition function. The findings prescribe the path. The report warns that the weather agency's shopping needed discipline. The function had to be strengthened. The weather agency's shopping needed discipline.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-894: The State Department could not find enough linguists in 2006, and GAO's report says staffing and foreign language shortfalls persisted despite the fixes. The findings count the gaps. The report warns that diplomacy in other tongues needed speakers. The shortfalls had to be filled.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-94: Energy cost-saving alternatives needed better planning in 2005, and GAO's report says improved guidance, oversight, and planning were required. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the department's dollars deserved smart saving. The planning had to improve. The department's dollars deserved smart saving.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1094: Four agencies were piping money to rural water projects in 2007 — and tripping over each other. GAO's report maps the overlapping taps for small-town water and sewer aid. The findings make the case for joining forces: one thirsty town should not need four federal pen pals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-594: Veterans hunting jobs got thin data in 2007 — GAO's report says Labor could do better tracking reemployment help and results for former troops. The findings demand real numbers on who got hired. The report's premise: you cannot fix what you do not count.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-94: Freight railroads were healthier but still worrisome in 2007, and GAO's report says the industry had improved, though competition and capacity concerns remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the boxcars' business needed watching. The rails' rivals needed refereeing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-294: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at best Practices: Increased Focus on Requirements and Oversight Needed to Improve DOD's Acquisition Environment and Weapon System Quality. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-594: The Government Accountability Office dug into offshore Marine Aquaculture: Multiple Administrative and Environmental Issues Need to Be Addressed in Establishing a US Regulatory Framework in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-94: In 2007, the Government Accountability Office published this report on bankruptcy: Implementation of Reform Act's Debt Reaffirmation Agreement Provisions. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
godwin-caleb-williams-1794: Caleb Williams, William Godwin's 1794 novel. The pursued servant. This book preserves that radical classic. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
harnack-history-dogma-vol-1-1894:
Adolf von Harnack's History of Dogma, Volume 1, appears in Neil Buchanan's translation of 1894. Harnack traces how Christian teaching became dogma in the early church. Dogma, in his famous thesis, is the gospel reshaped by the Greek spirit. Creeds and councils of the first centuries receive deep study.

He follows the Apologists, Origen, and the road to Nicaea. The work is a monument of church history in scale and learning. Protestant and Catholic scholars alike must answer its claims. Harnack's liberal reading shapes the narrative throughout. Volume 1 of seven lays the foundation. It remains essential for students of early Christian thought.
hegel-philosophy-mind-wallace-1894:
Part three of Hegel's Encyclopaedia turns from logic and nature to mind, or spirit. William Wallace translated that part into English in 1894. The German text reached its full form in the 1830 edition of the system. Hegel treats mind as the truth toward which nature was heading.

His account climbs three levels, named subjective, objective, and absolute spirit. The first covers soul, awareness, and the free mind of a person. The second covers law, morals, family, and the state. The third reaches art, religion, and philosophy itself. Wallace's version long served as the standard English text. It completes the Encyclopaedia in English dress.
hipparchus-commentary-aratus-manitius-18:
Hipparchus of Nicaea, who worked in the second century BCE, was the greatest astronomer of the ancient world. He found the slow shift called the precession of the equinoxes and built the first star catalogue. His commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus is his only work that survives whole. Karl Manitius edited the Greek text in 1894, with a German version.

Aratus had turned the star lore of Eudoxus into a poem, and Hipparchus checks its claims star by star against his own measures. The tone is dry and exact, a scientist correcting a poet. No English version in the public domain exists. The edition stands here as the record of Greek astronomy at its peak.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r: Gibbon's fifth volume in this edition follows Byzantium's thousand-year struggle: the Arab conquests, the Crusades, emperors and scholars holding the line at Constantinople. The history widens into a panorama of the medieval world. Gibbon's learning and irony sustain one of literature's great long narratives.
hobson-evolution-modern-capitalism-1894:
Hobson's first major book, The Evolution of Modern Capitalism, came out in 1894. He studies how machine production remade industry and labor. Great factories and joint stock companies crowd out small masters in his account. Workers face displacement as machines take over task after task.

The book founded Hobson's underconsumptionist economics, his lifelong theme. Markets, he argues, fail when wages lag behind what industry produces. That failure drives slumps, empire, and reform alike in his later work. Here the theme appears in fresh, early form. Historians of economics treat the study as a founding text. Its survey of industrial change still reads well.
hunter-blood-inflammation-1794:
John Hunter's Treatise on the Blood, Inflammation, and Gun-shot Wounds appeared in 1794, after his death. Friends published the work he had built over a lifetime of practice. Hunter studied how blood behaves in health and in injury. Inflammation, the body's response to harm, stands at the center of his account.

He applies that physiology directly to surgery, above all to gunshot wounds. When to cut, when to wait, and how wounds heal guide his rules. The book founded scientific surgery on observed fact rather than habit. Its first edition holds his mature system entire. Surgeons read it as a charter. The plain, hard won tone commands respect.
huxley-evolution-ethics-1894:
Late in life, Thomas Henry Huxley turned from defending evolution to asking what it means for how we should live. Evolution and Ethics, from 1894, centers on his Romanes Lecture of 1893. Companion essays round out the volume.

Huxley argues that nature's struggle is not a guide for human conduct. Society, he says, grows by checking selfish instincts, not copying them. The claim split him from friends who read morals straight out of evolution. The lecture remains a key text in debates about nature, ethics, and progress. The other essays return to his long fight for honest, open inquiry.
illuminatus-dirigens-1794:
Illuminatus Dirigens, oder Schottischer Ritter preserves the working of a high grade of the Illuminati. The German text was printed in 1794 as a companion to the latest works of Spartacus and Philo. It passed the Munich censors in February of that year. Few inner rites of the order ever reached print at all.

Inside are the rite's speeches, signs, duties, and lessons for men raised to the Scottish Knight grade. One quoted rule is blunt: a man fit for nothing better stays a Scottish Knight. The print lets readers see how the order trained and tested its senior men. Scholars value it as rare proof of how the higher grades worked.
jacobs-more-celtic-fairy-tales-1894:
Joseph Jacobs made this mate to his Celtic Fairy Tales two years on, in 1894. The first set had won a wide public, and more tales lay to hand. He retold them in the same plain, brisk style as the first. Jacobs held that a folk tale should be told as the folk tell it, with no stiff book words in the way.

Sea maids and water spirits run through this set, as they did through the first. The tales come from Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, the old Celtic lands of the west. With its mate, the set forms the main Victorian hoard of Celtic tales in English.
jay-treaty-1794:
John Jay negotiated the 1794 treaty with Great Britain to settle quarrels left over from the Revolutionary War. Britain still held forts on the northwestern frontier and owed payment for enslaved people carried away at the war's end. Trade disputes and the search of American ships had pushed the two nations close to war again.

Under the terms, British troops would leave the frontier forts, trade would resume, and old debts would go to joint panels for settlement. Many Americans hated the concessions, and the treaty split the young republic's politics for years. President Washington backed it anyway, buying peace while the fragile nation grew stronger.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michelson-alber:
Albert A. Michelson, born at Strelno in Prussia on December 19, 1852, became an American physicist of world standing, as Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly record in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father emigrated and settled in San Francisco, where Albert was schooled. He graduated from the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis in 1873.

Michelson resigned from the navy after study at Berlin, Heidelberg, and Paris, and took the physics chair at the Case School in Cleveland. He moved to Clark University in 1889 and, three years later, to the University of Chicago, where he still taught when the article appeared. Honorary degrees from Cambridge and Yale and membership in the Royal Society mark his reputation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mizrahi-10894:
Mizraḥi — the name simply means an Oriental — belongs to a family of rabbinical authors in the East, with branches at Constantinople and Jerusalem, as the Jewish Encyclopedia records in 1906. Persian Jews settled in Turkey often took it as a surname. The entry strings together the family's scholars across four centuries.

Abraham ben Baruch Mizraḥi was a ritual slaughterer at Jerusalem in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and wrote a handbook on the slaughtering laws, printed at Amsterdam in 1718. Absalom ben Moses Mizraḥi, three centuries earlier, wrote Imre Shefer, a work on Hebrew poetic form composed in 1391 and quoted by Abraham de Balmes. Carmoly printed it at Paris in 1841 from a manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ja:
Mordecai ben Jacob, known as Mordecai Singer, was a Polish translator who lived at Cracow and died in 1575, as the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and S. J. Levinson note in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His work was rendering Scripture into Judæo-German, the vernacular of Ashkenazic Jewry. Two books of his survive.

He translated the Book of Proverbs, printed at Cracow in 1582, and the Book of Job, printed at Prague in 1597 — both appearing after his death, if the dates hold. To each he supplied a commentary in Hebrew, so the volumes taught two languages at once: the text in the vernacular, the learning in the holy tongue. Steinschneider's catalogue is the entry's chief witness.
kipling-jungle-book-1894:
Rudyard Kipling published The Jungle Book in 1894, a set of stories about Mowgli, a boy raised by wolves in India. Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther teach him the Law of the Jungle. Shere Khan, the tiger, waits for a chance to kill him. Other tales in the book feature a mongoose, seals, and army animals.

Mowgli must learn when to trust the jungle and when to return to men. Songs and poems stand between the stories. Kipling writes with pace, humor, and respect for animal life. The tales have delighted children for generations. They also carry sharp lessons about law, courage, and belonging.
kroll-de-oraculis-chaldaicis-1894:
Wilhelm Kroll published his critical edition of the Chaldean Oracles in 1894, in Latin. The Oracles are cryptic Greek verses that guided Platonist philosophers of late antiquity. Only fragments survive, quoted inside later philosophical works.

Kroll collected every fragment he could find and arranged them in order. His numbering of the fragments remains the standard that researchers cite today. Greek text and scholarly apparatus serve specialists rather than casual readers. The Oracles themselves speak of fire, the soul, and ascent to the divine. Kroll's cornerstone edition made serious Neoplatonic studies possible. Every later translation of the Oracles builds on his foundation.
lockyer-dawn-of-astronomy-1894:
J. Norman Lockyer read old shrines by the stars in The Dawn of Astronomy, his bold book of 1894. Lockyer was a chief of star lore in Britain. In Egypt he found that shrines point to star rise and sun rise on set days. Those points shift slow with the ages, so a shrine's aim can give its date.

That trick gave the dig a new clock. It also tied the faith of the pharaohs to the sky they watched. Lockyer's book founds the study now called the lore of stars and stones. Its claims still get weighed.
machen-great-god-pan-1894:
Arthur Machen let loose an old god on modern London in The Great God Pan of 1894. A brain operation lifts the veil for a young woman, and what she sees unmakes her mind. Years later a trail of vice and death in the city leads back to that room.

Helen Vaughan, the tale's dark heart, moves through London leaving ruin and horror in her wake. Machen hints more than he shows, and the hints chill the blood. Lovecraft ranked the novella among the finest weird tales ever made. It is the most cited horror text of the Victorian mythos line.
marlowe-dido-1594:
Christopher Marlowe wrote Dido, Queen of Carthage early in his career, likely while still at Cambridge. The play was performed by a company of boy actors and printed in 1594, after Marlowe's death. It retells a famous episode from Virgil's Aeneid.

Aeneas, shipwrecked on his way from fallen Troy, is welcomed by Queen Dido of Carthage. The gods engineer their love, and Aeneas delays his mission to found Rome. When duty calls him away, Dido's grief turns to despair and a famous death. Marlowe's verse is already musical and grand, though gentler here than in his later tragedies of ambition.
marlowe-edward-ii-1594:
Christopher Marlowe wrote Edward II in the last years of his life, turning English chronicle history into tragedy. The play was printed in 1594, the year after his death. It covers the reign and fall of King Edward II in the early 1300s.

Edward showers favor on his beloved Gaveston, enraging his barons and his queen. Civil war follows, Gaveston is killed, and new favorites rise in his place. The queen and her lover Mortimer seize power and imprison the king. Marlowe treats Edward with growing pity as cruelty closes in. Many consider it his most humane and tightly built tragedy.
maspero-dawn-of-civilization-1894:
Gaston Maspero told the birth of the old East in The Dawn of Civilization, in English from 1894. Maspero was a chief of Egypt's study in France and ran its site guard. M. L. McClure turned his French tale to English. Egypt and Chaldaea share this first tome of his three tome past of the old world.

Land, folk, faith, and the first kings fill its sweep. Maspero writes with a tale smith's grace. His set was the main tale of its crop. This tome is its dawn in both name and theme.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s: This volume of the St. Cloud letters continues the imperial portrait. Napoleon's proud marshals and ministers parade through the pages. Hot ambition hums beneath the stiff ceremony. The machinery of empire laid bare for all to see.
mineralogische-chemische-und-alchymistis: Mineralogische, chemische und alchymistische Briefe, 1794. The mineral letters. This book preserves that collection. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
nansen-eskimo-life-1894:
Nansen wrote Eskimo Life after his crossing of Greenland in 1888 and 1889, when he wintered among the Greenland Inuit. The 1894 English edition shares his study of their life. Before the ski crossing, almost no European knew this coast well.

He describes kayaks, hunting, dress, food, family life, and tales told in winter houses. Nansen admires Inuit skill and kindness, and he attacks the harm done by trade and missions. His respect for his hosts was unusual for the age. The book is a founding work of modern writing on the peoples of the far north. His chapters on child-raising praise patience he rarely saw matched at home.
nashe-unfortunate-traveller-1594:
Thomas Nashe published The Unfortunate Traveller in 1594, and Edmund Gosse later edited the text found here. Nashe was the sharpest prose stylist among the Elizabethan pamphleteers. His hero, Jack Wilton, is a page who follows courts and armies across Europe.

Jack survives battles, plagues, executions, and rogues from Henry VIII's France to Italy's wicked cities. The tale veers from farce to horror in a page, in prose of amazing speed and color. Scholars call it the first English picaresque novel, a rogue's progress before the novel had a name. Its violence and wit still startle readers used to tamer Elizabethan prose.
neuesten-arbeiten-spartacus-philo-1794:
Printed in 1794, Die neuesten Arbeiten des Spartacus und Philo gathers later writings tied to the two heads of the Illuminati. Spartacus was the order name of founder Adam Weishaupt. Philo was Adolph von Knigge, the man who built the order up. The texts came from papers seized by the Bavarian state.

The editors present the higher grades as a warning, not a treat for the curious. Their foreword says the plans in these pages put peoples and princes at risk alike. Readers still get the founders' debates, aims, and inner rules in their own words. The volume stands near the close of the long Illuminati papers affair.
nizami-the-loves-of-laili-and-majnun-189:
Nizami, the twelfth-century Persian poet, told of Laili and Majnun in a long romance, here in an 1894 English version. Qays loves Laili from childhood, but her family weds her to another. Mad with longing, he wanders the desert, singing her name to wild beasts.

Grief refines his love into something near to worship of God. Poets, kings, and hermits cross the tale, yet Majnun's heart never turns. The story has been called the Romeo and Juliet of the East. Older than that pair and stranger in its mystic depth, it stands among the supreme love tales of world literature.
on-remedies-in-the-sloane-collections-an: On Remedies in the Sloane Collections, and on Alchemical Symbols, 1894. The Sloane remedies. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
openalex-w1993102294: Parasites drain Brazil's cattle industry. A 2014 reassessment by Grisi and colleagues estimated the economic toll of cattle parasites in Brazil. The study tallied annual losses across the animals at risk — a bill ranchers can't ignore.
openalex-w2130560194: The world's soils got a 1-km map. Hengl and colleagues' 2014 SoilGrids1km paper built global soil information from automated mapping. The system answered the growing need for soil data — soils being a non-renewable resource and carbon sink.
openalex-w2168509294: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is one of medicine's hardest fights: treatment takes years, the drugs are toxic and costly, and outcomes are often poor. This 2012 PLoS Medicine study pools individual patient data from 9,153 people to ask which drug combinations, and how many, actually work. The meta-analysis gives doctors evidence-based guidance on building regimens that cure more patients with fewer failures.
openalex-w2173759594: Filarial worms cause river blindness and elephantiasis, yet their family tree has been shaky. This 2015 PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases paper uses multi-locus sequence typing — comparing several genes at once — to redraw the evolutionary relationships of the Onchocercidae family. The new tree overturns older classifications and clarifies which worms threaten human and animal health.
openalex-w2279275894: Rare decays of B mesons are exquisite probes of new physics, because the Standard Model predicts their patterns precisely. This 2016 Journal of High Energy Physics paper analyzes the angular distribution of the decay B0 → K*0 μ+ μ− using 3 fb−1 of LHCb data. The full angular information tests for CP violation and for deviations that could hint at particles beyond the Standard Model.
openalex-w2610726194: Dark matter would slip through detectors unseen, betrayed only by missing energy beside a lone jet. This 2015 paper reports ATLAS's search for such signatures in 20.3 fb−1 of 8 TeV data from 2012 — an energetic jet plus large missing transverse momentum. No new phenomena appeared, but the hunt narrowed where they might hide.
openalex-w266195994: Every two years, the Particle Data Group publishes the 'Review of Particle Physics' — the field's indispensable reference. This 2008 edition, in Physics Letters B, compiles the measured properties of every known particle and force, plus expert reviews of theory and experiment. For physicists, it's the bible: the one volume that says what the universe is made of, as far as we know.
openalex-w2742723294: From 2010 to 2016, Brazil's semiarid Northeast endured its worst drought on record. This 2017 paper examines the drought's climatic characteristics — how El Niño and tropical Atlantic conditions conspired to parch the region. The analysis of an unprecedented event holds lessons for a region where droughts are a recurring fact of life.
openalex-w2752229394: Pregnancy requires the mother's immune system to tolerate a half-foreign fetus — a feat of precise timing. This 2017 Science Immunology paper reveals an 'immune clock' of pregnancy: using mass cytometry, the authors show immune adaptations unfold on a strict schedule in women delivering at term. The clock could one day predict preterm birth.
openalex-w2778861494: Brain-computer interfaces read intentions from EEG — and motor imagery (imagining movement) is a key signal. This 2017 BMC Bioinformatics paper improves feature extraction for these signals, using mutual information to select discriminative filter banks beyond the classic common spatial pattern method. Better features mean BCIs that understand imagined movement more reliably.
openalex-w2929535294: Malaria infections too faint for standard tests are common everywhere the disease is endemic — but do they sustain transmission? This 2019 Nature Communications paper studies the temporal dynamics and infectiousness of subpatent Plasmodium falciparum infections by parasite density. The answer determines whether elimination campaigns must hunt the invisible.
openalex-w4409349694: This 2025 Artificial Intelligence Review paper comprehensively surveys loss functions and metrics in deep learning — from regression and classification fundamentals to practical insights across applications. The review is a reference for anyone training neural networks.
openalex-w605005794: Proton-pump inhibitors rank among the most prescribed drugs — and some studies link them to pneumonia. This 2015 PLoS ONE systematic review and meta-analysis examines the risk of community-acquired pneumonia with outpatient PPI therapy. The synthesis weighs a common drug’s hidden cost.
openalex-w7129009194: DIC means clotting run wild through the whole body, and doctors need a sharper handle on it. This paper proposes a new framework for the syndrome, guided by patient types, for modern clotting care. The authors rethought the old idea for today's wards. A blood-medicine review bringing order to chaos.
openalex-w7204257294: Plastic is now in our blood, our lungs, and our food. This literature review studies what microplastics and nanoplastics do to human health: how they enter the body and how they harm cells. The authors weigh a young but alarming science. A sobering overview of pollution at the smallest scale.
openalex-w7204631294: Students' brains work in different ways, and schools are only starting to catch up. This study looks at neurodiversity in education: the challenge of training teachers to honor different styles of learning, communicating, and growing. The authors map what teacher education still lacks. A forward-looking piece on making classrooms fit minds, not the other way around.
paine-age-of-reason-1794:
Thomas Paine published The Age of Reason in 1794, while the French Revolution was shaking Europe. Paine, famous for Common Sense and the American cause, now turned on revealed religion itself. He wrote as a deist who believed in one God but not in churches or miracles.

Paine went through the Bible book by book, pointing to errors, cruel acts, and clashing stories. He argued that true religion is doing justice, loving mercy, and copying God's goodness. The book sold hugely and drew furious replies, trials, and bans. It remains a landmark of freethought, plain in style and bold in its attack on priestly power.
peladan-comment-devient-artiste-1894:
Josephin Peladan teaches how one becomes an artist in Comment on devient artiste, in French from 1894. The book forms the third volume of his Amphitheatre of Dead Sciences. The self-styled Sar, a Rosicrucian aesthete of fin-de-siecle Paris, treats beauty as a sacred mystery with laws, grades, and priestly duties.

Art becomes religion in his perfumed, imperious pages throughout the work. He ranks masters, damns the vulgar, and crowns the ideal artist-priest. Wagner, Leonardo, and the old masters serve as his saints. The volume distills an age's aestheticism into a system, strange and gorgeous, from a man who lived his doctrine in robe and beard.
philosophie-der-freiheit-steiner-1894:
Rudolf Steiner published Die Philosophie der Freiheit in 1894, in German. The young Austrian thinker later founded anthroposophy, a spiritual movement. This early book lays the ground for all his later work.

Steiner asks how humans can know the world and act in true freedom. He argues that clear thinking itself is a free, moral act. The book blends philosophy with close study of the mind. It is dense and demanding to read. For Steiner's followers it is his most key text, the root from which his schools and farms grew.
plos-pbio-0020294:
Yong-Xu Wang, Chun-Li Zhang, Ruth T. Yu, and a large team pinpointed a muscle control switch in PLOS Biology in 2004. Muscles have slow fibers for endurance and fast fibers for power. A receptor called PPARδ helps decide which type a muscle builds.

Boosting PPARδ shifted muscles toward the slow, tireless type, and mice with the change could run much farther. That is a striking result: one switch remakes both muscle build and stamina. It drew wide notice as a possible route to exercise in a pill. The paper's core claim is narrower and solid: muscle fiber type is not fixed, and a single pathway can reset it.
plos-pone-0000094:
Jingchun Zhu, Ashwini Jambhekar, Aaron Sarver, and their team modeled a yeast response with network math in PLOS ONE in 2006. Nitric oxide is a gas that cells use as a signal, and in high doses as a weapon. Yeast exposed to it switches on a defense program of many genes.

A Bayesian network model sorts which genes likely drive which others, rather than merely moving together. That causal map is the prize: it shows the chain of command in the response. Such maps help predict how the system reacts to new stresses or drugs. The paper is a good sample of systems biology, where math and gene data meet.
plos-pone-0000194:
Matthew E. Falagas, Ioannis Karydis, and Ilektra Kostogiannou published this hospital safety study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It prospectively tracked percutaneous exposure incidents, needlesticks and similar injuries, among health care staff in a newly founded tertiary hospital. Such injuries risk passing blood-borne infections from patient to worker.

Counting injuries as they happen, rather than from memory, gives a truer picture of the risk. The authors record how often exposures occurred and under what conditions. Their data help hospital safety teams target training and equipment where injuries actually cluster, in a setting that was still building its routines.
plos-pone-0000294:
Lei Li, Xiangfeng Wang, Rajkumar Sasidharan, and colleagues published this rice genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Much of any genome is silent at a given time. The authors carry out a global identification of transcriptionally active regions in the rice genome, the stretches actually being read into RNA. They also characterize what those regions contain.

An activity map shows which parts of the rice genome are working, including regions outside known genes. That map is a resource for breeders and biologists working on the world's most important food crop. It also reveals how much transcription happens in supposedly quiet DNA.
plos-pone-0000394:
Daniel Stockholm and colleagues asked why identical cells in a dish end up behaving differently, in PLOS ONE in 2007. They studied a clonal cell population, cells all copied from one ancestor and grown in the same conditions in vitro. Even so, the population showed phenotypic heterogeneity: cells with visibly different traits.

Where does difference come from when genes and surroundings match? The paper traces the origin of that spread within the clone. The question matters for medicine and biology alike. Cell populations that look uniform can hide rare cells with unusual behavior. That includes drug resistance in cancer. Understanding the source of the variety helps explain how it arises so reliably.
plos-pone-0000494:
Marie Benoit and colleagues measured immune signals in the blood of patients with Whipple's disease, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Whipple's is a rare infection that can smolder for years. The team found increased levels of circulating IL-16, an immune messenger. They also found more apoptosis markers, signs of cells undergoing programmed death. Both measures related to the activity of the disease.

Markers that rise and fall with disease activity are valuable in a rare illness that is hard to monitor. IL-16 and cell-death markers could help doctors tell a flare from remission without invasive tests. The study also hints at how the infection disturbs the immune system beyond the gut, where Whipple's usually shows itself.
plos-pone-0000594:
Byungwoo Ryu and colleagues read gene activity across many tumor cell lines to find marks of melanoma's advance, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Melanoma is a skin cancer that can be cured early but kills once it spreads. The team profiled gene activity in a broad panel of tumor lines. From those profiles they picked out patterns tied to how far the cancer had advanced.

Marks of advance could sort patients by risk, which is the key choice in melanoma care. Cell line panels let the team compare stages under the same lab rules. The patterns also name genes that may drive the advance, not just tag along with it.
plos-pone-0000694:
Wolfgang Jakob and Bernd Schierwater changed animal body plans by switching genes off, reported in PLOS ONE in 2007. Regulatory genes of the Antp class helped invent and spread animal bauplans, the basic body layouts of species. Cnidaria, the phylum of jellyfish and their kin, sits close to the root of animal life. Its members often live in two distinct generations with strikingly varied forms.

By silencing Hox-like genes in hydrozoans, the authors altered those body plans directly. Such experiments test whether the same gene toolkit that built animal diversity still controls form today. Few systems let researchers reach so close to evolution's starting conditions.
plos-pone-0000794:
Yukako Yokota, H. T. Ghashghaei, Christine Han and colleagues followed young neurons migrating into the growing cerebral cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Interneurons are born in a region called the ganglionic eminence and migrate tangentially, sideways, into the cerebral wall to reach their places. Faulty connectivity and differentiation of these interneurons are thought to cause several brain disorders.

Radial glia, the scaffold cells of the cortex, guide much migration. The study splits movements that depend on radial glia from those that go on alone. Knowing which routes need the scaffold tells scientists where migration can fail. Cortex building is transport at cell scale, and interneurons travel farthest.
plos-pone-0000894:
Christopher Martyniuk, Stephane Aris-Brosou, Guy Drouin and co-authors traced the early history of GABA receptors, for PLOS ONE in 2007. GABA is a major calming signal chemical in the brain, in both backboned and spineless animals. Its receptors help run learning and memory, yet little was known about how fast or in what pattern they evolved.

The team focused on two receptor parts found only in mammals, called theta and epsilon. They asked what kind of selection shaped them over time. Tracing receptor history can explain why drugs that act on GABA vary across species. It also shows how a key brain system was assembled piece by piece.
plos-pone-0000994:
Timothy Linksvayer showed that ant species differences can arise from interactions between brood and worker genes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In social insects, a trait is shaped by the genes of several individuals at once. A young ant's growth depends on its own genes and on the nurses that raise it.

Linksvayer focuses on epistasis, cases where genes interact so their joint effect is more than the sum of parts. Between brood and worker genomes, such interactions could drive species apart. The idea widens evolution theory for social life. It says the unit that evolves may be the colony's combined genome, not one ant's.
plos-pone-0001094:
Jean-Philippe Lachaux, Karim Jerbi, Olivier Bertrand and colleagues set out a blueprint for mapping brain function from inside the skull, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Before epilepsy surgery, patients undergo intracranial recordings to find the seizure network. Those same recordings can map eloquent areas, regions whose loss would cost speech or movement.

Recordings from inside the human brain are rare and precious. The authors propose a real time functional mapping approach built on them. Real time matters in the operating room, where decisions cannot wait for offline analysis. A shared blueprint also lets centers pool rare data. The paper is aimed at surgical teams and brain researchers alike.
plos-pone-0001194:
The asp viper, Vipera aspis, is one of Europe's venomous snakes, and its venom varies from place to place. Elisabeth Ferquel and colleagues reappraised the venom's neurotoxicity, its ability to attack nerves, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Venom diversity matters both for understanding snake evolution and for treating bites.

The authors revisit how neurotoxic the venom is and where the neurotoxic forms occur. Geographic variation within a species complicates antivenom use, since a serum raised against one population's venom may fit another's poorly. Their reappraisal updates the evidence on an old question in toxinology.
plos-pone-0001294:
Crosses between species often yield hybrids that survive, but only just. Hernán López-Fernández and Daniel Bolnick asked why that partial inviability happens, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Two explanations compete. Lethal genetic incompatibilities might fail to strike every individual, a property called incomplete penetrance. Or hybrids might vary genetically in which incompatibilities they carry.

The authors frame and test the two explanations for partial F1 hybrid viability. The answer matters for understanding how species split, since hybrid failure is a barrier to gene flow. Their analysis weighs the alternatives with data from hybrid crosses.
plos-pone-0001394:
Svetlana Shinkareva and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on reading minds from brain scans. Prior work had shown that scan patterns can reveal which class of thing a person views, such as tools. The team pushed the test to two classes that look quite unlike: tools and homes. They asked how sharp the read out could be.

By scanning brains as people viewed tools or dwellings, they learned the pattern for each class. They could then tell which class a new scan fit. The study adds proof that brain maps hold rich detail on what we see. It also refines ways to decode thought from scan data.
plos-pone-0001494:
Han Xiao and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how a coronavirus blocks host cell work. In infected cells, many defense genes are switched on at the RNA level. Yet their proteins often fail to rise as expected. The team traced that gap to the virus's spike protein, the part it uses to enter cells.

They show the spike binds a host factor and curbs the making of host proteins. That curb helps the virus blunt the defense reply. A spike job past cell entry was not in the standard view. It names a fresh point where drugs might free the host reply.
plos-pone-0001594:
Željka Pezer and Đurđica Ugarković wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on satellite DNA in beetles. Satellite DNA fills the dense zones at chromosome centers. Its RNA copies help form those zones and the grip points for cell division. How its copying is run within dense DNA was little known. The team tested which copying enzyme does the job in beetles.

They show the main gene copying enzyme drives satellite copying here. That is a plain answer to a murky point. It ties satellite RNA output to the cell's main work flow. The result helps frame how center zones are built and kept each cell cycle.
plos-pone-0001694:
Andrey V. Kajava, Maria Anisimova, and Nemo Peeters traced the origin of an unusual protein family in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The proteins are GALA-LRR, made by Ralstonia solanacearum, a bacterium that wilts many crops. GALA proteins are type III effectors, tools the bacterium injects into plant cells. They combine an F-box part with LRR repeats, a common protein-building module.

The GALA repeats did not fit any known LRR subfamily, so the authors used sequence analysis and structure prediction to place them. They argue GALA-LRR is a new member of the CC-LRR subfamily, with a history running from plants to bacteria. The full text gives the comparisons behind that claim. Effector family histories show how plant pathogens borrow and reshape host-like parts.
plos-pone-0001794:
Ben J. Harrison, Jesus Pujol, Hector Ortiz, and their co-authors studied how sad mood changes the resting brain in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Resting-state functional MRI reveals slow variations in the BOLD signal, the scanner's measure of blood oxygen. In humans these slow variations are thought to reflect intrinsic functional connectivity, the brain's standing networks.

The team induced sad mood in volunteers and measured how resting-state networks were modulated. The full text gives the mood induction method, the network maps, and which connections strengthened or weakened. Showing that mood alone retunes resting networks matters for depression research, where resting scans are used to find disease patterns.
plos-pone-0001894:
Xiaoli Ma and colleagues asked where the cells that clog grafted hearts come from, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. After a heart transplant, the new heart's vessels can thicken from within. That process, called neointima growth, is a top cause of late death. Stents can open such vessels, yet the thickening often comes back around the stent.

The team traced whether the cells in the new growth come from the donor heart or from the person who got it. They report on the share that comes from the recipient's own body. Knowing the source of the clogging cells shapes how doctors aim drugs to keep graft vessels open.
plos-pone-0001994:
Boris Zybailov and co-authors catalogued the proteins of the chloroplast, the green plant cell part that runs photosynthesis, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A full parts list is needed to grasp how the chloroplast aids plant growth. The team ran large-scale protein analysis on ten separate chloroplast samples, using two mass spectrometry setups.

They focused on three traits of each protein. These were the sorting signals that send it to the chloroplast, chemical changes at its start, and how much of it there is. A map of all three guides work on how proteins find their place and how the chloroplast is built.
plos-pone-0002094:
Mohammad Abdur Rab and co-authors audited ethics practice in health research across the Eastern Mediterranean, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Commentators had voiced concern about whether proper ethics review systems exist in developing countries. Rules mean little if studies in practice skip consent, review, or safeguards for volunteers.

The team ran a retrospective data analysis of studies from countries in the World Health Organization's Eastern Mediterranean Region. They explored how far investigators there consider several ethical practices when they conduct research. A regional audit gives reformers facts instead of impressions, and shows where review systems need support.
plos-pone-0002194:
Hugo Cousillas and co-authors asked whether a young songbird needs company to build a healthy hearing brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In human babies, direct social contact shapes speech growth and keeps perception sharp. The processes behind that link are still poorly known, so the team turned to a female songbird.

They tested whether social segregation during growth harms the development of a central auditory area, the part of the brain that handles sound. A bird kept apart from others may miss the vocal exchanges its brain expects. The study links social life and brain growth in a species that, like us, learns by listening.
plos-pone-0002294:
Belén Morón, Michael Bethune, Isabel Comino, and co-authors built antibodies for detecting a key gluten fragment, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Celiac disease is a permanent intolerance to gluten prolamins from wheat, barley, rye, and, for some patients, oats. Partially digested gluten peptides inflame the small intestine of people with the disease.

Fast, immune-based tests need antibodies that lock onto the main immunogenic peptide, the fragment that triggers the reaction. The team produced and characterized monoclonal antibodies against it. Reliable detectors of that fragment support both food testing, to guard patients. Assays that may one day measure toxicity of foods for celiac patients directly.
plos-pone-0002394:
In 2008, García-Contreras and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Rodolfo García-Contreras, Xue-Song Zhang, Younghoon Kim, and others. Its subject is protein Translation and Cell Death. The title goes on to note the Role of Rare tRNAs in Biofilm Formation and in Activating Dormant Phage Killer Genes. We discovered before that the small Escherichia coli proteins Hha (hemolysin expression modulating protein) and the adjacent.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002494:
A research team led by Garbuzova-Davis reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Svitlana Garbuzova-Davis, Cyndy Davis Sanberg, Nicole Kuzmin-Nichols, and others. Its subject is human Umbilical Cord Blood Treatment in a Mouse Model of ALS: Optimization of Cell Dose. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a multicausal disease characterized by motor neuron degeneration in the spinal cord and brain.

Cell therapy may be a promising new treatment for this devastating disorder. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002594:
Work from Chae and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Young Kwang Chae, Sung Koo Kang, Myoung Sook Kim, and others. Its subject is human AQP5 Plays a Role in the Progression of Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML). Aquaporins (AQPs) have before been linked to increased expression in solid tumors.

However, its expression in hematologic malignancies including CML has not been described yet. Here, we report the expression of AQP5 in CML cells by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002694:
Ofer Yizhar led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was modulating vesicle priming reveals that vesicle immobilization is necessary but not sufficient for Fusion-Competence. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ofer Yizhar, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. In neurons and neuroendocrine cells, docked vesicles need to undergo priming to become fusion competent. The summary also notes a further point. Priming is a multi-step process that was shown to be associated with vesicle immobilization. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002794:
Bengt Hansson led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was postglacial colonisation patterns and the role of isolation and expansion in driving diversification in a passerine bird. The catalog record names Bengt Hansson first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Pleistocene glacial cycles play a major role in diversification and speciation, although the relative importance of isolation and expansion in driving diversification remains debated. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002894:
Laure Franqueville, Petra Henning, Maria Magnusson and co-authors studied crystal-like clumps that form in cells infected with adenovirus type 5. These protein crystals appear late in infection, inside the cell nucleus. What the virus needs to build them was not well known.

Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, the work uses altered viruses plus electron and light microscopy to find the rules for crystal growth in the nucleus. It also probes what the crystals are made of and what they do. Virologists gain detail on a striking late stage of adenovirus infection that older studies had only described.
plos-pone-0002994:
Katherine Martin, Denis Patrick, Mina Bissell and co-authors derived a breast cancer prognosis signature from 3D culture in 2008. Early detection is vital in breast cancer because it widens treatment options and survival. The group had earlier used an unsupervised method to find genes whose activity predicts outcome.

Their new signature came from cells grown in three-dimensional culture, which mimics tissue better than flat dishes. It accurately predicted clinical outcome across independent datasets, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, cross-dataset success is the key test for any gene signature hoping for clinic use.
plos-pone-0003094:
Rofa Elfakess and Rivka Dikstein identified a DNA element governing genes with very short leaders in 2008. Transcription is controlled by regulatory elements, and elements sitting downstream of the start site, in the 5 prime UTR, could influence translation too. Evidence for such dual-purpose elements was limited.

Their element is specific to messenger RNAs with very short 5 prime UTRs and also regulates transcription, per the title. One element doing both jobs coordinates the two steps. Published in PLOS ONE, composite elements like this revise the tidy split between transcription and translation control. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003194:
Andries Kalsbeek, Ewout Foppen, Ingrid Schalij and colleagues study the brain clock's control of blood sugar in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The mammalian biological clock sits in the suprachiasmatic nuclei of the hypothalamus and imposes its time structure on the body through nerve and hormone outputs. To study clock control of the autonomic nervous system, the team focused on the daily plasma glucose rhythm.

Their title frames the result as an interplay of GABA and glutamate, two key brain signals. Readers learn how clock neurons may balance opposing signals to set a daily sugar rhythm. The work links timekeeping circuits to metabolic control.
plos-pone-0003294:
Vincenzo Calvanese, Angelica Horrillo, Abdelkrim Hmadcha and colleagues study cancer genes in embryonic stem cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Developmental genes are silenced in embryonic stem cells by a bivalent histone-based chromatin mark. This mark may also make DNA promoter hypermethylation of tumour suppressor genes more likely in cancer. The team report what they found in this setting.

The title states that cancer genes are hypermethylated in human embryonic stem cells. Readers see a stem cell state share marks with cancer gene shutdown. That overlap may explain why certain tumour suppressors are so often shut down by methylation.
plos-pone-0003394:
Fernando E. Herrera and co-authors studied a protein tied to Parkinson's disease in this 2008 paper. The protein, alpha-synuclein, can clump into fibers inside brain cells. Dopamine, the brain chemical lost in Parkinson's, seems to block that clumping. The team asked how dopamine does this at the molecular level.

They found the block runs through five building blocks at the protein's tail end. A spot in the middle region, called E83, also plays a part. Those contact points explain how dopamine holds the protein apart. The detail could help design drugs that stop the clumping too.
plos-pone-0003494:
W. Joost Wiersinga and co-authors studied defense against a lethal tropical germ in this 2008 paper. Burkholderia pseudomallei causes melioidosis, a severe infection of soil regions. Toll-like receptors spot germs and start innate immune defense. Two adapter proteins carry those alarm signals onward.

One adapter, MyD88, proved key to protective host defense here. Without its signaling, mice fared worse against the bacterium. The study ranks one alarm hub above others for this germ. That ranking may guide vaccines and immune therapies for melioidosis. Melioidosis is often missed at first, which makes its death rate worse.
plos-pone-0003594:
Ziv Frankenstein, Joseph Sperling, and Ruth Sperling released structure-fitting tools in this 2008 paper. Big molecular assemblies are often studied at low resolution. Electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy give unlike views of them. Comparing and docking such blurry models is hard.

Their Fit EM2EM tools match low-resolution models against each other. The tools support study of assembly and dynamics of large complexes. Quantitative comparison brings order to fuzzy structural data. Other labs can reuse the software for their own assemblies. Blurry views are often all that large complexes allow. So matching tools like these fill a real gap for labs that study the biggest machines inside cells.
plos-pone-0003694:
Melissa Piper Hunter, Noura Ismail, Xiaoli Zhang, and colleagues published this blood study in PLOS ONE in 2008. MicroRNAs are small RNA pieces that control how much protein a gene makes. Changes in them are linked to diseases such as cancer. What circulates in healthy people's blood was poorly mapped.

The team looked for microRNAs inside microvesicles, tiny bubbles shed into human peripheral blood. They detected microRNA expression in those vesicles from donors. The finding suggests a plain blood draw might one day report on the body's gene control activity, without taking tissue.
plos-pone-0003794:
Erxi Wu, Nathan Palmer, Ze Tian, and colleagues published this signaling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. PDGF is a growth factor that signals through two receptors, alpha and beta. The receptors can cover for each other in dishes, yet play distinct roles in animals. That overlap blocked clear study of the pathways.

The team used mouse cells genetically defined for each receptor: normal, missing one, or missing both. With that panel they dissected the PDGF pathways piece by piece. The map separates what each receptor truly does from what its twin can cover for.
plos-pone-0003894:
Arash Rafii, Pejman Mirshahi, Mary Poupot, and co-authors studied ovarian tumors and drug resistance in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article focuses on the setting around the tumor. Epithelial ovarian cancer often spreads within the belly cavity. There it meets mesothelial cells, which line that cavity.

The authors describe a process where tumor cells take material from stromal cells. They call that process oncologic trogocytosis in their report. After it, the tumors resist chemotherapy drugs more strongly. The finding names a route by which nearby normal cells can shield a tumor. Blocking that route could make standard drugs work better.
plos-pone-0003994:
K. Marie McIntyre, Simon Gubbins, Wilfred Goldmann, and co-authors described scrapie outbreaks in British sheep in 2008. Scrapie is a fatal prion disease of sheep flocks. Most earlier analyses used research institute flocks. Those flocks may not reflect conditions on real farms.

Their PLOS ONE article describes outbreaks in thirty naturally infected flocks. The flocks sat across the United Kingdom under farm conditions. Field patterns of spread and loss guide control policy better. The data help vets judge risk in commercial flocks. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004094:
Catherine M. Stein, Sarah Zalwango, LaShaunda L. Malone, and co-authors scanned Ugandan genomes for TB risk in 2008. Tuberculosis remains a major global health problem, worst in sub-Saharan Africa. Host genes were suspected to shape who gets infected or sick. Results across earlier studies had not agreed.

Their PLOS ONE article runs a genome scan for infection and disease. It separates catching Mycobacterium tuberculosis from developing active illness. Those two steps may have different genetic controls. Ugandan data add an African population long missing from genome scans. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004194:
Tomonori Hirose and colleagues published this kidney study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Podocytes are kidney cells whose interlocking feet form slit diaphragms, the selective filter that keeps protein out of urine. Mutations behind inherited kidney disease pointed the team to this filter's construction.

They studied aPKCλ, described as a universal polarity protein that helps cells keep their top and bottom straight. They report that this protein is essential for maintaining the slit diaphragms of podocytes. When polarity fails, the kidney's filter fails with it, which is why the finding matters for kidney disease.
plos-pone-0004294:
Samuel Lai and colleagues published this mucus study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mucus protects the body's wet surfaces. Its barrier power rests on viscous and elastic properties. Those properties are not well understood at the scale of pathogens and fine particles. The team worked with fresh, undiluted human cervicovaginal mucus.

They report on altering mucus rheology, its flow behaviour, so as to effectively solidify human mucus at the nanoscale. A tunable mucus barrier could one day block viruses and particles while leaving the tissue beneath unharmed. The team worked at the scale of single particles and viruses.
plos-pone-0004394:
In both main forms of diabetes, insulin-making beta cells are lost. A protein called AIF helps control cell death and energy work in mitochondria. Fabienne Schulthess, Sophie Katz, Amin Ardestani, and co-authors removed that protein in their test system. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper reports what happened to beta cells afterward. The protein's full name is apoptosis inducing factor, though its day job is cell upkeep.

Deleting AIF set off beta-cell death. It also shrank the total mass of beta cells. Fewer beta cells means less insulin for blood sugar control. The result shows this mitochondrial protein guards the cells diabetes destroys. Protecting such upkeep paths could matter for slowing the disease.
plos-pone-0004494:
Dysentery epidemics that swept refugee camps in Central Africa in the early 1990s are documented by Solen Kerneis, Philippe Guerin, Lorenz von Seidlein, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cause was Shigella dysenteriae type 1, a bacterium that brings severe bloody diarrhea. Children and displaced people in tropical countries are hit hardest by such outbreaks.

Although these epidemics keep happening, their features have rarely been written down in detail. The authors describe the outbreaks that struck refugee settings between 1993 and 1995, drawing lessons while the problem remains ongoing. Records like these help aid teams prepare for the next camp epidemic. They show what worked, what failed, and how fast this pathogen can move through a crowded settlement.
plos-pone-0004594:
Energy-dense food fattens young teens whether or not they carry a famous obesity gene variant, report Laura Johnson, Cornelia van Jaarsveld, Pauline Emmett, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dietary energy density means how many calories a food packs per bite. Its link to fat mass in children is not a simple straight line, suggesting some children are more susceptible than others.

Children carrying the FTO variant that raises obesity risk seemed prime candidates for extra susceptibility. The team tested whether FTO variants modified the effect of dietary energy density on fat mass in early adolescence. They did not: the diet effect stood on its own, as the title states. The result points prevention at food itself, for all children alike.
plos-pone-0004694:
Randolf Menzel asked if honeybees can learn the order of a set of items, for a PLOS ONE study in 2009. Learning a sequence means holding not just one item but what came before and after it. That skill is seen as a mark of a rich kind of memory in humans.

Menzel tested bees on tasks much like finding a path through a set of places. He asked if bees track true order or just single cues. Proof of order learning in bees would blur the line drawn around higher memory. It would also show how a small brain can still track complex patterns.
plos-pone-0004794:
Martina Johannesson and colleagues showed that FGF4 and retinoic acid direct stem cells into foregut endoderm, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Both signals control patterning of the gut lining layer and pancreas induction in embryos. Protocols to grow gut and pancreas cells from human embryonic stem cells often used retinoic acid, and Other growth factors, but excluded FGF4 from the mixture.

The team found the pair works in a time and dose dependent manner. Adding FGF4 improved formation of PDX1 expressing foregut cells. Better recipes bring lab grown pancreas cells closer. That matters for diabetes cell therapy research.
plos-pone-0004894:
Laetitia Carthagena and colleagues studied human TRIM gene output in response to interferons, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tripartite motif proteins share conserved architecture. The anti HIV activity found for TRIM5 alpha sparked interest in antiviral roles for the whole family. The team profiled gene output across the family after interferon treatment. They sought members switched on by interferon that likely join innate defense against diverse viruses.

Many TRIM genes respond strongly to interferons. The family forms a broad antiviral arsenal. Single members still await a defined role. Interferon therapy partly works through them. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004994:
Blood vessels and early blood cells arise together in the embryo. A transcription factor called Etsrp is required for both. Gustavo Gomez and colleagues searched downstream of it in zebrafish. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Forcing Etsrp on switches many vascular and blood genes on.

The team discovered new genes under Etsrp's control. Some build vessels, others build blood. The list fills out the blood-building program considerably. Its mammalian counterpart is also essential for these tissues. The work helps complete the blueprint of how circulation is born. New genes on the list are candidates for roles in human vascular disease.
plos-pone-0005094:
Solving a protein's structure needs crystals of it. Many proteins refuse to crystallize well. Amy Wernimont and Aled Edwards updated a trick for them in PLOS ONE in 2009. The trick is in situ proteolysis. A trace of protease is added to the crystallization trial. The protease trims floppy parts of the protein.

Only a fraction of purified proteins yield usable crystals. The 2007 method raised those odds. This update refines the recipe further. It reports what worked across many trials. Structural biology runs on such practical knowledge. Each rescued protein is a structure that can be solved. Some of those structures become drug targets. A humble methods paper can unblock a whole field.
plos-pone-0005194:
Much of the harm in malaria comes not from the parasite alone but from the host's fierce swelling response. Finding which parasite-linked molecules spark that response is key to new treatments. Orengo and colleagues pointed to uric acid in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Uric acid is a waste product best known for causing gout when it builds up. The team showed it acts as a go-between in the swelling response triggered by Plasmodium falciparum, the main malaria parasite. Naming that mediator gives researchers a fresh target in the chain that leads to severe disease.
plos-pone-0005294:
Global targets for HIV treatment assumed health systems in poor countries could expand fast. In Tanzania, the 2005 target was ten times higher than what was actually achieved. Hanson and colleagues estimated the country's real capacity for antiretroviral therapy in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their estimate used data on staff productivity and on patients lost from care. Honest capacity math shows where the bottleneck truly lies, whether in workers, clinics, or follow-up. Targets grounded in that math are likelier to be met and to guide real investment. Staff time is the true cap on care in clinics like these,. A count based on real work hours shows where one more nurse or one more clerk would help most.
plos-pone-0005394:
Narcolepsy with cataplexy has known genetic markers, including a variant between the CPT1B and CHKB genes and a specific HLA haplotype. Miyagawa and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether the same markers confer risk for related hypersomnia disorders in Japanese patients.

The conditions studied fall under central nervous system hypersomnias, including essential hypersomnia. Testing narcolepsy markers there checks whether these sleep disorders share genetic roots. Shared markers would blur the boundary between the diagnoses and guide genetic counseling. Sleep that will not lift is more than a quirk. it wrecks school, work, and mood, so a shared gene root with the best-known sleep disease would give these cases a firmer place in care and in law.
plos-pone-0005494:
Steve Kim and Loren Frank studied memory learning after brain damage in rats, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The hippocampus is vital for forming memories of events. Yet which exact patterns of its activity support new learning was not known.

The team used a task where rats must keep alternating between places without pause. Rats with damage to the hippocampus learned this fast, steady task poorly. The setup lets workers watch brain activity while learning happens. Rapid learning of a running routine needs the hippocampus just as much as learning facts does.
plos-pone-0005594:
Andrew Watson, Cesar Ramirez, and Ellen Salud worked on predicting how visible an aircraft is, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Seeing other aircraft in time is a basic part of flight safety. Judges of safety need a way to predict whether a pilot can spot a given plane.

Visibility depends on the plane's size, shape, distance, and colour against the sky. The authors set out a method that combines those factors into a forecast. A sound forecast lets designers and regulators test see-and-avoid rules without risky flight trials. A forecast tool also helps judge new plane colours and shapes before they enter service.
plos-pone-0005694:
Kailash Pandey and co-authors examined a malaria parasite enzyme in 2009, focusing on the brake built into its own front end. The enzyme, falcipain-2, helps the parasite digest hemoglobin, the red protein of blood. Without that food supply, the parasite cannot grow inside red cells.

Like many such enzymes, falcipain-2 is made in a longer form whose head piece blocks its action until cut away. The team mapped the parts of that head piece that do the blocking. Those details point to ways a drug might jam the enzyme. A blocked enzyme starves the parasite, a route drug makers prize.
plos-pone-0005794:
Gregory Glass and co-authors studied cats and rats sharing city alleys in 2009, and the odd effects that follow. Community webs can respond in counterintuitive ways when species are added or removed. City-dwelling species matter for biodiversity and for public health alike.

The team examined how cats, often assumed to control rats, actually interact with them in an urban setting. Simple predator logic may fail where shelter and garbage set the terms. Their phrase, trophic garnishes, flags the small interactions that season the whole system. The results warn city managers against easy fixes for rat problems.
plos-pone-0005894:
Pernille Hojman and co-authors showed in 2009 that raising erythropoietin in muscle protects mice against diet-driven obesity. Gene transfer into muscle raised blood EPO many-fold and lifted hemoglobin. Earlier work hinted EPO improves several metabolic measures beyond making red cells.

Protected mice burned more fat in their muscles on the rich diet. That extra oxidation kept weight gain down. Repurposing a blood hormone for metabolic defense is an appealing idea, though safety limits loom. The study details the muscle-fat link and gives the obesity field another hormonal angle to weigh.
plos-pone-0005994:
Rapamycin is a drug that quiets the immune system, prized for transplants. Laura Strauss, Malgorzata Czystowska, Marta Szajnik and colleagues found a twist in its action in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper compares how two kinds of human T cell answer the drug: regulatory cells, which calm attacks, and effector cells, which carry them out.

The drug helps regulatory cells grow and last, while effector cells react in a different way. That split favors the peacekeepers of the immune system. Learning exactly how the drug picks its winners could improve transplant care and autoimmune treatment, where boosting the calm cells while sparing the rest is the whole goal.
plos-pone-0006094:
Every tumor carries fresh mutations, and some of them make flags the immune system can target. Nisheeth Srivastava and Pramod Srivastava modeled that flag count in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper estimates the repertoire of true tumor-specific epitopes, the short protein pieces shown on MHC I molecules. These epitopes arise in a human tumor as its cells copy DNA with small errors.

Only some mutations become flags that are processed and presented, so the true repertoire is smaller than the raw mutation count. Knowing its size guides cancer vaccine design, which must pick real targets from a sea of near misses. The model turns an appealing idea into a number planners can build on.
plos-pone-0006194:
Chimpanzees in Uganda's Budongo Forest had long been seen chewing the soft core of rotting palm trees. Vernon Reynolds and colleagues finally tested why, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The palm species, Raphia farinifera, decays in the forest, and its pith is easy for chimps to tear and eat.

Lab tests found high levels of sodium in the pith. Salt is scarce in a fruit-based forest diet, so the pith works like a natural salt lick. The answer solves a small daily mystery of chimp behaviour. It also shows how animals track down minerals that their main foods lack.
plos-pone-0006294:
Two spinal fluid proteins can flag Alzheimer's disease even before symptoms show. Peder Buchhave, Kaj Blennow, and Henrik Zetterberg followed patients over time in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Earlier reports on how tau and amyloid-beta-42 change within individuals disagreed with each other.

The longitudinal study tracked both markers in patients and elderly controls over repeated samples. Settling their time course is essential if the markers will guide diagnosis or trials. Stable markers can confirm disease; changing ones might track its progress. The paper clarifies what clinicians can expect from these tests.
plos-pone-0006394:
Parasitic wasps pause their development to survive hard seasons, a state called diapause. Florian Wolschin and Juergen Gadau read proteomic signatures of early diapause in the jewel wasp Nasonia in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Diapause increases longevity and survival under harsh conditions, but its global metabolic adjustments were little studied.

Protein patterns mark the shift into standby mode. Broad protein surveys reveal which systems power down or stay ready. Insects time diapause to seasons with great precision. The signatures may help predict pest and pollinator timing under climate change. The marks may also help track how pests and crop foes shift as the climate warms.
plos-pone-0006494:
Erica Rosenblum, Thomas Poorten, Matthew Settles, and colleagues read gene activity in frogs facing a deadly fungus for PLOS ONE in 2009. Emerging infectious diseases worry both wildlife and human health experts. Several highly virulent fungal pathogens have recently been found in natural populations. The chytrid fungus is devastating frog species around the world.

The team measured the genome-wide transcriptional response of the frog Silurana tropicalis to chytrid infection. Which genes switch on or off shows how the frog fights back, or fails to. Such profiles may explain why some species crash while others survive. They also offer targets for conservation action.
plos-pone-0006594:
Nisha Badders, Shruti Goel, Rod Clark, and colleagues studied a Wnt receptor in mammary stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ectopic Wnt signaling induces increased stem and progenitor cell activity in the mouse mammary gland, followed by tumor development. The Wnt signaling receptors Lrp5 and Lrp6 relay those signals. The team examined Lrp5 specifically.

Their title reports Lrp5 is expressed by mouse mammary stem cells and is required to maintain the basal lineage. Without it, a whole branch of the gland's cell family fails. The finding ties a signaling receptor to stem cell maintenance. It also bears on breast cancer, where Wnt signaling often goes wrong.
plos-pone-0006694:
Cédric Alaux and colleagues studied how a honey bee signal changes the brain of the bee that sends it in PLOS ONE in 2009. Animal signals are known to cause large gene changes in receivers. Far less was known about effects on the sender. Honey bees use a modulatory communication signal during colony life. The authors asked whether producing it alters the sender's brain state.

They linked signal performance to a distinct neurogenomic state in the bees. In other words, sending the signal came with its own pattern of brain gene activity. That pattern differed from bees not performing the signal. The result widens how scientists think about communication. Sending a message, not just hearing one, can reshape the brain.
plos-pone-0006794:
Akira Masuda and Shuji Aou studied how rats pass avoidance behavior to each other in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rats learn from watching or interacting with companions. Social learning helps animals adapt when situations switch. Avoiding dangerous places quickly is a survival skill. Learning it from others beats learning by injury.

The authors compared learned and unlearned rats under changed situations. Avoidance behavior spread socially between the animals. They examined how the transmission held up when conditions changed. Social transmission can preserve useful caution across a group. It can also spread outdated fears, making the dynamics worth mapping.
plos-pone-0006894:
Yi Cao, Dongmei Zhang, and Weiqing Pan built a mouse malaria germ to test vaccine leads in PLOS ONE in 2009. One part of a surface protein, MSP1-19, does the same job in far-kin Plasmodium kinds. That steadiness makes it a vaccine lead. The man's germ, Plasmodium falciparum, is hard to test head-on. A fused protein called 2.9 joins lead bits in one chain.

The team bred the man's lead into Plasmodium berghei, a mouse germ. A green glow protein served as a flag in the build. Vaccine leads can now be tried in mice through this stand-in germ. Leads that pass can move on with more trust.
plos-pone-0006994:
Richelle Charles, Jason Harris, Michael Chase, and colleagues compared two Salmonella types in PLOS ONE in 2009. Salmonella Typhi causes typhoid fever, a whole-body infection in humans. Its relative Typhimurium causes gut illness in people but typhoid-like disease in mice. Both are steered by a control system called the PhoP regulon.

The team compared the proteins that system controls in each type. Side-by-side proteomics shows where their programs diverge. Those differences may explain why one type stays in the gut and the other invades the whole body. They also hint at targets for typhoid-specific tests or vaccines.
plos-pone-0007094:
Judith Favier, Jean-Jacques Brière, Nelly Burnichon, and others studied tumor fuel use in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most cancer cells favor a wasteful way of making energy, known as the Warburg effect. Why they do so is a long debate. The team turned to pheochromocytomas, rare tumors that can run in families. These tumors carry known gene faults.

They measured how the tumors breathe, grow blood vessels, and burn sugar. The Warburg pattern turned out to be set by the gene faults themselves. In short, the mutations fix the tumor's fuel style. That ties tumor genes straight to a classic puzzle of cancer biology.
plos-pone-0007194:
Andrea M. Matter, Sara B. Hoot, Patrick D. Anderson, and colleagues traced the history of an antibiotic gene cluster in 2009. Many Streptomyces bacteria make valinomycin, an antibiotic compound. The gene cluster that builds it had been described in two separate isolates before this study.

The authors compare the cluster across strains and study its family relationships. They use both parsimony and likelihood methods, two ways of building evolutionary trees. Their paper covers conservation, ecology, and evolution of the cluster. It shows how an antibiotic-making toolkit persists and changes across related bacteria.
plos-pone-0007294:
Zhao Qin, Laurent Kreplak, and Markus J. Buehler studied the mechanics of vimentin filaments in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Intermediate filaments are one of three major cytoskeleton components in eukaryotic cells. They give cells mechanical stability and help transmit forces, a process called mechanotransduction across tissues.

Despite their importance, filament mechanics were not fully explained. The authors show that hierarchical structure controls the nanomechanical properties of vimentin filaments. In other words, structure at several size scales sets strength and flexibility. Their computational models connect molecule-level design to cell-level mechanical resilience.
plos-pone-0007494:
Javier Simón-Sánchez and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 testing a reported genetic risk for frontotemporal lobar degeneration. That condition is a form of dementia that shrinks the front and side regions of the brain. A variant near the GRN gene, called rs5848, had been linked to risk in a North American group. The Dutch team checked the same variant in their own population.

In the Dutch sample, the variant showed no association with the disease. A negative result like this is a useful check on earlier claims. It shows the reported risk does not hold in every population. Genetic effects can depend on ancestry and on how cases are selected. Narrowing where the link is real sharpens future research. The paper is a reminder that replication decides what genetics can claim.
plos-pone-0007594:
Dong Liu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 cataloguing microRNAs in the liver of a human fetus. MicroRNAs are very short RNA molecules, and they regulate gene expression in human cells. Different sets appear in different tissues as development proceeds. Liver cells were known to carry particular types. The team used a modified method to identify the fetal liver's microRNAs more completely.

The census lists which tiny regulators are present as the human liver forms. Each one is a potential hand on the organ's development. A reference list like this anchors later work on liver growth and disease. It also shows a tweaked method can find molecules standard surveys miss. Developmental biology runs on such maps. The fetal liver's control panel is now better charted.
plos-pone-0007694:
Farid Rahimi, Kazuma Murakami, Jamie Summers and their co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Alzheimer's disease. The disease is linked to clumps of a protein fragment called amyloid-beta. Short strands of RNA called aptamers can stick to chosen targets. Yet they had rarely been used in amyloid research.

The team raised aptamers against a form of amyloid-beta made of small clusters. The aptamers latched onto shared features found across amyloid deposits. They were highly sensitive but not very specific. That trade-off matters for anyone hoping to use aptamers to detect or treat amyloid diseases.
plos-pone-0007794:
Jakob Benedict Seidelin and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks for faulty sensing in Crohn's disease beyond the known genetic cases. A gene called CARD15 helps cells sense muramyl dipeptide, a bacterial fragment. Patients with certain CARD15 variants sense it poorly.
