Animal work suggests healthy CARD15 signaling helps prevent bowel inflammation. The authors tested patients without any disease-linked variants. They found evidence of impaired CARD15 signaling in those patients too. The defect may thus be wider than the gene's mutation list. That widens the search for what goes wrong in Crohn's disease.
plos-pone-0007894:
Herman van Haagen and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It predicts protein interactions from the literature itself. Proteins rarely work alone; their partnerships drive cell life. Knowing which proteins interact is central to biology.

The team's method compares the context in which proteins appear in papers. Proteins mentioned in similar contexts are predicted to interact. The approach outperformed earlier algorithms that needed both names in one sentence. Literature context is a rich, untapped data source. The method turns the published record into a discovery tool. It grows stronger with every new paper that appears.
plos-pone-0007994:
Chang-Jiun Wu and colleagues searched lung tumors for a pattern of chemical tags in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tags are phosphates, added to proteins when signal chains fire. In cancer, those chains often fire at the wrong times and in the wrong cells.

Reading many tags at once, the team found a compact pattern that marks lung cancer. Such a signature could help doctors spot the disease or sort its kinds from a tissue sample. The work also shows which signal chains run hot in these tumors, a map for drug ideas that aim to cool them.
plos-pone-0008094:
Shannan Ho Sui and colleagues checked whether germ weapon genes really cluster on genome islands in PLOS ONE in 2009. Islands are blocks of genes that look borrowed from another species. Many past reports, each on one kind of germ, placed virulence genes inside such blocks.

Across many genomes at once, the team tested the link with care. Clusters did tend to hold weapon genes more often than the rest of the genome. A borrowed block can thus arm a mild germ in one stroke, which is one way new disease strains are born.
plos-pone-0008194:
Mohamed Elrefaei and colleagues studied immune control in HIV infection in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. HIV weakens the immune system and raises levels of several blocking signals. These include CTLA-4, TGF-beta, and IL-10. The team examined HIV-specific CD8 T cells, killer cells that target the virus. They asked what controls their output of suppressive signals.

The authors found that CTLA-4 signaling on CD4 T cells regulates this output. Helper CD4 cells thus shape what the killer cells release. That finding clarifies one route of immune dysregulation in HIV. It may help efforts to restore stronger immune responses during treatment.
plos-pone-0008294:
Desheng Lu, Jerry X. Liu, and Tomoyuki Endo tested a drug on leukemia cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Abnormal activation of Wnt/beta-catenin signaling promotes several cancers. That pathway is switched on in chronic lymphocytic leukemia cells. Uncontrolled signaling may contribute to the defect in apoptosis, the death of faulty cells. The team studied ethacrynic acid, an existing drug.

Ethacrynic acid showed selective toxicity to the leukemia cells. It acted by inhibiting the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway. Selectivity matters, because a useful drug must spare healthy cells. The result suggests a new use for an old drug.
plos-pone-0008394:
Henri Blehaut and colleagues tested a vitamin treatment in children in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. Seven genes for folate metabolism sit on chromosome 21. Folate deficiency may contribute to intellectual disability in Down's syndrome, which is trisomy 21. The team investigated oral folate supplementation, given as leucovorin or folinic acid. Children received a daily dose based on body weight.

They measured effects on the developmental quotient of the children. Thyroid status was also examined as an influence on results. If a cheap vitamin improves development, the benefit would be large. The study tests that hope rigorously.
plos-pone-0008494:
Jiahui Yang and co-authors build a rabbit model of lupus in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Lupus, or SLE, is an autoimmune disease with wide effects. A factor called BAFF helps B lymphocytes survive as they mature. Blood BAFF levels have been tied to disease activity in patients. The team study BAFF and its receptors in rabbits with a lupus-like illness. Rabbits offer a larger animal model than mice.

They track how BAFF levels relate to disease signs in the model. They also map which receptors the B cells carry. The model may help test BAFF-blocking drugs before human trials. It adds a system for study of lupus mechanisms.
plos-pone-0008594:
Ryan Kelly and co-authors compare genetics across fifty species in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their setting is the northeastern Pacific rocky intertidal community. Comparing many species across the same seascape can identify differing structure. Some species show strong population structure, others very little. Those contrasts suggest hypotheses about processes causing variation. Larval dispersal and habitat may drive the differences. The team gather population genetic data for all fifty species.

They find wide variation in genetic structure among neighboring species. Species sharing a shoreline do not share a genetic pattern by default. The comparative approach focuses marine protection on species with isolated populations. Such species are most vulnerable to local extinction.
plos-pone-0008694:
Martin Rosvall and Carl Bergstrom offered a fresh way to watch networks change over time. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Networks show up in cell biology, travel, trade, and science itself. Links inside them shift constantly, yet most maps freeze a single moment. A frozen map can hide the very change that matters.

The authors built a method that follows clusters as they form, merge, and fade. It squeezes long records into clear pictures of change. Readers get a tool for spotting turning points in large systems. The approach suits fields from disease spread to money flows.
plos-pone-0008794:
Jacqueline Merrill, Tiffany Melhuish, Michael Kagey, and colleagues gave a supporting role to loose protein handshakes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells tag proteins with SUMO, a small modifier that changes their behavior. Enzymes attach the tag in a relay chain. The last enzyme in the chain, an E3, picks the targets. Some proteins also grip SUMO without a chemical bond, through short motifs.

For the E3 enzyme Pc2, also called CBX4, those loose grips mattered. Motifs that bind SUMO boosted the enzyme's tagging activity. Loose contacts thus help steer a covalent tagging system. The insight refines models of gene control by SUMO.
plos-pone-0008894:
Elaine Long, Stephanie Baker, Vanessa Oliveira, and colleagues showed peacekeeper cells need sugar trimming to reach grafts. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Donor antigen plus a gentle antibody can teach mice to accept transplants. The lesson enriches regulatory T cells that guard the graft. Those cells must travel to the right tissues to work. An enzyme that trims sugar chains on proteins proved essential.

Without alpha-1,2-mannosidase and proper N-glycosylation, Treg cells migrated poorly. Graft tolerance failed along with their travel. Sugar processing, an unlikely suspect, gates transplant success. The link opens a new angle on inducing tolerance in patients.
plos-pone-0008994:
Alfredo Csibi and co-authors followed a protein switch that lets mouse muscle grow, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Building muscle needs the mTOR pathway, a master controller of protein making. Young muscle cells must both mature and bulk up, and mTOR drives each step. The switch in question, eIF3f, is a part of the cell's protein-building machine.

The team showed eIF3f passes signals from mTOR to the machine that builds muscle protein. Without it, muscle cells failed to mature and enlarge normally in mice. The part acts only when the mTOR signal calls for growth. Knowing this link helps explain wasting diseases where muscle growth stalls.
plos-pone-0009094:
Miguel Aste-Amézaga and co-authors built antibodies that switch off a key development signal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Notch receptors guide cell fate choices throughout animal development and growth. When Notch1 signalling runs out of control, several cancers can follow. The signal also feeds the growth of tumour blood vessels.

The team characterised antibodies that block Notch1's signal directly. The antibodies inhibited the normal receptor and mutated versions alike. Mutant receptors drive some leukaemias and can resist simpler blockers. A blocker covering both normal and mutant forms could serve as a cancer drug scaffold.
plos-pone-0009194:
Sean Menke and co-authors published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cities are the fastest-growing habitat on Earth, yet few native species thrive in them. One that does is Tapinoma sessile, a widespread native ant often treated as a pest. The authors asked how this ant conquered city life in place after place.

They used DNA barcoding of one gene to compare ant populations across habitats and regions. The genetic patterns showed separate lineages succeeding again and again in cities. In other words, urban success was convergent, not a single lucky invasion. That makes this ant a model for how native species adapt to human-made habitats.
plos-pone-0009294:
Hong Zhang and co-authors published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV still passes from mother to child where treatment is scarce. The first virus to take hold, the founder virus, sets the course of infection. Its outer coat protein is the immune system's main target.

The team studied coat genes from Zambian infants infected around birth. They focused on subtype C, the form common in southern Africa. The infants' viruses showed restricted genetic diversity in the coat. A narrow founder population tells vaccine designers what the virus looks like at its most vulnerable moment, right at transmission.
plos-pone-0009394:
Patricio Retamal and co-authors published this typhoid study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Salmonella Typhi causes typhoid fever in humans only. Its cousin Typhimurium infects many animals. Comparing their DNA, the team found a shared island of genes called SPI-3, but three genes are broken in Typhi.

They built a Typhi strain carrying working SPI-3 sequences from its cousin. The rebuilt strain showed changed behavior inside host cells. Those changes reveal what Typhi lost as it specialized on humans. Understanding the trade helps explain why one Salmonella causes typhoid while another causes food poisoning.
plos-pone-0009494:
Chang-Shi Chen and colleagues found a new player in worm defense in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many bacteria attack cells with pore forming toxins, which punch holes in cell coats. The worm C. elegans resists such toxins in part through a signal path led by DAF-2. That same path also controls lifespan and stress responses. The team searched for new parts of the defense network.

They identified a protein named WWP-1 as a modulator of the DAF-2 path in this defense. Changing WWP-1 changed how well worms stood up to toxins. The result links aging biology with immune defense in one small animal. It shows a single network guarding against both time and attack.
plos-pone-0009594:
Cameron McDonald and colleagues joined two health problems in a mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Schistosomiasis is a worm infection that burdens many poor nations. Iron deficiency is common in the same regions, often from poor diet and from the infection itself. The team varied iron stores in mice infected with the worm. They then measured how severe the disease became.

Mice with higher iron stores had worse disease outcomes. That result warns against assuming iron supplements always help in worm regions. Iron can feed the very processes that harm the host. Care programs may need to weigh iron and infection together, not separately.
plos-pone-0009694:
During the 2009 flu pandemic, doctors noticed that very heavy patients often fared worse. Oliver Morgan and colleagues checked whether morbid obesity itself raised the risk of hospital care and death. Their analysis of pandemic cases appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The team separated obesity from other chronic illnesses that often travel with it. Even apart from those conditions, morbid obesity stood out as a risk factor. That finding helped doctors spot which flu patients needed the closest watch. It also shaped advice on who should get vaccine and early treatment first.
plos-pone-0009794:
Before birth, the placenta and its support tissues grow from a handful of early cell types. Ilya Chuykin and colleagues described two of those cell lineages in rats. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The lineages are trophoblast cells, which help form the placenta, and extraembryonic endoderm cells. Both were derived from rat preimplantation embryos, embryos at the earliest stage. Describing these lineages gives researchers reference points for lab-grown cells. Rats are a standard model for studying how mammals develop. Such references support studies of early development and pregnancy.
plos-pone-0009894:
Many genes switch on and off in cycles, like cell division or daily rhythms. Ning Li and colleagues built a way to group those cycling genes by the shape of their cycles. Their method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Functional clustering groups genes that behave alike over time. The profiles were periodic transcriptional profiles, waves of gene activity that repeat. The grouping tool is ARMA, a time-series model with two tuning parts, p and q. Better groups help scientists find genes that share one clock. The cycles repeat on set schedules, hour by hour or day by day.
plos-pone-0009994:
A colon cancer gene also helps run the cell division clock, through its grip on a DNA enzyme. Yang Wang and colleagues mapped that connection in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The gene is APC, adenomatous polyposis coli. APC mutations start most inherited colon cancer syndromes.

APC has binding domains for topoisomerase II-alpha, an enzyme that untangles DNA. Those domains influence cell cycle progression, the march toward division. They also influence aneuploidy, having the wrong number of chromosomes. The link ties a famous cancer gene to chromosome stability. Aneuploidy is a hallmark of many cancers.
plos-pone-0010194:
The authors were Andreas Neueder, Steffen Jakob, Gisela Pöll, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used yeast to study ribosome building. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, built from RNA and many proteins. A protein called rpS5 is a primary binder of the small subunit, one of the factory's two main parts.

Removing rpS5 in yeast broke new subunits and disturbed their assembly. The team also found a local role for rpS5 in the final processing of 18S ribosomal RNA. Such detail helps explain how cells finish building working ribosomes, step by step.
plos-pone-0010294:
The authors were Emma Stokes, Samantha Strindberg, Parfait Bakabana, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study counted great apes and elephants across a wide conservation landscape. Protected areas anchor conservation, but many species need far larger ranges than parks provide. Landscape-scale programs try to meet those needs across mixed land, and managers must show whether that broader work actually pays off.

The team monitored animal abundance at large spatial scales to judge effectiveness. Reliable counts of apes and elephants are hard to gather over such areas. Their methods and results help other landscapes measure real impact.
plos-pone-0010394:
Ming-Show Wong, Der-Shan Sun and Hsin-Hou Chang built a bacteria-killing coating lit by normal light for PLOS ONE in 2010. A known catalyst, titanium dioxide, kills germs but usually needs ultraviolet light. UV is risky indoors and absent from most room lighting. Newer versions respond to visible light and work more efficiently under sunlight. The team added tiny silver structures to boost the effect.

Their material killed bacteria well under ordinary visible light. Such coatings could disinfect hospital or kitchen surfaces without UV lamps. The study measured how strong the killing was under set conditions. Safe, light-driven hygiene is the aim. The work sits where materials science meets infection control.
plos-pone-0010494:
Fernando Wolff and colleagues described hepatitis C co-infection among HIV patients in southern Brazil for PLOS ONE in 2010. The two viruses often travel together through shared routes. Rates of co-infection and the mix of hepatitis C types vary widely around the world. Some people clear hepatitis C on their own; most do not. The team measured all three features in their patient group.

Local genotype data matter because hepatitis C treatment response depends on type. Knowing how many co-infected patients need care shapes clinic planning. The study fills a regional gap in a global patchwork. It also gives Brazilian clinicians numbers from their own population, not imported estimates. Co-infection care is a growing load on HIV services.
plos-pone-0010594:
Stella Tommasi and colleagues examined how a smoke-related chemical rewrites cell markings, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The chemical stood in for the harmful compounds found in tobacco smoke. The team focused on methylation, the chemical tags that help control gene activity.

Human cells exposed to the compound showed widespread changes in those tags. Some regions lost tags while specific genes gained them. That double pattern matches changes seen in lung cancers linked to smoking. Mapping where the tags move helps explain how smoke can push normal cells toward cancer over time.
plos-pone-0010694:
Audrey Chaput-Bardy and colleagues watched damselflies decide whether to leave home, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The damselfly Calopteryx splendens lives along streams, and young adults may stay or disperse. Leaving brings chances to breed elsewhere but costs energy and safety.

Wing length, sex, body state, and local conditions all swayed the choice. The team also tracked how leaving affected survival. Stronger fliers in good state took the risk more often. Dispersal is the engine of range change, so knowing who leaves helps predict how stream insects will shift as their habitats warm and dry.
plos-pone-0010794:
Rim Al Safadi and colleagues studied a surface protein in group B streptococcus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This germ is a leading cause of sepsis and meningitis in newborns. Its surface proteins help it grip and enter human tissues. One, called Lmb, grips laminin, a protein found throughout the body's scaffolding.

Strains carrying a mobile DNA element, IS1548, near the lmb gene made more of the gripping protein. The element sits in the spacer between two surface protein genes. A small hop of DNA can thus turn up a germ's grip. Tracking which strains carry the element may help predict which ones invade newborns most readily.
plos-pone-0010894:
Stéphanie Lorain, Cécile Peccate, Maëva Le Hir and co-authors published this gene therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by errors in the huge dystrophin gene. One repair idea is RNA surgery: swapping a faulty exon, a coding segment, for a good copy inside the cell's message. Earlier tools could replace only the start or end of a message.

The team built a double-sided trans-splicing tool that targets a single middle exon, using the mouse version of the disease gene as a test bed. Their constructs replaced the mutated exon accurately and efficiently in the test message, and adding a downstream helper segment improved the result. Lorain and colleagues prove mid-message exon exchange is feasible, widening the range of mutations that RNA repair could one day treat.
plos-pone-0010994:
Raychel Chambers and Toru Takimoto published this virus study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sendai virus, a relative of measles and mumps viruses, assembles its new copies at the cell surface. Its inner core, the nucleocapsid, must travel from the cell's interior to those budding sites, but that journey had never been watched, so the team built a glowing version of the virus.

They fused a fluorescent tag to the L protein, part of the core, in a virus that still grew like the normal one. Time-lapse microscopy showed the tagged cores moving in directed, jumpy runs, and follow-up work tied that transport to intracellular vesicles rather than free drifting. Chambers and Takimoto give the first live view of a paramyxovirus core in transit, a step viruses must complete to spread, and therefore a possible point of attack.
plos-pone-0011094:
Rehle, Hallett, Shisana and colleagues published an HIV study from South Africa in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used three large national surveys, carried out in 2002, 2005 and 2008. From those surveys they estimated how many new infections occurred in each period.

Their estimates showed a fall in new infections over the six years covered. That fall suggests prevention work in the country was starting to pay off. Careful estimates like these help leaders judge which programs to keep or expand. The study offers hope, while still showing a very large epidemic to manage.
plos-pone-0011194:
Hasegawa and Miwa characterized mutant worms in PLOS ONE in 2010. A tiny roundworm is widely used to study how bodies handle toxins. Certain mutants fail to control a large set of detox enzymes, the second phase defenses that make poisons safer to expel.

By describing the genes and cells behind those mutants, the team mapped part of the control circuit. That circuit guards against chemical threats from food and the environment. Its parts may have counterparts in people, informing drug safety science. The worm's simplicity lets researchers find control genes that would be hard to spot in complex animals.
plos-pone-0011294:
Bergerot, Julliard and Baguette studied broken habitats in PLOS ONE in 2010. When habitat is cut into fragments, species do not just decline one by one. The working relationships between species also fade. The team measured how those functional links change along a gradient of fragmentation.

Links declined as fragmentation grew more severe. That loss can unravel pollination, predation and other services that hold communities together. Conservation that protects only single species may miss the ties between them. Corridors that reconnect fragments could restore relationships as well as movement. The study gives that argument measured support.
plos-pone-0011394:
Daniel Hess, Jeffrey Chisholm, and Ariel Igal tested in 2010 whether blocking one fat-making enzyme can stop lung cancer cells. Cancer cells need large amounts of fat building blocks to keep dividing, and the enzyme they studied helps make those fats. The team blocked it in lung cancer cells grown in the lab and watched what followed.

Blocked cells stalled in their division cycle and then died by the cell's built-in self-destruct program. Hitting both growth and survival with one block makes the enzyme an attractive drug target. The result also supports a broader strategy in cancer research: starve tumors of the building materials they need most. More work is needed before any drug reaches patients, but the study names a clear weak point in lung cancer cells.
plos-pone-0011494:
Nadège Salvi and co-authors reported in 2010 changes in the breathing muscle of rats with type 1 diabetes. Diabetes is usually tracked in pancreas, eyes, kidneys, and nerves, but the diaphragm, the muscle that powers every breath, also lives under high blood sugar. The team examined its structure and function in diabetic rats and measured a metabolic regulator called PPAR beta delta.

The regulator was turned up in the diabetic diaphragm, alongside structural and functional changes in the muscle. Diabetes thus quietly remodels the machinery of breathing itself. That remodeling could help explain why people with diabetes fare worse in respiratory illness and intensive care, where a tired diaphragm is dangerous. The study argues that the diaphragm belongs on the list of tissues diabetes care should watch, not just the classic four.
plos-pone-0011594:
Cajsa Isgren and colleagues surveyed a muscle disease of Standardbred racehorses in PLOS ONE in 2010. The condition, exertional rhabdomyolysis, makes muscles seize and break down after hard exercise. It occurs in many athletic horse breeds, yet little was known about its pattern in Standardbreds used for racing worldwide.

The survey mapped how common the problem is and which factors raise the risk. Surprisingly, horses prone to the condition also tended to show stronger racing performance. That trade-off between speed and muscle fragility is useful for trainers and vets, who must balance fast training against a real risk of breakdown.
plos-pone-0011694:
José Aguilar-Yáñez and co-authors made a flu vaccine component inside bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic exposed the need for faster, higher-yield vaccine production. Growing virus in eggs or cell culture is slow, so the team tried a different factory: the common bacterium Escherichia coli.

They produced a fragment of the pandemic virus's hemagglutinin, its main surface protein, in the bacteria. A bacterial pipeline could be scaled up far faster than egg-based production during an emergency. The work supports a shortcut that might deliver pandemic vaccines while they can still do the most good.
plos-pone-0011794:
Guohua Wang and co-authors studied how an immune signal controls microRNA production, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Building gene regulatory networks is a central theme of systems biology. As understanding of how microRNAs are made and what they do grew, mapping the networks they form became a natural next step.

Working in HeLa cells stimulated with interferon gamma, the team showed the transcription factor STAT1 regulates microRNA transcription. One protein thus conducts both the classic alarm genes and the small-RNA response. That double duty reshapes how the interferon network should be drawn.
plos-pone-0011894:
Virginie Renaud and colleagues reported in 2010 that the way a protein folds can hide it from the immune system. The protein is MMP-2, an enzyme that cuts matrix material outside cells. Part of MMP-2 forms a peptide that killer T cells can recognize when it is shown on a cell's display molecules, as happens with human melanoma cells.

Presenting that peptide required an unusual cross-presentation route, and the protein's own folding prevented the immune-visible piece from being generated inside the cell. In effect, correct folding works as camouflage. The result matters for cancer immunology, since a tumor protein that hides from T cells is a harder target for immune-based treatments.
plos-pone-0011994:
Gitanjali Jayachandran and co-workers reported in 2010 that putting back a lost tumor guard gene makes lung cancer cells far easier to kill with a standard drug. The guard, called NPRL2, sits in a stretch of chromosome 3 that tumors often lose. Its yeast kin helps the cell sense nitrogen, and the human gene had shown signs of holding tumors back.

With NPRL2 restored, human lung cancer cells of the most common type grew much more prone to death from cisplatin, the workhorse drug for this disease. The gene works by steering key parts of the DNA repair path: cisplatin harms DNA, and weak repair makes that harm fatal. A test for NPRL2 could one day help doctors pick who will gain most from the drug.
plos-pone-0012094:
Christopher Ciccolella, Nathan Raynard, John Mei, and colleagues studied how legume root nodules handle hydrogen gas, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inside these nodules, partner bacteria pull nitrogen from the air so the plant can grow, but the process also makes hydrogen. In most nodules that gas simply escapes, which wastes energy the plant and bacteria worked hard to store.

The authors found that some nodules use two kinds of bacterial enzymes to catch the hydrogen and recycle it. Recycling turns a waste product back into useful fuel for the nodule. Work like this matters for farming, since better nitrogen use by legume crops could cut the need for added fertilizer.
plos-pone-0012194:
Melita Dvorak-Ewell, Dan Wendt, Chuck Hague, and co-authors developed an enzyme treatment for a rare storage disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In Morquio A syndrome, a missing enzyme lets a sugar chain called keratan sulfate build up, deforming bones and cartilage, and no treatment existed. The team made the human enzyme in the lab as a candidate replacement therapy.

They tested it on human cells in culture and tracked where it travels in the bodies of normal mice, with attention to cartilage. Reaching cartilage is the hard part, since that tissue has no blood supply of its own. A therapy that gets there could change a disease that now can only be managed, not treated.
plos-pone-0012294:
Elke Bergmann-Leitner, Ryan Mease, Patricia De La Vega, and co-authors tested a malaria vaccine antigen in PLOS ONE in 2010. CelTOS is a protein malaria parasites use to cross through host cells, both in the mosquito and in the mammal they infect, and infection cannot succeed without it. Because the protein barely changes across malaria species, it raised a rare hope: one vaccine part protecting against several species at once.

Immunizing with CelTOS from the deadliest human malaria species protected animals against challenge with a different, mouse malaria species. Cross-species protection is the exception in malaria vaccinology, where most candidates guard only their own strain. A conserved weak point like this is exactly what a broadly useful vaccine needs.
plos-pone-0012394:
Xevi Biarnés, Alessandro Marchiori, Alejandro Giorgetti and colleagues modeled how a bitter taste receptor grabs its target, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The receptor TAS2R38 sits on the tongue and detects a bitter compound called PTC; people differ sharply in whether they taste it at all. Hard data on the receptor's shape were lacking, so the team built a computer model.

Their model shows the pocket where PTC fits and which receptor parts grip it. The fit explains why small gene changes make some people strong tasters and others blind to the bitterness. Models like this guide research on taste, appetite, and why patients differ in tasting bitter medicines.
plos-pone-0012494:
Roopa Kothapalli, Asif Khan, Basappa and colleagues used computer design to find blockers of a cartilage-chewing enzyme, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme MMP-13 cuts type II collagen, the main protein of joint cartilage, and it is active in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis but not in healthy adult tissue. That selectivity makes it a tempting drug target.

The team aimed at a side region of the enzyme, its hemopexin domain, whose special residues differ from sister enzymes. Blocking there could spare related enzymes and cut side effects. Computer-first design narrows thousands of candidates to a testable few, saving years of bench screening for arthritis drug hunters.
plos-pone-0012594:
Chris Bauch, Samit Bhattacharyya and Robert Ball modeled vaccine free-riding in brand-new child immunization programs, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. When vaccination is voluntary, some parents skip shots while relying on others' immunity — free-riding that can erode coverage. Classic models studied settled programs, but new programs, like those for newly licensed vaccines, start with no habits or trust built up.

Their model shows free-riding behavior can emerge rapidly in new programs, threatening coverage early. Early erosion is dangerous because a shaky launch can fix public doubt for years. Program designers should pair new vaccine rollouts with strong default policies and communication from day one.
plos-pone-0012694:
Stiebler, Hoang, Egan and co-authors studied how malaria parasites safely store iron-rich waste. Blood-feeding parasites turn loose heme, which is toxic, into a crystal called hemozoin. Their 2010 study used a lab stand-in crystal, beta-hematin, to find what starts crystal growth.

In sour conditions the amount of loose heme that stays dissolved rises, and that rise helps crystals form on their own. Because many malaria drugs act on this waste path, its details matter. A clearer picture of crystal birth may guide better drug design.  The chemistry was followed over time in controlled solutions.
plos-pone-0012794:
Lovatt and Bijlmakers showed that T cell receptor signals steady a growth protein called beta-catenin. Beta-catenin signalling is essential while T cells develop in the thymus. Its role in mature T cells, the finished defenders in blood, had only lately come into view when they wrote in 2010.

Their study found that when the T cell receptor is triggered, beta-catenin destruction slows and the protein builds up. A steadied pool can then switch genes on in the mature cell. The result extends a development pathway into adult immunity.
plos-pone-0331994:
Silke Velghe and colleagues asked parents what changed after their children with developmental coordination disorder finished an intensive week of balance training, forty hours packed into five days. These children struggle with movement in ways that spill into play, friendship, and family life. Questionnaires from one group of parents and group discussions with another were analysed in sequence for shared themes.

Parents reported children joining in more, starting activities on their own, and carrying themselves with new confidence, with calmer family dynamics alongside. Features of the week mattered: a dedicated therapist, a welcoming setting, and the sheer amount of practice. Parents also grew in understanding and spoke differently with teachers and others, which helped the changes hold three months on. The authors treat empowerment, in child and parent alike, as the engine.
plos-pone-0336194:
Jessica Ainooson and colleagues report a quality fix at one medical centre for day surgery on the womb and ovaries for non cancer causes. Too many patients stayed over two hours in recovery. Chart review pointed at a routine pre surgery drug, gabapentin, given for pain, which can also sedate. The default order for a set dose was removed.

Average recovery stay fell from about three hours to about two hours and forty minutes, a drop near thirteen percent. Use of the drug collapsed from nearly all patients to almost none, with no rise in pain scores. Age gaps in stay time also vanished. Dropping a routine drug, the project shows, can speed recovery safely.
plos-pone-0341194:
İbrahim Kırçova and three co-authors study why people intend to buy their own electric scooter. A survey of more than three hundred people, followed by interviews, tested a chain of reasoning. Enjoyment shapes how useful scooters seem. So do hopes for the technology's future, and how price feels. Those beliefs then shape buying intent.

Perceived performance proved to be the hub of the whole model. It raised buying intent mainly by making people feel free and capable. The urge for novelty played only a small part. Interviews added key conditions. Safe roads, clear parking rules, and honest running costs strengthened the whole chain. The authors advise sellers to prove usefulness and support, not chase novelty. This matters most for young city buyers.
plos-pone-0341994:
Nicholas Steel, Paola Zaninotto, Oby O Enwo, and James Banks published this 2026 study of health care preferences among older adults in England. Using a nationally representative aging survey of people fifty and over. They examined six general preferences, from appetite for risk to whether quality or length of life matters more, and how preferences vary by person.

Clear age and sex patterns appeared: women leaned toward deciding jointly with doctors and prizing quality of life, while the oldest participants preferred delegating decisions and avoiding risk. Steel offers these patterns as conversation starters, never substitutes for asking the individual.
plos-pone-0343894:
Middle schoolers who cannot organize homework lose marks they could easily earn, and a coaching program called HOPS teaches those missing skills. Jenelle Nissley-Tsiopinis and colleagues present a replication trial plan, in PLOS One in 2026, testing the program when ordinary school staff deliver it.

About thirty schools will join, with students aged eleven to fourteen assigned by school to the program or a waiting list. School-employed providers are the point: the original trial used research staff, which schools cannot afford at scale. A third arm, taught by researchers, lets the team compare delivery styles directly. Results will show whether the program survives real-world staffing.
plos-pone-0345394: Antosik and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on hardship early in life in nineteenth-century Poznan. The birth cohort ran from 1830 to 1855. The team traced how harsh early conditions shaped who people could marry and how far they rose in society. Old city records let them follow whole lives. The study shows how early hardship can echo across a lifetime.
plos-pone-0345694: Wang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on fishways, the channels that help fish pass dams. They used computer fluid modeling to study water flow in overflow weir fishways. The aim was to map the hydraulic regimes, the zones of fast, slow, and swirling water fish must cross. Flow maps help engineers shape passages that tired fish can actually climb.
plos-pone-0346794:
Note on status: this is a protocol for a systematic review, written by Collen Mafira Ngadhi and colleagues and published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The planned review concerns family group decision making, a child welfare approach in which extended families meet to build their own safety plans for children instead of having officials decide alone.

The team will gather studies from 2014 through the end of 2024, in English, covering this model and its variants in both numbers-based and interview-based research. Their focus is how the approach is applied and used, with lessons for developing countries where child welfare systems face distinct strains. The goal is guidance grounded in what has actually been tried.
plos-pone-0346994:
Amber Bennett-Weston and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE building a one-question measure of therapeutic empathy, the warmth and understanding patients feel from their clinician. Empathy improves outcomes for both sides, yet existing questionnaires are long and differ, making services hard to compare. The team designed a universal single item, in pictorial and text versions, usable by patients, practitioners, students, and observers, then tested the patient version with experts and over five hundred patients.

Both versions tracked an established empathy measure closely, and barely tracked a clinical neutrality measure, the opposite pole, as intended. The agreement held for patients of every gender and ethnicity, and across practitioner types. Ethnic minority patients rated their practitioners' empathy lower than White patients did, the kind of known group difference a valid scale should detect. The measure is offered for settings where a full questionnaire is impractical, such as routine feedback.
plos-pone-0347194:
Lindsey D Cameron and Jirs Meuris investigated when unpredictable pay pushes low- and middle-wage workers to quit. Variable paychecks are common in gig and hourly work and are suspected of corroding well-being. Their 2026 study combined interviews and surveys with ride-hailing drivers to build predictions, then tested them on matched records for more than seven hundred truck drivers at a national carrier.

Pay variability did raise quitting, but not evenly. The effect concentrated where lower-than-usual checks came often, where workers felt little control over earnings, and where the household depended on that paycheck. Even top-performing drivers quit over variability, and leavers likely ended up earning less annually. Interviews backed the same pattern. The authors frame unstable pay as a distinct source of precarity, beyond how much workers earn on average.
plos-pone-0347994:
Barsha Gadapani Pathak and colleagues used a social autopsy approach to trace how twenty-five women in rural Palwal district, India, came to lose their babies before birth. Structured interviews reconstructed each woman's path through pregnancy and care, and five health workers added the system's view. India's programmes target stillbirth on paper, yet these deaths are seldom reviewed and often never counted.

Three layers of delay appeared. Care was barely sought, because of beliefs, low sense of risk, and women's limited say. Care was hard to reach, through poor transport and restrictive norms. And there were gaps in what happened to mothers afterwards, a phase the system largely abandons. The authors argue that preventing stillbirth means fixing decisions at home and roads to care, not only clinic quality, and remembering the mother after the loss.
plos-pone-0348094:
Foster Amponsah-Manu and colleagues surveyed two thousand two hundred students in Ghana's Eastern Region about why so many refuse to give blood voluntarily, even though hospitals depend on donated blood. Their 2026 cross-sectional study asked about knowledge, beliefs, cultural pressures, and practical obstacles, then looked for patterns in who said no.

About four in ten students were unwilling to donate. Believing oneself ineligible, thinking donation is unsafe, and knowing little about it all pushed students away, as did discouragement from family or faith. Long waits, awkward locations, and lack of incentives mattered too. Free health check-ups were the most wanted reward. The authors recommend better education plus easier donation sessions.
plos-pone-0348494:
Feilong Qin and co-workers combine two analysis tricks to predict where hidden copper and gold ore bodies lie deep underground. Rock chemistry patterns can betray buried metal, but single elements give noisy hints. Their 2026 study first groups elements that travel together, then maps where their combined signal grows unusually strong, using a pattern rule tied to how signals cluster in space.

Applied to a known mining area in China, the combined map matched the real ore bodies well. The model also flagged a possible new ore body far below ground between two drill holes. Smarter reading of soil and rock chemistry could steer expensive drilling toward the most promising ground.
plos-pone-0348594:
Veterans of the 1990 to 1991 Gulf War worried their wartime exposures might make COVID-19 hit them harder. Donna L White and colleagues checked that fear in the national Million Veteran Program, in this 2026 PLOS One study of the pre-vaccine year 2020.

The team compared deployed veterans with era veterans who stayed home, looking at infection, hospital care, intensive care, and death. A surveyed subgroup let them test whether Gulf War Illness, the chronic multi-symptom condition affecting many deployed veterans, added extra risk. Records came from the veterans' health system's COVID data resource, giving the study nationwide reach.
plos-pone-0348794:
Weiqiang Zheng, Modan Su, and Changwei Gao work on virtual synchronous generators, devices that let solar and battery systems imitate the steadying behaviour of old-fashioned spinning power station machinery. A known flaw links two key settings: raising the virtual inertia that supports grid frequency also makes power output swing and overshoot when loads change. Their 2026 paper proposes a fix.

The team adds a lead-differential element to the controller and analyses the redesigned system both off-grid and connected. Experiments showed the power swings during sudden changes could be calmed by tuning the new element, while steady performance stayed intact. The change effectively separates quick response behaviour from long-run stability.
plos-pone-0348894:
Virginia T Scarlett and colleagues surveyed open source software contributors across University of California campuses. Just under three hundred students, faculty, researchers, and staff answered. Nearly all students and researchers called open source vital to their work, and well over half of seasoned contributors had served as project maintainers, not just users.

Lack of time, above all for documentation, was the top barrier. Respondents most wanted robust computing access and dedicated grants to sustain projects. Campus norms sometimes blocked contribution outright. Universities that prize open source in words, the survey argues, must fund maintainer time in budgets or lose the infrastructure their research stands on.
plos-pone-0349094:
Maaz Waseem, Zainab Kamran, and Amjad Ali reviewed trials of precision vaccines, built from tiny protein fragments or peptides, against a poultry E. coli that causes costly bird disease. Conventional vaccines and antibiotics struggle against the bacterium's diversity and rising drug resistance. Their 2026 meta-analysis combined ten studies measuring deaths, illness, immune response, production, and resistance outcomes, and summarized how machine learning is entering vaccine design.

Fragment-based vaccines significantly cut both deaths and illness, and advanced formats like membrane vesicles and nanoparticle carriers produced strong immune responses with protection across types. Results varied between studies, and evidence on cutting antibiotic use is still thin. Machine learning showed promise for choosing fragments and delivery routes. The authors call for large field trials and cost analysis before farm adoption.
plos-pone-0349194:
Kompal Sinha and co-authors set out a study plan in 2026 for measuring how business founders bounce back from hard times. Experts disagree on what founder resilience even means, so support programs lack a shared yardstick. No results are reported yet.

Guided by a view of resilience as a skill that can grow, the team will review past work, consult experts in rounds, and run interviews and group talks with people in business. Their aim is a tested set of measures that fits local context. Such a tool could help governments aim help where it keeps firms alive in unstable times.
plos-pone-0349394:
Yajun Dong and colleagues in China followed a very large group of women through their first fresh IVF cycle in 2026. Rather than asking only whether treatment ended in a baby, they tracked each stage, from a positive hormone test to a clinical pregnancy and then a live birth.

Hormone levels measured before treatment, including one that reflects egg supply, did not act in a simple more-is-better way. Mid-range values were linked with the best odds at some stages, forming a sweet spot. Different hormones mattered at different steps. The stage-by-stage view may help doctors set fair expectations and tune treatment for each woman.
plos-pone-0349794:
Caoimhe McKenna and co-authors used linked health records in 2026 to count illnesses and cancers in people with Down syndrome over twenty years. This group faces many health conditions, yet the full relative burden had not been tallied in one matched study.

Records for more than four thousand six hundred people with Down syndrome were compared with five times as many matched controls. Most conditions were more common, led by thyroid trouble, heart defects present from birth, and epilepsy. Risks of autism, kidney disease, and bowel inflammation were several times higher. Cancer patterns differed too. The tally helps clinics plan screening matched to real risks.
plos-pone-0350094:
Canan Sayın Temur authored this 2026 PLOS One study of future gym teachers. It looks at two kinds of attitudes. One is how aware they are of looks on social media. The other is what they believe about people with obesity. Future gym teachers shape how schoolchildren feel about bodies. So their own biases matter. The study surveyed more than one hundred fifty teacher trainees. It compared answers by gender and by year of study.

Women and men did not differ much on either measure. Awareness of looks was lower in second- and third-year students than in fourth-years. Some attitude gaps by year also appeared. Notably, the two measures were not linked to each other. Temur argues that teacher training should tackle both topics head-on. That would keep social media pressure and weight stigma out of school gyms.
plos-pone-0350194:
Van-Thuc Nguyen and co-authors simulated friction stir welding of aluminium and magnesium at the atomic scale in 2026. The process joins metals without melting them, using a spinning tool, and the mix of the two light metals is prized for vehicles.

Their simulation varied tool travel speed, spin speed, and pin shape, watching atoms mix and strain build. Aluminium atoms spread into the magnesium side more readily than the reverse. Faster travel and spin raised heat and disorder in the joint. The atom level view helps explain why some weld settings give strong joints and others leave weak, messy seams.
plos-pone-0350294:
Mochou Liu and co-authors weighed whether inclisiran, a twice-yearly injection that durably lowers harmful cholesterol, is good value for Chinese patients who already have cardiovascular disease. Many such patients miss cholesterol targets on statins alone. Their 2026 model simulated a lifetime of treatment from the health system's viewpoint, comparing the injection plus statins against statins alone and testing the result against China's accepted cost threshold.

Adding inclisiran bought extra healthy life years at a cost per year below the national threshold. The answer depended most on how much the drug cuts deaths, on discounting choices, and on its price, yet it stayed cost-effective in every scenario tried. A probability analysis put the chance of good value above ninety-five percent. The authors back wider use within the Chinese system.
plos-pone-0350394:
Justin C Cheung and Shirley S Ho surveyed just over one thousand people in Singapore about driverless delivery drones run by smart software. Public backing for new tech is often blamed on lack of facts. Their survey weighed hard knowledge against mental shortcuts like trust, news attention, and faith in scientists and officials, plus views of risk and gain.

Raw knowledge did not predict backing directly. Trust in the tech, attention to news, and respect for expert sources did, as did seeing more gain than risk. Knowledge still mattered in a roundabout way, by shaping trust and risk views. Campaigns that only pour out facts, the authors warn, will miss how people really judge new tools.
plos-pone-0350994:
Sadia Akter and colleagues ran a case control study in Bangladesh with two hundred and fifty one heart attack patients and the same number of matched controls. Two variants in a gene that activates vitamin D were tested against heart attack risk and blood vitamin D levels. Heart patients carried clearly lower vitamin D than controls.

One variant raised heart attack odds roughly two and a half times for carriers versus non carriers, with a clear link in men but not women. The second variant showed no link. Gene guided vitamin D checks will not replace classic risk care, but in South Asian groups this variant may mark extra risk worth watching.
plos-pone-0351194:
Expression of Concern: The PLOS One Editors warn readers to treat the findings in the study of the ING5 protein and cell growth with caution. Concerns cover overlapping figure panels, missing detail on statistical tests, partial loss of original data, and values under two figures that do not match the published charts. The original authors could not explain those mismatches.

One figure was replaced with repeat experiment images and its chart updated, which settled that part. Other worries remain open, including charts whose statistics cannot be confirmed. Editors advise special caution for results in the final figures. The underlying claim, that the protein is altered by a growth enzyme and guides cell division apart from a known guard protein, stays unproven until data are complete.
plos-pone-0351394:
Teenagers and their teachers often see the same student's personality differently, and Marek Blatný and co-authors tracked those gaps over two years. Their 2026 PLOS One study followed about three hundred early adolescents and twenty-eight class teachers, comparing self-ratings with teacher ratings of traits and social skills.

Agreement ran highest for traits that are easy to watch from outside, like talkativeness. Teachers and girls agreed more on social skills than teachers and boys did. Both sides' ratings stayed fairly steady over time, and the gaps neither widened nor closed much. The authors advise care when judging quiet, hard-to-see traits from the classroom alone.
plos-pone-0351494:
Cristhian Rojas-Miliano and a large team audited how well qualitative health studies by Peruvian authors were reported between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-five. Qualitative work can reveal how patients and communities experience illness, but only if readers can judge how it was done. The reviewers gathered a hundred forty-seven studies and scored them against a standard reporting checklist for qualitative research.

Reporting was strongest in abstracts, aims, and findings, where nearly all studies did well. It was weakest where it matters for trust: many papers skipped the study's qualitative approach, the researchers' own position, and a quarter never mentioned ethics approval at all. Most studies came from Lima and half appeared in Spanish-language or regional outlets. The audit gives Peruvian journals and trainers a concrete fix list for raising the credibility of local qualitative work.
plos-pone-0351694:
Good medical reasoning weighs prior chances before test results, a style called Bayesian. Robert Parisien and colleagues surveyed about one hundred fifty bone and joint surgeons from an international study group, presenting eight clinical scenarios, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Average scores sat at three quarters of the fully Bayesian mark, showing decent but incomplete use. Almost nobody reasoned in a fully Bayesian way every time, while most reached it at least once. The dominant style was mixed: surgeons noted prior chances but underweighted them instead of updating cleanly. The authors hope naming the habit helps training programs normalize sharper reasoning at the bedside.
plos-pone-0351794:
Barbie dolls have long faced criticism for unreal body shapes. Sara Grafenauer, Belinda Durey, and Kevin Norton measured the newer dolls. They studied the 2016 Fashionista range. That range includes Curvy, Petite, and Tall Barbie. A redesigned Ken was included too. The study updates a famous 1996 comparison.

Each doll was measured carefully by hand. Math then scaled the dolls to adult height. Their proportions could then meet real population data. Waist and hip ratios now sit much closer to real ranges. The Curvy doll landed nearest the average woman. Gaps remain, the authors note. But the direction of change is clear.
plos-pone-0352094:
Dan Santos Alves and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One virus survey from the Brazilian Amazon. They tested stool samples from five hundred sixty children with stomach illness. The samples were collected between 2013 and 2022. All had already tested negative for the usual culprits, rotavirus and norovirus. The team screened for astroviruses, a less-watched cause of gut illness, in both common and rare forms.

About one in ten samples carried a classical astrovirus. Diarrhea, vomiting, and fever were the typical picture. School-age children were the most affected group. Sequencing found three classical types, plus one striking find. A rare non-classical type had never been reported in the Americas. A probable mixed-parentage strain also turned up. The authors say astroviruses deserve a place in regional checks on childhood diarrhea.
plos-pone-0352194:
Nona Attaran Kakhki and co-authors reviewed research on what cancer treatment does to the mouths, and the daily lives, of children who survive cancer. Mouth sores, damaged teeth, and dry mouth can shadow survivors for years, yet reviews of their quality of life were a decade old. The team searched five databases for studies since twenty twelve on survivors diagnosed before eighteen.

The review set out to update the older picture and to check how often studies asked children themselves, not only parents or charts. It maps what is known about how oral complications weigh on eating, comfort, confidence, and well-being after treatment ends. For survivorship programs, the map shows where mouth care and follow-through are documented, and where the child's own voice is still missing from the record.
plos-pone-0352394:
Mary Collier and six colleagues read the cargo of tiny vesicles shed by blood vessel cells. Their 2026 study cultures human vein cells and provokes them two ways. One stimulus is a classic inflammatory signal. The other is oxidised cholesterol, the kind tied to artery disease. Vesicles released into the medium were collected and their proteins catalogued by mass spectrometry. Over thirteen hundred proteins were measured. Cell death was checked alongside, to separate activation from dying.

Only the inflammatory signal increased cell death. Its vesicles carried a distinct protein signature. Two proteins, E-selectin and a phosphatase called DUSP7, rose as candidate markers of that death pathway. Vessel-lining cells under fatal inflammatory stress broadcast their state in vesicle cargo. Blood tests reading such cargo could someday report on hidden vascular injury. That would give cardiovascular doctors information from the vessel wall itself, long before symptoms or scans declare damage.
plos-pone-0352694:
Saran, Wood, and Marotta tested whether how a hand is drawn changes a mind task in a 2026 study. In the task, people judge whether a shown hand is left or right, which quietly makes them imagine moving their own hand. Sixty-two young adults judged both lifelike hands and simple line drawings.

Hands in easy positions were judged faster and more accurately than hands in awkward twists, as expected. Palm views showed the usual inner-side advantage. Whether the hand looked lifelike or drawn mattered only in certain views and angles, not across the board. Researchers choosing task images should know that picture style can nudge results in subtle ways.
plos-pone-0352794:
Volgemute and colleagues, in a 2026 study, refine a short Latvian personality questionnaire for use with athletes. Personality shapes who sticks with sport and who reaches the top, but many questionnaires in sport lack proper testing in athletes or fair comparison scores. More than nine hundred athletes from eighty-four sports took part, split into two linked studies.

The first study polished the fifty-three-item questionnaire, confirming a structure of five broad factors covering fourteen traits, with decent reliability. Scores could be compared fairly between men and women, and the team built age- and sex-adjusted standard scores. The second study linked traits to competitive level: a few traits, notably anxious insecurity, sociability, and orderliness, differed slightly between elite and non-elite athletes. The authors offer the tool as evidence-based support for athlete assessment, while warning that personality explains only a little of who wins.
plos-pone-0352994:
Yang Cheng, Yangzhi Jiang, and Qizhao Zhang present this 2026 PLOS One consumer study. It is built around an airline's breast cancer awareness campaign. Nearly eight hundred Delta Air Lines customers answered a survey about the campaign. The authors modeled how ethical judgments and social norms relate to doubt about company good deeds. They also modeled how that doubt relates to engagement and buying intent.

Customers who judged the campaign sound, and who felt peers approved, doubted the airline's motives less. Doubt, in turn, dragged down both engagement and buying intent. Engagement itself lifted buying intent. The authors advise companies to win real engagement, not just exposure. That is what turns cause campaigns into lasting goodwill.
plos-pone-0353394:
Victor Olivero-Ortiz and four colleagues sort salvaged laptop battery cells into well-matched families so they can live a second life, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Recovered cells vary wildly in capacity and resistance, and a battery pack is only as strong as its weakest member. The team measured each cell's discharge capacity and internal resistance, then used clustering and an iterative selection routine to assemble the most uniform set.

Their refined selection built a pack with more usable capacity, lower resistance, and higher peak power than the baseline method, using the same layout. Careful matchmaking of this kind turns electronic waste into dependable storage for solar systems and backup power.
plos-pone-0353694:
Chenchun Ding and colleagues search in 2026 for genes linked to cell ageing that could help diagnose a scarring lung disease with no clear cause. They combined public gene data from patients with a curated list of ageing related genes, then used learning methods to narrow the field. Lab tests in cells and animals checked the top candidates.

Two hub genes stood out, but only one showed a clear disease specific pattern and a close tie to ageing of lung surface cells. A drug already in use bound that gene's product in computer models and eased ageing signs in tests. More work is needed before clinical use.
plos-pone-0353794:
Rongpeng Liu and co-authors combine in 2026 large scale and single cell gene data to probe how a metabolic compound called fumarate may shape gum disease. The long term gum illness destroys tissue and bone around teeth, and metabolism is increasingly tied to immune behaviour. Their search looked for fumarate linked genes and cell groups that stood out in diseased tissue.

A fumarate linked immune pattern was enriched in diseased gums, and three genes rose consistently in both human tissue and a mouse model. Those genes sat mainly in immune and support cells and showed promise as markers. Computer screening flagged two drug candidates for future lab checks.
plos-pone-0354294:
Akinsola and colleagues, in a 2026 study, map the genes of goats across Nigeria and nearby countries in West Africa. Local goats support many families across forest, savanna, and dry Sahel lands, yet their shared history across borders was poorly traced. The team read tens of thousands of genetic markers in about two hundred animals.

Three broad genetic backgrounds emerged, and each crossed national borders rather than matching them. One linked the dry north, one linked southern dwarf goats, and one stood apart in Cameroon. Signs in the DNA point to very recent mixing across borders layered over much older exchanges. Numbers of breeding animals have shrunk sharply over the long term, and some herds showed more inbreeding than others. The team also flagged dozens of regions that may carry traits shaped by local conditions. Their map gives breeders and planners a clearer base for guarding these herds.
plos-pone-0354394:
Sharleen L O'Reilly leads a multi-country team setting out a study plan, published in 2026, to deliver a pregnancy coaching program across four European health systems. The program supports women at risk of diabetes in pregnancy through a phone app with personal coaching, and an earlier version showed promise. The new plan refines it and tests how well it lands in Ireland, Spain, Poland, and Norway, whose systems and populations differ sharply.

Women will be screened with a machine learning tool, then coached from early pregnancy to a year after birth, with app sessions, messages, and connected scales. The design studies rollout and health effects together, comparing periods before and during delivery of the program. O'Reilly and colleagues aim to learn what makes such coaching stick in routine care.
plos-pone-0354594:
Lv and colleagues, in a 2026 review, ask whether letting athletes choose their own rest breaks between efforts works as well as fixed rest times set by a coach. Fixed rests ignore that people recover at different speeds. Letting athletes rest until they feel ready is gaining fans, but study results were mixed.

The team gathered sixteen experiments with about two hundred eighty participants that compared self-chosen and fixed rests head to head. Overall, performance did not differ clearly between the two styles. When a few outlying studies were removed, a small edge appeared for self-chosen rest. Heart rate and blood lactate, a marker of hard effort, did not differ at all. The authors conclude that self-chosen rest is at least as good as fixed rest and may suit athletes who know their own recovery, while calling for larger, cleaner studies.
plos-pone-0354694:
Runfang Tian and colleagues track in 2026 how deaths from heart defects present at birth changed in China over two decades. Their data covered people up to age sixty four and came from national health yearbooks. They split trends by town and countryside, by sex, and by age, and they tested one rural insurance policy for children.

Death rates fell in both town and countryside, with a larger fall in towns and among males. Rates stayed higher in rural areas and for males overall. After the rural policy began, rural deaths kept easing. The authors urge stronger, targeted steps for groups still left behind.
plos-pone-0354794:
Michael A Kisley, a single author, published this 2026 survey study linking what people believe about animal feelings to how they shop. Two American surveys asked adults whether animals experience emotions, and how often they avoid products or foods that involve animal use; the second survey deliberately recruited many vegetarians and vegans.

Belief in animal emotions predicted avoidance of animal-tested goods, animal events, and animal foods, beyond age, schooling, and gender. Pet contact and personal moral or spiritual outlooks fed those beliefs. Kisley argues consumer ethics toward animals rests partly on how real their inner lives seem.
plos-pone-0354894:
Feng An and Wenyin Tao tackle a hard safety problem: spotting when a large language model reasons in deceptive ways. Older monitors label whole answers as safe or deceptive and lean on heavyweight teacher models. Their 2026 paper instead trains a tiny monitor that reads the model's hidden chain-of-thought states.

The monitor maps those states into a space where honest and deceptive reasoning sit apart. Training pulls similar cases together and pushes unlike ones away, so gradual shifts toward deception become visible. On a sycophancy test set, the contrastive monitor beat a standard classifier at flagging deceptive tendency. An and Tao argue that watching reasoning geometry offers a lighter path to self-supervised safety checks.
plos-pone-0355194:
Hailong Zong and colleagues assess in 2026 genetic variety and yield links in soybean lines from many origins, grown in two settings. Soybean is a key food and oil crop first raised in China, and breeders seek higher yield with good quality. A small set of DNA markers was run across the lines, and a dozen plant traits were measured for variety and grouping.

Plants varied widely in traits such as height, pod count, and seed weight. Marker analysis showed rich variety and split the lines into a few clear groups. Dozens of markers linked to yield traits, with a handful confirmed in both settings. Breeders can use those stable markers to pick parents.
plos-pone-0355294:
Tushna Vandrevala and her team asked Black and South Asian adults in Britain how they decide if health advice can be trusted. Good choices need facts that people can use and trust. Yet groups like these often get leaflets and web pages that ignore their lives, their faith, and their past care. The team held long talks with dozens of people and watched how advice moves in group settings.

Friends, kin, and social media ranked as the most trusted sources of health facts. Dry, stiff advice that felt cold pushed people to search in other places first. Some ways of checking matched those of the wider public. But past events and group norms shaped how checks were made, and why. The team urges health staff to write warm, plain advice with known local voices, or risk being tuned out for good.
plos-pone-0355394:
Mayu Takizawa and co-authors develop in 2026 a fast DNA test that can single out and count the exact bacterium strain used to ferment soybeans into natto. The strain looks almost identical to close relatives, and older markers fail on some odd isolates. Comparing dozens of genomes, the team found one communication gene that stays perfectly intact across the natto line while other markers wobble.

A test built on that gene measured amounts across a very wide range and stayed accurate even when swamped by other bacterial DNA. On shop bought fermented soy foods, test counts matched living cell counts closely. Food quality checks and hospital tracking could both use it.
plos-pone-0355494:
Tingxuan Li, Ziyu Liu, and Deping Zou survey in 2026 Chinese university students who use artificial intelligence tools to write in English as a second language. Their model links confidence with the tools, ease of use, felt usefulness, felt risk, and how actively students engage. Several hundred valid replies were tested with a structural model.

Confidence raised both ease and usefulness ratings. Oddly, students who found the tools most useful also reported stronger risk awareness, rather than less. A positive attitude drove active engagement, which linked more to good than to bad writing outcomes in students' own reports. The authors note self reports cannot prove real gains.
plos-pone-0355694:
Juying Li and five colleagues published a heart attack study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They focused on a cell alarm system that senses stray DNA and triggers inflammation, known as the cGAS-STING pathway. After a heart attack, that alarm may add to the damage in heart tissue.

Li's team searched for markers tied to this pathway that could flag injury, and they traced how the pathway acts after an attack. Their work names candidate markers that doctors might one day measure, and points to steps in the pathway that drugs could target. Both leads matter because limiting early damage is key to how well a patient recovers.
plos-pone-0356294:
Till Kastendieck, Ursula Hess, and Christophe Blaison test how a threat in one place stains feelings attached to places around it, in PLOS ONE in 2026. In two experiments totaling several hundred participants, people faced a threat of electric shock tied to one spot in a screen based environment, the hotspot. Theory predicted the surroundings would split: soured close by, sweetened farther away, a pattern called affective polarization of space.

Self reports confirmed the pattern. Near the hotspot, the area felt negative and highly arousing; farther out, it felt positive with low arousal. Body measures told a narrower story: skin and heart responses showed people felt more threatened near the spot, but did not mirror the polarization. Nor did feelings toward strangers shown at spots shift as predicted. The subjective geography of fear, the authors conclude, is real, but its reach into body and social judgment is limited.
plos-pone-0356394:
Shuang Shi developed a way to align roadside laser scanners and cameras without placing special targets in the street. Matching the two sensors is essential when they are fused to watch traffic across wide areas. The 2026 method reads natural features from real traffic scenes instead of artificial markers.

Shi matches shapes and structures across the two data types, working from rough matches to fine ones. Time consistency across frames steadies the result in busy, changing scenes. On a self-built roadside dataset, average errors stayed very small. The method also held up in dim light, with blocked views, and in dense traffic, which supports its use on real roads.
plos-pone-0356494:
Ronald Kibirige and colleagues studied epilepsy care in two districts of central Uganda, Buikwe and Mukono, in 2026 work based on fieldwork from 2024. People with epilepsy there attend community clinics and depend on daily anti-seizure medicine to stay safe. The team set out to learn how many patients actually take their medicine as directed, and what helps or gets in the way.

About two thirds of the nearly three hundred patients surveyed were taking their medicine well. Better adherence was linked with a modest steady income, while long waits at the clinic and too-low doses were linked with worse adherence. Interviews added human detail: fear of stigma, money worries, family support, and mistaken beliefs about the drugs all shaped whether patients kept up their treatment.
plos-pone-0356694:
Monika Dobrogowska studied young girls and beauty culture in a qualitative PLOS ONE paper from 2026. The trend nicknamed Sephora Kids involves preteens buying skincare and anti-aging products aimed at adults. Dobrogowska examined how concern with appearance and body capital takes hold so early in adolescence.

Through close qualitative work, the study traces how marketing and social media reach ever younger buyers. It also weighs what that early pressure costs the girls it targets. Parents, schools, and regulators debating age limits on such products gain grounded insight here. The work adds a careful voice to a debate often driven by headlines rather than by listening to young people themselves.
plos-pone-0356894:
Khaled A Alrasheed led a team of six authors studying digital tools in green construction, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Building information modeling, or BIM, lets teams design and test a building in software before building it. The team studied how BIM support affects the adoption of green building practice in the construction industry.

Alrasheed's findings show where the digital tool speeds up sustainable construction and where it stalls. Green features often fail on coordination, not intent, and BIM is built for coordination. Knowing its real effect helps firms decide how much to invest in the software and training. As building codes tighten on energy use, evidence on what actually drives adoption is valuable.
plos-pone-0356994:
Samuel J Enumah, Xue Wu, Xueya Cai, and Yue Li examined how reliance on contract labor, such as travel nurses, relates to hospital finances across the United States. Their 2026 study combined national hospital datasets covering nearly three thousand hospitals over multiple years, and tracked operating margins, total margins, and signs of financial distress against spending on temporary staff.

Hospitals spending more on contract labor ran thinner margins and faced more distress. Hospitals with high surgical volume fared better financially overall, but volume did not soften the drag from contract labor costs; the penalty appeared at busy and quiet hospitals alike. With closures threatening access to surgical care, the findings warn that stopgap staffing quietly erodes the hospitals it keeps afloat.
plos-pone-0357094:
Sarah E Stansfield and colleagues modeled a question about HIV prevention pills for women in South Africa. Could women take them only around the time of sex, rather than daily, and still be protected? Their 2026 study built a simulated group from a real Cape Town trial. The trial's records gave sex frequency and pill taking. The team then tested four schedules of the preventive drug combination. Each ran over six months.

Daily use protected best, with effectiveness in the mid-eighties percent range. On-demand schedules landed lower. But women who managed fewer than about three daily pills a week gained slightly from switching. The before-and-after schedule helped them, and they took fewer pills doing it. Offering on-demand options, the authors argue, could rescue protection for women whom daily routines defeat.
plos-pone-0357294:
Stephanie Rupp and Hanna Schwendemann listened to mothers in Germany whose children have speech or developmental concerns, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. Getting help means moving through referrals, waiting lists, and handovers between services. The authors studied that path as mothers live it, focusing on guidance, transitions, and communication.

Rupp and Schwendemann's qualitative work exposes where the system helps families and where it leaves them stranded. Breaks usually happen at transitions, when one service ends and another has not begun. Naming those weak points gives German health and education services a repair list. The mothers' accounts also remind planners that a pathway is only as good as its worst handover.
plos-pone-0357594:
Shili Yang and colleagues run a fully computational hunt for molecular links between a food toxin and liver cancer. The toxin, made by molds that contaminate stored grain and nuts, is known to harm the liver, but its cancer pathways stay fuzzy. The team merged toxin targets and cancer targets from public databases. They overlapped them with genes changed in a public liver tumor dataset. Then they ranked the survivors. Selection algorithms, docking, and motion simulation did the ranking.

A few hundred shared targets clustered in signaling, cell death, metabolism, and immune pathways. Five candidate genes rose to the top, some raised and some lowered in tumors, each sorting tumor from normal tissue well within the dataset. Docking predicted snug toxin binding, strongest for a major drug-processing enzyme. Yang and colleagues offer the five as leads for lab confirmation.
plos-pone-0357794:
Rili Yu and coauthors published a 2026 anesthesia study in PLOS ONE on why so many shoulder surgery patients wake up nauseated. Surgeons often lower blood pressure deliberately during shoulder arthroscopy to keep the view clear, but pressure dips can provoke nausea. The team reviewed just over three hundred patients and asked whether sustained low pressure, a drop of at least a fifth lasting an hour, independently predicted postoperative nausea and vomiting.

Nearly a third of patients suffered it.
