pmc-3418594:
Pearce, Salotti, Little, and co-authors study radiation exposure from CT scans in childhood and later risk of leukaemia and brain tumours. CT scans are very useful clinically. Their ionising radiation, though, may carry cancer risks, in particular for children, who are more sensitive to radiation than adults.

The team followed a cohort of children and young people who had scans, tracking later cancers. Their retrospective study gave some of the first direct estimates of excess risk after childhood CT. The results inform how doctors weigh scan benefits against dose in young patients.
pmc-5491694:
Omata, Cheng, Kokudo, and their co-authors updated Asia-Pacific guidelines in 2017 on hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. There is great geographical variation in this cancer's distribution. The majority of cases worldwide are found in the Asia-Pacific region, where it is a leading public health problem.

The guidelines cover how to detect, stage, and treat the disease in light of regional realities, including widespread hepatitis infection. Updates matter because imaging, surgery, and drug options keep changing. Shared regional guidance helps hospitals offer consistent, evidence-based care. It also supports screening programs for people at highest risk, such as those with chronic liver disease.
pmc-5499094:
Williamson, Altman, Bagley, and their team published the COMET Handbook in 2017. Picking the right outcomes is key when a trial is designed, so that the effects of rival treatments can be compared head to head. Outcomes must also matter to patients and to those who fund and use care.

COMET backs core outcome sets: a small agreed set of outcomes that every trial in a field should measure. The handbook shows how to build such a set with patients, doctors, and researchers at the table. When all trials report the same core outcomes, their results can be pooled and judged as one body of proof. That cuts waste and speeds firm answers for practice.
pmc-6061794:
Wouter De Coster, Svenn D'Hert, Darrin Schultz, and coauthors described the NanoPack tool set in 2018. Long-read sequencers from Oxford Nanopore and Pacific Biosciences produce very different data from older machines. Users need plots and filters tuned to long reads.

NanoPack gathers small Python tools that chart read length and quality and trim poor data. Reports can be built for a single run or compared across runs. The tools are free under an open license. Labs adopting long reads use them as a first check before assembly, since bad input quietly ruins downstream results.
pmc-7566194:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators measured in 2020 how much illness and early death can be traced to eighty-seven risk factors worldwide. The analysis spans more than two hundred countries and territories over three decades, from 1990 to 2019. It sits inside the wider Global Burden of Disease Study, which applies one set of methods to every country so results can be compared.

The risks covered range from smoking, high blood pressure, and air pollution to unsafe water and poor diet. For each, the team estimates the share of deaths and lost healthy years it explains. Rankings like these show health ministries where prevention buys the most health, and how those priorities shift as countries grow richer or older.
pmc-8005494:
Peng Yu and co-authors reviewed in 2021 pyroptosis, a fiery form of programmed cell death tied closely to the immune system. Unlike quiet cell death, pyroptosis makes the cell swell and burst, spilling signals that summon inflammation. Interest in the process grew sharply after the discovery of the gasdermin family, proteins that punch the holes that finish the cell.

The review explains the machinery step by step, from the sensors that detect danger to the gasdermins that carry out the rupture. It then surveys the many diseases this process can influence, including infections, inflammatory disorders, and cancer. Knowing how to trigger or block this death pathway could give doctors a new lever over illnesses driven by inflammation.
pmc-8023694:
Maxime Taquet and colleagues studied in 2021 the brain and mental health outcomes that follow COVID-19, using electronic health records for well over two hundred thousand survivors. Early reports had raised concern about lasting neurological and psychiatric effects, but firm numbers were scarce. The team tracked which new diagnoses appeared in the six months after infection.

They estimate how often conditions such as stroke, dementia, anxiety, and mood disorders occurred, and how the risks compared with those after other illnesses. Their large scale records gave some of the strongest early evidence that COVID-19 can leave a measurable mark on brain health. The results helped clinics plan follow up care and set priorities for longer studies.
pmc-8810394:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Dementia Forecasting Collaborators estimated in 2022 how many people live with dementia now, and how many will in 2050. Populations are growing older around the world, which pushes dementia numbers upward on its own. At the same time, solid evidence links several changeable risk factors to the disease.

The team models the expected rise country by country, separating the part driven by aging from the part that risk factor trends could soften. Their forecast shows cases climbing steeply by mid century, especially in lower income regions. The analysis gives governments a planning horizon: care systems, budgets, and prevention campaigns all need to be ready well before 2050 arrives.
podcast-joerogan-36NpaOg5594:
Comedian Brian Simpson joins Joe Rogan for episode 2491. Simpson rose fast with a sharp, cool style and dry wit. Late-night sets made his name among comic peers.

Rogan explores his path from foster care and service to the stage. Simpson tells his story with calm, cutting humor. They talk about craft, luck, and staying sane in comedy. The episode gives new fans a full intro to a rising voice. His mind works in clean lines, and the talk shows why peers rate him so high. His rise feels earned, and he knows it.
podmore-apparitions-thought-transference:
Frank Podmore weighed the proof for thought leaps in Apparitions and Thought-Transference, his study of 1894. The book draws on the great case hoard of Phantasms of the Living. Podmore sifts those cases with a doubt man's care. He asks which tales stand when fraud, flaw, and chance are cut from the count.

His sums are strict, yet he grants a strange rest that won't fade. The book is the core of the great work in brief, sharp form. It shows how the new field tried to be a science. Its care is its claim.
pyramid-texts-maspero-1894:
Spells carved inside Egyptian pyramids more than four thousand years ago are the oldest church texts in the world. The Pyramid Texts, in Gaston Maspero's French rendering of 1894, gives them whole for the first time. Maspero was the French scholar who opened these tombs' walls to print.

The spells speak to the dead king, ward off snakes and foes, and lift his soul to the stars. They name old gods, rites, and foods for the life beyond the grave. No older body of religious writing survives on earth. Maspero's version first let the modern world read that dawn of faith.
saxo-grammaticus-danish-history-elton-18:
Saxo Grammaticus, a Danish clerk of the twelfth century, wrote the Gesta Danorum, the Deeds of the Danes, a vast Latin history of his people. Oliver Elton translated the first nine books into English in 1894. Saxo wrote to give Denmark a past as grand as Rome's, and he filled it with kings, heroes, and gods grown into men.

Amleth, the brooding prince who feigns madness, walks here in his first form, the seed of Shakespeare's Hamlet. Wars with the Wends, sea kings, shield maidens, and the feuds of the royal house crowd the books. Saxo's Latin is rich and rolling, a skald in a clerk's robe. His history is the great well of Danish legend.
sbe-36-milinda-part-2-1894:
Volume 36 of The Sacred Books of the East appeared in 1894, with T W Rhys Davids translating Part 2 of The Questions of King Milinda. The Milinda is a dialogue between King Milinda, a Greek ruler in India, and the monk Nagasena. Part 1 had appeared earlier in the series.

Nagasena answers the king's hard questions on the soul, rebirth, and karma with famous images, such as the chariot that is no single part. Part 2 presses into finer points of Buddhist teaching. Rhys Davids, a leading scholar of Pali, gave the text full notes. This volume completed the fifty-volume Sacred Books of the East, a landmark of world religious publishing.
spr-proceedings-vol10-1894:
A single long part, number twenty six, makes up volume ten of the Proceedings in 1894. The Society for Psychical Research devoted the year to weighty reports. Results from the census of hallucinations reached print around this period. Telepathy experiments appear with their ledgers of hits and misses.

Trance mediumship keeps its place, with sittings reported almost word for word. Physical phenomena get brief, wary notices beside the mental evidence. The society's leaders argue in print over what the mass of cases proves. Volume ten is a compact sample of the whole enterprise. It suits readers who want one year of the archive entire. The standards of proof are the real subject.
spr-proceedings-vol9-1893-1894:
Parts twenty four and twenty five form volume nine of the Proceedings, for 1893 and 1894. The Society for Psychical Research carries its inquiries into a second decade here. Telepathy work continues, though the glow of the first trials has cooled. Reports on apparitions still arrive, sifted by committee standards.

Mediumship investigations fill long sections, with trance sittings written out in detail. The society also prints studies of hypnotism and allied states of mind. Every claim meets investigators trained to suspect error first. Volume nine keeps the archive's steady rhythm of case, check, and argument. Historians of the occult and of science both use it. Plain primary evidence is its strength.
stoever-life-linnaeus-1794:
Dietrich Stoever wrote the life of Carl Linnaeus, the great Swede who named the kinds of life. Joseph Trapp turned the book into English in 1794. Linnaeus had died not long past, and tales of his life were still fresh. One tale in the book draws fans of strange lore.

In 1735, at Hamburg, Linnaeus saw a famed seven-headed hydra on show. He found the thing a fake, made from skins and parts of beasts. The show men fled the town when his word spread. The tale shows the great name giver at work as a fraud hunter.
the-alchemical-essence-and-the-chemical-: The Alchemical Essence and the Chemical Element, 1894. The essence and element. This book preserves that episode. Later readers can locate it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Time has kept the file intact.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-2-pg2594: Volume two of the Forsyte Saga: the family chronicle continues through changing England. Soames, Irene, and the new generation in Galsworthy's masterly hands. The saga deepens. The Forsytes face the new century with old values.
the-hermetic-and-alchemical-writings-of-: The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Aureolus Philippus Theophrastus Bombast, 1894. The Paracelsus writings. This book preserves that collection. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
the-new-pearl-of-great-price-a-treatise-: The New Pearl of Great Price, 1894. The precious treatise. This book preserves that work. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Those who study the era will use it.
tob-0094:
Jean Bodin, the French thinker famed for his work on the state, wrote four books on the madness of sorcerers in 1580. De Magorum Daemonomania argues that witchcraft is real, deadly, and far more common than judges admit. Bodin demands the harshest response: death for witches, and punishment for those who defend them.

He sets rules of evidence so loose that denial itself becomes a sign of guilt. Coming from a mind of the first rank, the book gave the witch hunts learned cover across Europe. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. It remains a chilling read.
tob-0194:
Dudley Wright reconstructed the Eleusinian Mysteries, the secret rites of Demeter and Persephone celebrated near Athens for well over a thousand years. Initiates were promised a blessed lot after death, and the central acts were kept secret on pain of death. What happened inside the Telesterion hall is still argued among scholars.

Wright gathers the ancient testimony: hymns, inscriptions, hostile Christian reports, and archaeology, then narrates the festival's procession, fasting, and revelations as far as evidence reaches. V1 evidence calls his account the best plain tale of antiquity's most famous secret. Readers get both the known outline and an honest view of where the secrecy still holds.
tob-10794:
Georg Ebers could read Egypt's old hieratic script, a rare skill he put to work in Uarda, subtitled A Romance of Ancient Egypt. Ebers set his novel in ancient Thebes under the pharaohs. At its center stands Uarda, whose story entangles court plots, priestly power, and a love that crosses ranks.

Real learning fills the grand scenes: temples, medicine, festivals, and daily crafts are rendered from Ebers's Egyptological research. For nineteenth-century readers, Uarda was a favorite window on pharaoh-era Egypt, offering scholarship disguised as romance. Modern readers can enjoy both the melodrama and a period picture of what Europe then knew about ancient Egypt.
tob-4094:
Hermann Jacobi translated the Jaina Sutras for volume forty-five of the Sacred Books of the East, and part two holds two major Jain scriptures. The Uttaradhyayana gives monastic discourses on the disciplined life. The Sutrakritanga argues against rival schools and defends the Jain path.

Jain teaching prizes non-violence above all, extending care to the smallest living things. Monks and nuns bind themselves to strict vows of truth, poverty, and harmlessness. Jacobi, a leading scholar of Jainism, equips the texts with full notes. Checked from the 1919 edition, part two completes the series' Jain canon for English readers.
tob-4166-36794:
Volume two of Lang's Myth, Ritual and Religion presses his case against the solar-myth school. Lang explains rituals as acts tied to real belief, not as faded sun worship. He traces fairy tales back to older, rougher originals shared across continents.

Case after case, he sets Greek myth beside the lore of peoples his rivals ignored. The sun theorists get brisk, witty answers throughout. Lang also defends the view that some peoples held a high-god belief very early, a claim that stirred lasting debate. Readers who enjoy learned argument at full stretch will find volume two as sharp as the first.
tob-4194:
Leo Tolstoy, in his religious crisis, cut the four Gospels into one harmony and called it The Gospel in Brief. Published in the 1890s, it strips away miracle and church doctrine to leave the Sermon on the Mount as Christ's true teaching. Non-resistance to evil stands at the center of Tolstoy's reading.

The Russian church excommunicated him, which only spread the book. Gandhi read Tolstoy and carried the ethic of non-resistance into another century's struggles. Tolstoy retells the story in plain, urgent prose, as if copying out orders for his own life. Verified from the 1919 edition, the harmony shows the novelist turned prophet at his starkest.
tob-4294:
James Haughton Woods published his Yoga-System of Patanjali with Harvard in 1914, and the academic study of yoga in the West dates from it. Woods translates the Yoga Sutras and prints the classical commentaries with them, so the root text arrives with its oldest interpreters in attendance.

Aphorism by aphorism, readers can test the short sayings against centuries of gloss. Woods writes as a philologist: exact, patient, and clear about hard places. Verified from the 1919 edition, his volume introduced yoga thought to universities. Teachers who want Patanjali with scholarly ballast still start on Woods's pages.
treaty-of-tordesillas-1494:
Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. The pact draws one line down the Atlantic Ocean's wide map. Lands west of the line fall to Spain, east to Portugal.

The line runs 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands. A papal grant stands behind the bargain of the two crowns. Brazil's bulge falls on Portugal's side, a fact of lasting weight. Neither power asks the peoples who live on those lands. The treaty that split a new world still shapes its tongues and maps. Portuguese in Brazil and Spanish elsewhere trace back to this line.
un-ga-res-194:
Palestine's refugees stand at the heart of Resolution 194, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 11 December 1948, months after the war that created the state of Israel. The text first honors the late UN mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, killed while working for peace. It then sets up a three-state Conciliation Commission to take over his task in Palestine.

The commission is told to help the sides reach a final settlement of all open questions. The resolution is best known for its stand on the refugees who had fled or been driven from their homes. It says those wishing to return and live in peace should be let back, and those who do not return should be paid for lost property.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 194 (III), adopted on 11 December 1948, addressed Palestine after the first Arab-Israeli war. The Assembly thanked the late United Nations Mediator, who had given his life in the work. It set up a three-state Conciliation Commission. The commission was to take over the search for a final settlement between the parties.

The text gave Jerusalem and its area special treatment under United Nations control, with protection for holy places and the freest possible access. Its best known passage states that refugees who wished to return home and live at peace should be let to do so at the earliest workable date. It states that pay should be made for lost or harmed property.
un-sc-res-1094:
Guatemala's peace accords gained military verification in January 1997. The final accords signed at Guatemala City on 29 December 1996 ended the long internal war. A definitive ceasefire signed at Oslo on 4 December would take force once a United Nations mechanism stood ready. MINUGUA had verified human rights in the country since 1994.

The Council authorized a group of 155 military observers, with medical staff, to attach to MINUGUA for three months. Their task was to verify the definitive ceasefire, as the Secretary-General's report of 17 December 1996 advised. The Secretary-General had to tell the Council when deployment was complete and the ceasefire had begun. Both parties were called to carry out their pledges under the accords in full. The international community was invited to keep backing the peace process. The step gave the Guatemalan settlement the armed watchers its last military clause required.
un-sc-res-1294: Security Council business produced Resolution 1294, catalogued in this library as a 2000 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1394:
For Western Sahara, the long-disputed territory in northwest Africa, the Council bought more time on 27 February 2002. It renewed the mandate of MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara. The mission exists to prepare a vote on the territory's future. The Secretary-General had urged the short renewal in a report dated 19 February.

The new mandate ran only until 30 April 2002. In that window the Council planned to weigh the options in the Secretary-General's report. Those options concerned the stalled search for a just and lasting settlement. The Council also asked for a fresh report before the mandate ended.
un-sc-res-1494:
The Council took up Georgia's breakaway region of Abkhazia in Resolution 1494, adopted on 30 July 2003. Talks on Abkhazia's future status had gone nowhere for years. Four mission staff had been seized as hostages in June, the sixth such seizure since the mission began.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 31 January 2004. It adds a civilian police team of twenty officers to the mission. Those officers would help make the Gali district safe enough for displaced people to return. The Council urges the Abkhaz side to at last discuss the paper on sharing powers.
un-sc-res-1594:
Côte d'Ivoire's United Nations mission gained one more month in April 2005. On 4 April 2005 the Security Council extended the mission and its French support force until 4 May. The Council recalled the Linas-Marcoussis peace deal it had endorsed in 2003. It also recalled sanctions set the year before. South Africa's president was then mediating between the Ivorian parties. The Council pointed the parties toward his African Union effort.

All Ivorian sides had to pursue a lasting and just solution at once. The short term kept pressure on the talks. The mission's troops and the French force stayed in place meanwhile. Within weeks, the Pretoria talks produced a new agreement. The Council remained ready to extend the mission again.
un-sc-res-1694: Resolution 1694, from 2006, belongs to the Security Council's continuous formal output preserved in this collection. The source transcription is English Wikisource's copy of the UN record. Inside the text, earlier resolutions are recalled like precedents in a court ruling, and the new decision builds on them; the entry keeps that legal chain visible.
un-sc-res-1794:
Formal Council action on the Democratic Republic of the Congo arrived as Resolution 1794, adopted on 21 December 2007. Fighting in North Kivu had caused a grave humanitarian crisis. Foreign and Congolese armed groups still held ground in the east. The Congo and Rwanda had just signed the Nairobi joint statement on a shared approach.

The Council extends the United Nations mission, called MONUC, until 31 December 2008. Up to 17,030 troops stay authorized. The Kivus come first, above all guarding civilians. Armed groups must lay down their arms and demobilize without delay. The government must hold a round table on peace in the Kivus. Reform of the army, police, and courts is pressed as urgent.
un-sc-res-1894:
Resolution 1894 was the Council's answer on Protection of civilians in armed conflict, adopted on 11 November 2009. The Council marked ten years of work on this theme. It was also sixty years since the Geneva Conventions. Civilians still suffered badly in wars, and aid often could not reach them.

The Council says protection must shape peacekeeping mandates from the start. Such mandates must be clear, credible, and within a mission's real reach. Protection work takes first call on a mission's troops and funds. The Secretary-General must draft a working plan for protection in the field, plus rules for how missions report on it. Respect for the laws of war and safe passage for aid sit at the center.
un-sc-res-194:
The Cyprus peacekeeping force lost its mediator to death in office in the autumn of 1964. A report from the Secretary-General judged that the force was still necessary on the island. Cyprus's government wanted it to stay beyond 26 September 1964. A new mediator had been appointed to take the dead man's place. Resolution 194 was adopted unanimously on 25 September 1964.

The Council paid tribute to the memory of the mediator who had died in office. It renewed its thanks to the Secretary-General and to the states supporting the force. Its earlier Cyprus resolutions were reaffirmed. The force's stationing was extended for three more months, ending on 26 December 1964. The text joins two tasks of that season: mourning a mediator lost mid-mission, and keeping the force that guarded a fragile quiet.
un-sc-res-294: Listed under 1963, Resolution 294 preserves formal action taken by the United Nations Security Council. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-394: The Republic of Seychelles sought a United Nations seat in 1976. On 16 August 1976 the Security Council examined its application. It recommended to the General Assembly that Seychelles be admitted to membership. The vote was unanimous. The whole text is one sentence long. The Indian Ocean island state had gained independence from Britain weeks earlier. It joined the world body that September.
un-sc-res-794:
On the Council's agenda, Somalia drew Resolution 794, adopted on 3 December 1992. Warlords fought over food aid while famine spread across the country. Relief ships and planes came under attack, and supplies were looted. The small United Nations effort on the ground could not cope with the scale of the crisis.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs a member state's offer to lead a large relief operation. States taking part may use all necessary means to make aid delivery safe. A shared command would run the force, with a fund to channel gifts of money and goods. The Secretary-General had fifteen days to plan how the United Nations would take over later.
un-sc-res-94:
Resolution 94 is a short court-related decision the Security Council adopted without dissent on 29 May 1951. It followed the death on 7 May of Judge José Philadelpho de Barros e Azevedo, a member of the International Court of Justice. His death left a seat on the Court empty for the rest of his term.

Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Council sets the date for the vote that fills such a vacancy. The Council decided the election would be held during the sixth session of the General Assembly. It also ordered that this vote come before the regular election at the same session, which would fill five seats ending on 5 February 1952.
un-sc-res-994: The library catalogues Resolution 994, a Security Council decision, under the year 1995. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Guatemala's peace gets UN verifiers in Resolution 1094, adopted on 20 January 1997. Guatemala's government and the URNG rebels had signed a string of accords since 1994, capped in December 1996 by a definitive ceasefire signed at Oslo and a final peace agreement. The parties had asked the UN to verify the whole package, and a UN human rights mission, MINUGUA, was already in the country.

The Council expressed full support for the peace process. It authorized military observers to attach to MINUGUA so the ceasefire and the demobilization of URNG fighters could be verified on the ground. China had lifted an earlier veto days before, after Guatemala adjusted its stance on Taiwan, clearing the vote.

Security Council resolution 1294, adopted on 13 April 2000, keeps the United Nations Office in Angola, UNOA, in place for a further six months, until 15 October 2000. The Council endorses the decision in the Secretary-General's report of 11 April 2000. It asks him to keep carrying out the Office's tasks under resolution 1268 (1999). He is to report every three months on developments in Angola. The reports include advice on further measures the Council might take to advance the peace process.

Western Sahara's stalled vote gained only a two-month bridge in 2002. On 27 February, the Council adopted Resolution 1394 without dissent. The territory's fate pits Morocco against the Polisario Front. The UN mission, MINURSO, was set up to run a vote on the people's future. That vote had waited a decade by then.

The text follows the Secretary-General's February report. It extends MINURSO's mandate just to 30 April 2002. In the same breath, the Council says it will weigh his options with care. His report laid out paths from the old vote plan to a split or a political deal. The short leash showed the Council's fading patience.

Georgia's Abkhazia deadlock deepens in Resolution 1494, adopted on 30 July 2003. Those who shot down a UNOMIG helicopter in October 2001, killing nine people, had still not been found. The Abkhaz side kept refusing even to discuss the draft paper on sharing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi. Four more UNOMIG staff had been seized in June 2003, the sixth hostage-taking since the mission began.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, until 31 January 2004. It approves adding 20 civilian police officers to help create conditions for the safe return of displaced people and refugees. It strongly urges the Abkhaz side to receive the powers paper and open real talks on Abkhazia's status within Georgia. It demands an end to impunity for attacks on UN staff and presses both sides to protect returnees, starting in the Gali district. A report is due in three months.

A split land bought one more month of UN cover in 2005. Côte d'Ivoire had been cut in two since a 2002 revolt. A peace force, UNOCI, held the line with French troops. Talks ran through South Africa's Thabo Mbeki for the African Union. Resolution 1594 passed with no dissent on 4 April 2005.

The mandate for both forces grew by one month, to 4 May 2005. The short span showed doubt, not calm. All Ivorian sides were told to chase a just and lasting fix with fresh zeal. Mbeki's talks got the Council's full weight. The text cites the chief's report of 18 March. It rests on the 2003 Paris peace deal and the Accra pact of 2004. Each month's vote kept the force alive while talks ground on.

The balance of Liberia's mission, UNMIL, is adjusted on 13 July 2006. The Secretary-General had reported that many of the mission's military tasks were complete and had recommended changes to its shape. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council increased UNMIL's authorized civilian police component by 125 officers and cut its military component by the same number, keeping the overall size broadly steady.

Congo's mission is extended with the Kivus as top priority in Resolution 1794, adopted on 21 December 2007. Fighting between the army and a dissident militia in North Kivu had caused a humanitarian crisis. The FDLR and other armed groups remained in the east. Congo and Rwanda had signed the Nairobi Joint Communiqué of 9 November 2007.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC's mandate and capacity, as set out in Resolution 1756 (2007), until 31 December 2008. It keeps up to 17,030 military personnel, 760 observers, and 391 police plus formed police units. MONUC must give highest priority to the Kivus crisis, above all protecting civilians and supporting the Nairobi Communiqué. The Council demands the FDLR, ex-FAR/Interahamwe, the dissident militia, and the LRA lay down their arms and enter demobilization and repatriation without delay. It authorizes MONUC to support Congolese brigades in disarming them.

Protecting civilians in war is the subject of Resolution 1894, adopted on 11 November 2009. That was ten years after the Council took up the theme. It was sixty years after the Geneva Conventions. Civilians still made up most casualties, humanitarian access was often blocked, and aid workers were attacked. The Secretary-General's May 2009 report listed five core challenges, from compliance with the law to accountability.

The Council demands that all parties to armed conflict obey international humanitarian, human rights, and refugee law and protect civilians and their basic needs. It condemns attacks on civilians and the use of human shields, and opposes impunity, insisting states investigate and prosecute war crimes and genocide. It says peacekeeping mandates must give protection activities priority in using mission resources, promises action against deliberate attacks on humanitarian personnel, and asks for systematic reporting on access constraints.

Cyprus again filled the agenda in the autumn of 1964. On 25 September, the Council adopted Resolution 194 without dissent. The Secretary-General held that the peace force must stay past its late-September end date. The Cyprus government wanted it to stay as well.

The text extends the posting for a further stretch. It also pays tribute to Sakari Tuomioja, the Finnish envoy who had served as mediator in the dispute. He had died in office weeks before. The Council notes with warmth that a new mediator has been named. The pairing speaks clearly. Soldiers held the quiet on the ground, while a mediator chased the political deal.

Resolution 1994, adopted on 30 June 2011, renews the Golan observer force while noting unusual trouble in its zone. UNDOF had supervised the Israel-Syria disengagement since 1974, and the Secretary-General's June report was before the Council. Serious incidents on 15 May and 5 June, when protesters approached the ceasefire line from the Syrian side, had put the long-held truce in jeopardy.

The Council called on the parties to carry out the 1973 ceasefire resolution at once and to respect the 1974 disengagement agreement fully, exercising maximum restraint. It extended UNDOF's mandate for six months, to the end of 2011. Parties were told to give UN personnel unhindered access and keep them safe.

Senegal complained again about Portuguese attacks in 1971, two years after an earlier Council resolution on the same charge. Portuguese forces based in Guinea-Bissau had grown more violent. Mines were being laid inside Senegalese territory. Resolution 294 was adopted on 15 July 1971.

The Council demanded that Portugal stop all acts of violence and destruction in Senegal at once. Portugal had to respect Senegal's sovereignty, territory, and security. The attacks carried out since 1963 against Senegalese villages and people were condemned. So was the unlawful laying of anti-tank and anti-personnel mines. The Council also sent a special mission of its own members, with military experts, to investigate the facts on the spot.

The Seychelles, a scatter of Indian Ocean islands, became independent from Britain in June 1976. Its leaders applied for UN membership that summer. Resolution 394 was adopted unanimously on 16 August 1976. The meeting was the Council's 1952nd. The application papers were filed as document S/12164.

Members recommended the Republic of Seychelles for admission. The General Assembly welcomed it in September. With barely ninety thousand people later, it ranked among the UN's smallest members. Its vote still counts the same as any giant's. Tourism and fishing dominated its economy. The text preserves a neat example of decolonization's final wave reaching even the ocean's remotest island groups.

Somalia's famine forces an exceptional step in Resolution 794, adopted on 3 December 1992. Civil war was blocking food and medical aid; relief shipments were looted, aid workers attacked, and the Pakistani UNOSOM contingent in Mogadishu had been hit. The Secretary-General judged the existing course inadequate. A member state had offered to lead an operation to secure relief.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes the Secretary-General and cooperating member states to use all necessary means. The aim is to establish, as soon as possible, a secure environment for humanitarian relief operations in Somalia. That is the mandate behind the US-led Unified Task Force. It demands all factions cease hostilities, protect aid staff, and stop breaches of humanitarian law, warning that those who commit or order such acts will be held individually responsible. States are asked for forces and money, under unified command.

The death of a World Court judge in May 1951 left a seat to fill. Judge José Philadelpho de Barros e Azevedo, named in the text, died on 7 May 1951. His seat stood vacant for the rest of his term, and it had to be filled under the Court's Statute. Resolution 94 was adopted unanimously on 29 May 1951.

Under Article 14 of the Statute, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for such a vacancy. The Council decided that the election would take place during the sixth session of the General Assembly. It would be held before the regular election for the five seats falling vacant in February 1952. That timing let the Assembly fill the empty seat first, then turn to the planned elections.

Croatian government forces attacked a Serb-held area of Western Slavonia on 1 May 1995. The area, known as Sector West, was covered by a cease-fire agreed in 1994. The attack broke that cease-fire. An agreement reached through United Nations mediation on 7 May had also not been carried out in full. Resolution 994 was adopted unanimously on 17 May 1995.

The Council backed the statements its president had made on 1 and 4 May. Both sides were told to finish pulling all their troops out of the zones of separation, without delay. UNCRO, the United Nations operation in Croatia, had to regain its authority and deploy fully once the troops withdrew. Croatia was told to respect the rights of the local Serb population in full. Free movement was part of that duty, and aid groups had to reach the people. United Nations staff would assess their situation.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
Early growing pains of the first peacekeeping force fill the second report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/3694, from 1957. UNEF had been thrown together during the Suez Crisis months before. It now had to settle into a lasting role on Egyptian soil, with Egypt's consent as its legal base.

The report covers the force's move into its positions, its size, and its first full season of patrols. It deals with supply, housing, and ties with local authorities. The text shows peacekeeping being built in real time, with few models to copy.

The seventh report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/5494, reviews the force around 1962 and 1963. UNEF had by then spent six years on the Egypt-Israel frontier. Its presence was credited with keeping that border quiet while other fronts in the region flared.

The report covers patrol work, troop rotation, costs, and the force's ties with Egypt as host. It also notes strain over funding among member states. The yearly reports, read in order, show a crisis force turning into a fixture, until its sudden end in 1967.
vespucci-letters-markham-1894:
Amerigo Vespucci, a Florentine voyager in Spanish and Portuguese service, wrote letters in 1503 and 1504 that changed the map of the world. Clements R Markham edited them for the Hakluyt Society in 1894, with other documents that trace Vespucci's career. Among the letters stands Mundus Novus, the New World letter that spread across Europe in print.

Vespucci argued that the lands across the Atlantic were no edge of Asia but a world unknown to the ancients. Mapmakers took the claim so far that they named the continents after him: America. His letters are short, vivid, and bold in their reach. Reading them, one watches a new world enter the European mind.
voltaire-letters-on-england-morley-1894:
Exile in England taught Voltaire a new country, and Letters on England shared the lesson with France in 1734. The Cassell edition of 1894, edited in the Morley line, holds the famous Lettres philosophiques. Letter by letter, Voltaire praises English trade, tolerance, and science, and lets France judge itself.

Newton and Locke enter French thought through these pages, carried by a writer in playful, deadly earnest. Churches that coexist, merchants honored, poets buried with kings: each custom lands as quiet reproach. The letters count as a founding document of the French Enlightenment, the spark of much that followed.
warfield-the-kentucky-resolutions-of-179: The Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, an historical study, Warfield's 1894 work. The nullification resolutions. This book preserves that study. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Its pages add to the record of the past.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-2-189:
Volume two of Westcott's Collectanea Hermetica reissued John Everard's Divine Pymander in 1894. Everard had translated seventeen Hermetic tracts into English in 1650. His version was the first Hermetica English readers could own.

The tracts present Hermes Trismegistus teaching about God, mind, and creation. Everard's vigorous early modern prose gives the sermons real force. Westcott added his own preface for Golden Dawn readers. The reissue put a landmark translation back into circulation after centuries. Before Everard, Hermes spoke to England only through Latin and rumor. Westcott understood the book's historic place and presented it as a founding text.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-3-189:
An anonymous Short Enquiry Concerning the Hermetic Art, dated 1714, fills volume three of Westcott's series. Westcott reissued it in 1894 with his preface. Florence Farr, a leading Golden Dawn adept, added an introduction to alchemy and notes.

The Enquiry argues that the Hermetic art is true philosophy, not fraud. Its author, calling himself a lover of Philalethes, defends adepts against scoffers. Farr's introduction guides Victorian beginners through alchemy's terms and aims. The volume preserves a spirited period piece from alchemy's last fighting century. Alchemy still had public defenders in 1714, and this text shows their case. Westcott's series rescued such pamphlets from oblivion.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-4-189:
Volume four of the Collectanea Hermetica presents Aesch Mezareph, or Purifying Fire, in 1894. The treatise came from Knorr von Rosenroth's Kabbala Denudata in its 1714 English form. Westcott edited the reissue with preface and notes.

Aesch Mezareph weds alchemy to Kabbalah in a short, strange treatise. Metals become emblems of divine emanations in its scheme of correspondences. Hebrew letter lore and furnace work interpret each other throughout. The text was central to the Western mingling of Jewish mysticism with alchemy. Christian Kabbalists of the seventeenth century prized such material highly. Westcott offered it to Golden Dawn students as advanced reading in symbolic alchemy.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-5-189:
Cicero's Dream of Scipio anchors volume five of Westcott's Collectanea Hermetica, issued in 1894. Percy Bullock contributed an essay reading the Dream as a fragment of the Mysteries. The Golden Verses and Symbols of Pythagoras complete the small volume.

In Cicero's tale, Scipio rises in sleep through the spheres of heaven. He sees the earth's smallness and hears the music of the cosmos. Bullock argues the vision preserves initiatory teaching from ancient mystery cults. The Pythagorean pieces add moral maxims and riddling symbols for meditation. Westcott gathered three classics of pagan wisdom in one pocket book. Golden Dawn members used such volumes as graded study texts.
wilde-salome-1894: Salome, a tragedy in one act, Wilde's 1894 play. The dancer's tragedy. This book preserves that play. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
yeats-land-hearts-desire-1894:
Yeats wrote this one-act play in 1894, when he was building an Irish theater from folklore and longing. It is a fairy play: small, musical, and sad, set in a peasant cottage in the west of Ireland.

A young bride, Mary Bruin, grows restless with hearth, husband, and priest. A faery child comes singing of the Land of Heart's Desire, where sorrow never enters, and calls her away. The household fights for her soul with prayer and holy water, but the call is stronger. The play distills Yeats's early dream Ireland into a single evening's enchantment.
yoruba-speaking-peoples-ellis-1894:
Major A. B. Ellis published The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa in 1894. Ellis, a British officer long stationed on the West African coast, wrote the founding English study of Yoruba culture. His chapters cover religion, manners, customs, laws, and language in turn, with a grammar and vocabulary appended.

His account of the orisha system, the gods and spirits of Yoruba worship, became a classic source. Ifa divination, sacrifice, and the worship of Shango and other powers are set down in detail. Later scholars have corrected Ellis where his colonial lens distorted, yet they still start from his record. The book preserves knowledge gathered on the ground in the 1890s.
yukteswar-holy-science-1894:
Swami Sri Yukteswar wrote The Holy Science in 1894 to show one truth shining through two scriptures. Yukteswar, later known as Yogananda's guru, sets Hindu teaching beside the Christian Bible passage by passage. His frame is the yuga cycle, the vast ages through which mankind rises and falls in wisdom.

The book's Sanskrit title, Kaivalya Darshanam, names its goal: the vision of unity. Its teaching became the doctrinal bridge of modern Kriya Yoga, the path Yukteswar's line carried west. Short and dense, it still serves as the root text for that tradition's view of the ages.
zola-germinal-ellis-1894:
Émile Zola wrote Germinal in French, and Havelock Ellis made this landmark English version in 1894. Zola's novel of a mining strike is the chief glory of his Rougon-Macquart cycle. Ellis, a bold editor, kept the book's force when other translators shrank from it.

Étienne Lantier finds work in a coal mine in the grim north of France. Miners live on debt and crusts while owners feast and cut their pay still more. A strike rises, starves, riots, and breaks, and the mine floods in a vast collapse. Zola renders heat, dark, hunger, and crowd rage with crushing physical force and detail. The title, a spring month of germination, hints that new revolt will grow.
